en: A General Discourse on the Buddhist Teachings concerning the Constant Nature of Humanity: This is the innate endowment bestowed by the Supreme Lord (*Shangdi*) that all people equally possess.

Because it is without thought and without action, it is called "quiescence" (*ji*). Because it cannot be seen or heard, it is called "subtle" (*wei*). Because it is devoid of material substance, it is called... [the text continues].
It is called emptiness because it is free from desire; it is called stillness because its wisdom encompasses all things; and it is called awakening for the same reason.
Yet their ultimate destination does not go beyond the One, which is Non-being. To speak of non-being is to point to the foundation of being.

Thus, through stillness, it penetrates the responses of the world; through quietude, it rectifies the movements of the world; through the subtle, it manifests the manifest of the world; and through emptiness—
The reality of governing the world lies in awakening the spirit to respond to the world. This is what is called the "unreliant learning" transmitted by the thousand sages.
The Han Confucians took mere glossing and exegesis as their study; they patched together and exaggeratedly scrutinized the trivialities of forms, names, vessels, and numbers.
They took the traces of the ancient sages' already practiced deeds and codified them as essential canons, adhering to them as if they were fixed laws.

Regarding worldly phenomena, they do not know to employ the "non-being" (wu). Those followers of the Buddha, seeing the decline of our Confucian scholarship, vigorously thrust their arms into its midst;
they seized the refined principles of our learning and claimed them for themselves.

They swept away all the traces of the conduct practiced by the ancient sages and worthies, reducing them entirely to non-existence, while we Confucians merely maintained our integrity with anxious diligence, remaining bound by [tradition].
Stuck within the confines of physical forms and vessels, they remain troubled by worldly anxieties throughout their lives without realizing it.

When the subject of emptiness and stillness (*śūnyatā* and *śānti*) is mentioned, they declare, "This is the teaching of heretics," avoiding it for fear they cannot escape it. They do not realize that what the Buddha calls emptiness and stillness is originally the ancestral property of our own Confucianism;
those [heretics] have simply stolen and seized it. [The writings of] Han Yu’s "On the Origin of the Way" and Ou-yang Hsiu’s "Essential Discourse" were intended to...
To intimidate with empty words is merely to point out their coarse traces; let us speak instead of their essence.

Some claim that the learning of our Confucian school is centered on governing the world, while the learning of the Buddhists is centered on transcending the world, thereby making a distinction between the public and the private.

Some say that it is to indulge in the flavor of dhyāna, becoming biased toward stillness and emptiness. Some say that it is to sever emotions and eliminate thoughts, falling into the error of nihilism.
Some say that although the sutras are verbal expressions, the direct pointing and single transmission do not rely on words and letters.
Now, the Buddha’s way consists of compassion, joy, and equanimity, universally delivering all sentient beings. Even at the cost of his own body and life, he never hesitated;
he never acted out of self-interest. To be biased toward stillness and emptiness is the view of the Two Vehicles.

As for the Chan of the Supreme Vehicle, it performs the work of a Buddha amidst the dust and toil of afflictions, seeking the Buddha-dharma within the mental activities of sentient beings, never wearying of movement.
There is a partiality here. Even the Chan of the Supreme Vehicle regards annihilation as a heterodox path.

To be neither with thought nor free from thought, neither with emotion nor free from emotion—this non-identity and non-separation is the ultimate Dharma; it has never involved severing emotion or discarding thought.
How could the sutras be at fault? How could they hinder recitation? This "non-reliance on words" is itself the very mark of words. Exhaling...
Not entangled in manifold conditions, the inhalation does not abide within the aggregates (skandhas) or realms (dhātus). This is called the essential method for turning the sutras.
Failing to awaken to this through the mind, one is instead turned by the *Lotus Sūtra*, only then falling into the trap of verbal expression;
such is the general principle. Excellent indeed are the words of the Master of Wén: "The Buddha is a sage of the West; he is a hindrance (*niraya*) to the Central Kingdom. For we are Confucians.
The study of this [Confucian] Way holds that the perfection of one’s nature consists in each and every thing obtaining its proper place.

The teaching of the Buddhists seeks to cause all things to return together to quiescent extinction; it cannot be used to govern the state or bring order to the family—this is what is meant by "mud" (mired in abstraction).
This is further something that those who are Confucians ought to know. Composed by Wang Ji of Longxi.

For a long time, I have been unable to find the meanings of the two characters for the *bimbamālī* flower and fruit; recently, however, I found them in the Song edition of the *Fanyi mingyi ji*."
I have examined them and, as if suddenly finding a ship laden with pearls, I have recorded all those instances where common words in Buddhist texts were not understood,
or where the meaning was known but the pronunciation was unknown.

(Wenling says: Those referred to in the Sūtra as Pratyekabuddhas of sharp faculties are called "Rhinoceros-like" (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*). This metaphor compares them to the rhinoceros, which appears alone in a world without a Buddha;
observing the transformation of phenomena, they personally realize non-arising. Those of duller faculties are called "Group-dwelling" (*vargacārin*);

they also appear in a world without a Buddha, but they travel in groups, training and transforming their disciples. These Pratyekabuddhas rely on the Buddha's teachings to contemplate the Twelve [Links of Dependent Origination]...)
[He was] the one who practiced the two types of contemplation regarding dependent origination: that of the process of transmigration and that of its cessation).
At that time, King Prasenajit [invited his father, the former king], and furthermore personally extended invitations to the great bodhisattvas.
Gushan says: *Prasenajit* means "Victorious Army" (*Shengjun*). Wenzheng says: King Prasenajit was the king of Śrāvastī.
"Palace quarters" refers to the king's inner court; by inviting the Buddha into his inner court, he demonstrated the utmost reverence.
Within the city there were further elders, householders, and all sentient beings of immeasurable merit.
[The commentary] states: *Kṣatriya* refers to the royal caste; *caṇḍāla* means "killer," specifically those who engage in butchering, slaughtering, prostitution, or the sale of liquor.

Wenling says: This passage describes the cause of his falling into a lewd chamber. According to the Vinaya regulations, when a monk travels far from home, he must be accompanied by at least three companions:
one senior elder (*upādhyāya*) and one preceptor (*ācārya*). This is intended to strictly regulate his conduct and movements, thereby preventing errors and transgressions.
The bowl is called the "proper vessel" (saṃbhoga-pātra). The last donor refers to one who has not yet fed the Saṅgha.

Through impartial compassion, one transforms them with an equanimous mind toward oneself, causing them to give with an equanimous mind. Those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma;
thus, they are able to accomplish immeasurable merit.
At that time, while Ānanda was on his almsround, he arrived at [the house of] Mātaṅgī; she touched and fondled him, nearly causing him to destroy his precept-body.
(Chao Li says: "Mātaṅgī" means "filthy and utterly lowly. Since Ānanda made no discrimination, he thus fell into error.
(Changshui says: "Mātaṅgī" is translated as "Original Nature"; the person referred to as the "bhikṣuṇī by nature" in the subsequent scripture is she.)
Wenling says: Mātanga was a courtesan. Śābikara is translated here as the "Yellow-Haired Heretic.
The illusory incantation he transmitted is named "Primal Brahmā," but it is actually a demonic artifice.

"The lecherous body [of Mātanga] was about to destroy the essence of the precepts" means that by physically pressing against [the Buddha], he intended to corrupt the substance of his pure precepts. The later statement, "because the mind is pure," refers to this.
Before they had yet succumbed to drowning, [the spell] was merely about to destroy them.
The Tathāgata knew that the sorcery of lust had been cast upon them, and that Mātanga’s daughter had returned to the Buddha’s presence.
(An added note states: Generally, a sutra is divided into three parts: first, the introduction; second, the main body; and third, the dissemination. The introduction concludes here.

The following text constitutes the main body. This is because Ānanda’s retrospective examination of his former errors and his request for the sublime *śamatha* and so forth mark the very beginning of the main body.)
Zizhong said: "It is the constant custom of the Tathāgata that after accepting an invitation for a meal, he always delivers a Dharma discourse.
Since he has now returned so quickly, there must be a specific purpose. Wenling said: "The crown of the head represents the unsurpassed fruit.

That the light possesses the colors of a hundred jewels and is called 'Fearless' means that it can subdue demons and heretics, such that no thing can surpass it. The World-Honored One did not himself recite the mantra."
Regarding the statement that "the transformed Buddha speaks from the light upon the crown": this indicates that this mantra is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) mind-Buddha, the unsurpassed mind-dharma.
Zhenji states: Master Huan divided the *Zhengzong* into one section, further subdividing it into five parts.

First is the Section on Seeing the Path (*darśanamārga*), which begins here and ends within the fourth fascicle. Second is the Section on Cultivating the Path (*bhāvanāmārga*), beginning in the fourth [fascicle].

The second section concludes at the end of the seventh fascicle. The third section, "The Division on Realizing the Fruit," begins at the end of the seventh fascicle and concludes within the eighth fascicle.

The fourth section, "The Division of the Sūtra," follows after the division on realizing the fruit. The fifth section, "The Division on Aids to the Path," begins within the eighth fascicle and concludes at the end of the tenth fascicle.
Thus ends the text of the "Correct Teaching" (Zhengzong), and one subsequently enters the "Flow" (Liu).
[The text] concludes with the word "penetrating" (*tong*).
Ānanda saw the Buddha, prostrated himself, and wept with grief... [until] he sat far off, silently receiving the Sage’s instructions.
(Supplementary Note: The three names, *śamatha* and so forth, are the names for the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama*. Formerly, Guishan...)
I have previously applied the three types of cessation from the Tiantai school to these: first, cessation that realizes the true nature, which ceases within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

second, cessation that follows conditions through skillful means, which ceases within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); and third, cessation that stills the discrimination of the two extremes, which correctly aligns with the primary truth of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
This is because cessation is categorized under meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Wenling says: *Śamatha* means stillness; *samādhi* means contemplative illumination;
*dhyāna* means the non-duality of stillness and illumination. Though three names are established for its meaning, its essence is but a single dharma.
To raise one is to possess all three; to speak of the three is to speak of the one. Because the three are mutually integrated, they are called "wondrous.
Such wondrous cultivation is what is truly termed the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama*. This is the essential purport of this entire sutra and the profound gateway for attaining the principle.
Although Ānanda was ignorant of this, he consequently encountered calamity. It is only now that [the Buddha] limits him by means of his limited learning and minor wisdom, and...
The Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama is the request [for instruction]. Although the Great Samādhi serves as the request, there is no other specific method shown by the Tathāgata in the subsequent text.
First, there is the discernment of the real and the false; next, the harmonious integration of the real and the false;

and finally, the unification with the *tathatā-garbha* (store-nature), profoundly exhausting the nature of all phenomena. All of this, up until the fourth fascicle, serves to elucidate the ultimate reality.
It is simply the principle of perfection. Indeed, this principle of perfection is the foundation of Great Samādhi.
(Wuxing says: Regarding "the initial expedient means," there are both general and specific aspects to what Ānanda requested.

The general refers to *śamatha* and so forth, which are the methods by which all Buddhas attain enlightenment. The specific refers to the "initial expedient means," which corresponds to the awakening of the immediate capacity.)
[This is] the path by which one practices).
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and I share the same vital breath... [up to] "...therefore, with thirsty longing, they followed the Buddha to shave their heads and be ordained.
(Gushan says: When the perceived marks are seen as truly existent, birth and cessation appear vividly; by taking the resolve based on this, one securely proceeds toward the fruit of permanence.)

The Sutra below states: "If, during the causal stage, one takes a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible."
Wenling says: Ānanda means "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi). He was the son of King Droṇodana. On the night the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, he was born.
When King Śuddhodana heard that the Prince had attained enlightenment, and King Droṇodana further announced that a son had been born in the palace, the entire kingdom rejoiced;
thus he was named "Joyous Celebration. As he was the Buddha’s cousin, it is said they shared the same breath and the same root—this refers to the natural order of siblings.

They are brothers. Wuxing said: "Since Ānanda had grown weary of extensive learning and delighted in wondrous concentration, and the Tathāgata wished to discourse on this principle, he first interrogated him regarding false conditions.
Thus, the gate of the origin of the awakening mind and the vision [of reality] serves as the foundation for ceasing distraction and entering stillness;
the essentials of delusion and liberation both reside herein."
(An appended note states: Ānanda’s perception of forms is a vision that discriminates based on sensory objects;

the mind he generates is precisely a mind of deluded thought and clinging attachment. This is what will be repeatedly and thoroughly refuted in the subsequent "Seven Investigations and Eight Clarifications.")
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Ānanda! You and the others should know that because this perception is not true, there is cyclic existence" (Ziqing says:
Its essential nature is firm and concentrated, not involving worldly delusions; it is called the eternally abiding true mind, wondrous, perfect, and free from defilement).

Free from all obscurity and delusion, it is called the essence of innate purity and luminosity. Because sentient beings do not recognize this wondrous essence of their eternal mind, they are falsely entangled by thoughts of craving; thus, there is cyclic existence.
Gushan says: "The eternally abiding true mind" refers to the Tathāgatagarbha-mind that perfectly integrates the three truths, as discussed below.
"Employing various deluded thoughts" refers to sentient beings of the nine realms who fail to realize that these three are fundamentally devoid of even a single thought.

Consequently, those in the six destinies perceive the conventional (the mundane), the followers of the two vehicles perceive the real (the ultimate), and Bodhisattvas perceive the middle; all of this arises from a failure to understand [this truth].
Through the perfect fusion [of delusion], one gives rise to false grasping and attachment; thus, one is brought to revolve within the two kinds of birth and death.
Now that you wish to investigate unsurpassed Bodhi, I therefore resolve my mind to abandon birth and death.

[Zhang] Xing said: "The Way is inherently level and direct; it becomes crooked due to delusion. To investigate the crookedness and exhaustively seek the Right Path, one must eliminate inverted delusions;
therefore, I speak of the 'direct mind. When the mind is direct, the Way can be reached by a shortcut. 'One Way' means that all [practitioners] should employ the direct mind.
This is because I have diagnosed the illness and prescribed the medicine accordingly. To employ my own eyes and mind is immediately to give rise to various [delusions]."
[This refers to] various deluded thoughts). Letan said: "This precisely describes the substance of delusion. 'The eyes' refers to the visual faculty; 'the mind' refers to the mental consciousness.

These faculties and consciousnesses are empty and false, like flowers in the sky. If one clings to them as having a real substance that can see and can enjoy, one is not only deluded regarding phenomena."

Even regarding emptiness, one gives rise to views of self and person, as well as attachment. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The six [sense organs] act as intermediaries for thieves, who plunder the family treasure.

The beginningless, empty habitual tendencies and the ground-abiding ignorance all arise from the root consciousnesses and are nothing other than these. Perceptual images constitute the dust, and the consciousness-mind constitutes the defilement;
the cycle of birth and death does not fail to proceed from this. Thus, the following section investigates and examines [the nature of the senses] so that one may come to know [this].
False and illusory.
(Xie Li says: "The question 'Who is it that loves and delights? exhausts the root of delusion. The answer 'Because of the mind and eyes' reveals the root of delusion.")
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said... (up to) 'where now are the mind and the eyes located? [Lectan said:
Deluded mind and deluded seeing originally possess no substantial reality; they arise through clinging to objects.
This is called the root of beginningless birth and death; therefore, one must recognize their location]."
Gushan said: "The king is a metaphor for the true mind; the bandits are a metaphor for delusive thoughts. When the true is turned by the delusive, it is like a kingdom being invaded by bandits.
Sending forth troops to suppress and eliminate them is a metaphor for cultivating Great Samādhi. You should correspond to the king, while the mind and eyes correspond to the bandits."
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...thus the consciousness-mind truly resides within the body.
(From this point until the third section, Ānanda maintains that the mind resides within the body, while the Buddha refutes this by pointing out that one does not see the internal organs.)
Wenling says: This means that the mind is within and the eyes are without; this is true for everyone from ordinary sentient beings up to the Tathāgata, and Ānanda is no exception.

Thus, the text should clearly show this. There are twelve classes of distinct beings (*visabhāga-sattva*); those consisting of earth, wood, space, or scattered matter are excluded, as they do not belong to the category of the mind and eyes.
The supplementary note states: "The four sensory objects of the floating roots" refers to the eyes. This is explained in detail in the fourth fascicle.
(Zhendi said: "The eye-faculty floats outward and is provisionally formed by the four objects—earth, water, fire, and wind.
When it disperses, it returns once more to these objects; therefore, it is named after the objects.")
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you are now sitting here [until] 'therefore I am able to see from within the hall at a distance.
(Wuxing says: "The mind that is inside must necessarily see what is inside; therefore, he asks what was first seen within the hall.")
Wenling says: To settle the internal and external objects, one wishes to clarify the mind that exists within; thus, one must first perceive the internal and subsequently perceive the external.
To refute the mind that exists within, one does not first perceive the internal. Your observations and so forth all serve, for the time being, to cite specific instances to establish this point;
what follows below is the formal refutation.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said... (up to) 'it abides within the body'—there is no such possibility. (Supplementary Note:
The preceding passage presented both the locations of the mind and the eyes; now, he first refutes the deluded mind.
Although this is called a refutation of the deluded mind, he merely states that this mind has no location, yet does not explicitly state that this mind is deluded. This is because...)
He led Ānanda from place to place, examining and presenting [the mind] to him, so that his emotional attachments were exhausted and his logical reasoning brought to an end.
It was only after these seven locations had been used to interrogate the mind that he finally told him: "This is not your mind," and so forth.
Thus, the refutation of the seven locations was intended merely to refute the false mind as having no fixed location.

Wenling said: "If the mind were within the body, it would be somewhat plausible that it could perceive what is inside the body. However, when one asks the multitude whether they can do so, they are certainly unable.
The heart and stomach are internal organs; even if [the mind] cannot know them, the nails and vessels are external and manifest.
How can it not perceive these? Since it does not know what is internal, it is clear that it is not located within."
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "How can one person cause the multitude to be satiated?
(From this section to the second section, Ānanda held that the mind exists outside the body; the Buddha refuted this by demonstrating the separation of body and mind). (Supplementary Note:
Whereas previously it was said he "accepted the invitation," here it says he "sought alms from me. This was to encourage Ānanda...)

[Objection: It is difficult [to maintain that the body knows itself]. On the day one goes to accept an invitation, one must preach the Dharma for the host; this matter requires an overnight interval. Therefore, it refers to that very same day.
Following the precedent of begging for food, "I have already fasted overnight" means that I alone am already satiated. (Wenling says:
"That one person cannot satisfy the others is a metaphor for how the external mind cannot know the body.)"
Wenling says: Because the refutation of [the mind] not being internal gives rise to further false conceptualization, one claims that the mind is external.
If that were so, food could not satisfy it; this would mean that an external mind could not perceive the body. "Sustained" (宿預) refers to the four kinds of nutriment. "Lump" (摶) means a morsel;
it refers to physical matter that can be grasped as a segment, distinguishing it from the nutriment of volition (思食) and the nutriment of consciousness (識食).
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you were to perceive [the hand] as being outside the body, such a thing is impossible.
(Wuxing says: *Tūla* here means 'fine fragrance. Its cotton is like frost in color; the Buddha’s hands are as soft as this.)
(Gushan says: "Seeing is in the hand; it is in the eyes. Discernment is in the mind; thus, the mind is not something external.
Wenzheng says: From "The body and mind are external to one another" downward, he distinguishes that [the mind] is not external. From "I now show you" downward, he verifies that it is not external.)
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One... [up to] "...because those without obstructions have their faculties hidden within.
(From this point until the second section, Ānanda uses the "faculties hidden within" as his argument, which the Buddha refutes using the analogy of the lapis lazuli cage over the eyes).
(Changshui says: "The eye sees the lapis lazuli, but the mind does not see the eye. Even if it could see the eye..."
The eye itself becomes the object. Since the sense organ has already become the object, how could it immediately perform discernment?
Changshui said: "Lapis lazuli is a metaphor for the sense organ; the eye is a metaphor for the mind. The visual faculty is pure in form and does not obstruct the mind."
It is like a lapis lazuli bowl; it does not obstruct the eye. As it illuminates a single object, the mind follows the faculty and perceives it.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said... [up to] ...it is as impossible as a lapis lazuli vessel being joined [to itself]; such a thing cannot exist."
(Letang said: "If it does not conform, then as previously stated, 'conforming' implies discrimination; now, since the eye is that which sees, the meaning of 'conforming' is not established.")

Zhenji said: "This rebuke of Ānanda contains the fault of a discrepancy between the dharma and the analogy. In the analogy, one sees the lapis lazuli; in the dharma, one does not see the faculty (indriya).
Even if one were to concede that the faculty is seen, the faculty is itself an object (viṣaya). If it is an object, one cannot say that [the eye] follows [it]."
The preceding text states: "Those faculties follow the views; as soon as they [arise], they immediately engage in discrimination. Wénlǐng comments: "This contradicts both fact and principle;
it is not that the faculties remain latent."
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, [from the passage] up to 'this is called seeing within,' what is the meaning of this?
(Lectan said: *The Baihutong* states: "The five viscera are the liver, heart, lungs, kidneys, and spleen. The six bowels are the palaces and offices of these five viscera.
The stomach is the office of the spleen; the bladder is the office of the kidneys; the triple burner is the life... )
The gallbladder is the repository of the liver; the large and small intestines are the repositories of the heart and the lungs (respectively).
Wuxing said: "Initially, one might calculate that the heart is within the body; the Buddha refutes this by pointing out that its internal organs are not visible.

Next, one might calculate it is outside the body, which again invites the difficulty of the body and mind being separated. Furthermore, one might calculate it is hidden within the sense-roots, yet this still contradicts the analogy of the crystal cage."
Regarding the analogy of the eye, we now establish the distinction between internal and external in order to avoid the three aforementioned faults. Why?

Because that which possesses concealment is dark; therefore, when one perceives darkness, it is designated as "internal. It is not necessary that one must perceive an internal object [to call it internal].
Where there is an aperture, there is light; therefore, when one perceives light, it is immediately designated as "external. How could one further demand that the external be irrelevant?
If the internal and external are thus established, it naturally reveals that this mind does not reside in a single location, nor is it hidden within the sense organs.

That being so, although it is said that one perceives the substance of the mind as something external that is grasped, it actually remains within; for when one opens one's eyes and sees light, this is not the same as a lamp being outside a room.
(Wenling says: Since [the opponent] further calculates that the mind is within, they take seeing darkness as seeing the internal organs.
The following three sections refute this.)
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You should close your eyes... (up to) if there is no correspondence, how can seeing be established? [Létán said:
There are the five spirit-treasures and the six transformative viscera. The *sānjiao* (triple burner) is one of the six viscera;
it can transform the five grains and distribute moisture to the tissues and pores. It has distinctions between upper and lower, clear and turbid; therefore it is called the *sānjiao*.]
Wenling says: You should immediately question it; if he agrees with what follows, you should challenge him; if he does not agree, it is a conclusion.
If one is separated from external views, internal opposition is established (up to the point where) if one does not see the face, internal opposition is not established.
(This means that the eye sees only outwardly; there is no possibility of it facing inward. If it could face inward, why would one not see your own face when the eyes are open?)
Wenling says: "The realm before one's eyes is called 'external seeing'; the realm within the body is called 'internal facing.

Previously, because the eye was taken as external, it could not constitute the internal. Now, even if one sets aside external seeing to form internal facing, this would mean the eye is able to look back upon itself.
Furthermore, if it can look back upon the body while closed, then when opened, it should likewise be able to look back upon its own face. If...
If it were not so, the meaning would not be established.
To claim that seeing the face constitutes this "clearly knowing mind" (extending to what is called "seeing within") is impossible. (Wenling says:

"Through successive clarification, there is no principle of reflexive observation. (Wuxing says: "Therefore, one should know that [the following...]"*. *Note: The text fragment provided ends with "下" (below/next), indicating a continuation of Wuxing’s commentary.*

It cannot be said that it is seen. To clarify that it is external is merely a brief statement. Furthermore, seeing what is external serves to establish the seeing of what is internal. Now, this is concluded according to the correct calculation). [The Master] said:
"Your eye has already known that the body's contact is not the perceiver. Since it exists in empty space, it is certainly not you."
This is the essence. If one were to insist that both possess cognition, then two distinct entities would result.
Ānanda said: "I have heard from the Buddha... [it is] neither within, nor without, nor in between—these three locations."
(Zhenji said: "This means that the mind is itself the object, and the object is itself the mind. (Gushan said: "The mind arises and phenomena arise;
the object originates from the mind. Phenomena arise and the mind arises; the mind follows the object and shifts.")
Xingfu said: "When Ānanda recognized the delusion of a single thought-moment, the transformation of the root-body and the vessel-world arose;
this is 'the mind giving rise to dharmas. Furthermore, when moved by the wind of objective realms, the waves of consciousness surge up;
this is 'dharmas giving rise to the mind. Wenzheng said: "In terms of the mutual arising of mind and dharmas, to contemplate according to the realm is precisely the substance of the mind."
Where the mind and its objects meet, that is where the mind resides.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Now you say [that the mind comes from outside]; if it were to come from outside, it should first encounter the face."
[Regarding the nineteen realms: The householder Śūra said, "The Four Noble Truths that I previously taught are not the ultimate truth.

Now, for your sake, I shall further teach the five truths, the six aggregates, the thirteen bases, and the nineteen realms. Upon hearing this, Ānanda reflected upon the characteristics of dharmas and realized that there was no such principle at all.
Wenling says: To take the substance of thought itself as the mind is merely to regard it as a floating ideation; therefore, it is difficult to determine whether its substance exists or not.
If it were without substance, it would exist in name only, so how could it respond to and combine with objects?
It would be like the nineteenth element or the seventh sense-object—merely empty names. If it does have a substance, where should it be located such that one could point to it on the body?
[This is] a verification. It clarifies that the essence [of seeing] actually has no location.
"Tas" means to touch. Ānanda said: "If seeing is the eye... (up to)... if it were the seeing of objects, how could one be called dead?"

(Gushan said: "Ānanda’s statement here means that the mind can only know; it cannot be called 'seeing. He never realized that the capacity to see resides within the mind, and thus his eyes were merely unable to see [the mind itself])."
Wenling says: Under the words "Ānanda said," he resolves the preceding objection. Under the words "The Buddha said," he cites the analogy of the gate.
By stating that the capacity to see resides in the mind, he clarifies that it is merely the eyes that do not see when one dies.
Ānanda, furthermore, as for this mind of yours that is aware and capable of cognition—[from here until] "it follows the existence or non-existence [of the body];

such a thing is impossible" (Wuxing says: First four propositions are established; below they are analyzed in detail. The analysis of its not being a single entity shows it has no location, meaning it has no fixed place.
○ The analysis of its not being a manifold entity. ○ The analysis of its not being an all-pervading entity. ○ The analysis of its not being a non-all-pervading entity).
Wenling said: "One should know that the true mind is neither one nor many, and neither pervasive nor non-pervasive.
Since these four attributes do not apply, it cannot be said that the mind exists wherever it happens to conjoin with an object."
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One... [up to] "...furthermore, if there is no seeing within, it ought to exist in between.

(Wuxing says: This cites a Great Teaching yet misinterprets it. Changshui says: Since they do not know each other externally, it should say 'externally they also know each other'; I suspect this is a textual error.)
Wenling says: If one considers it to be within, the internal organs are not perceived; if one considers it to be without, the body does not perceive itself.
Since neither of these two positions holds, it must reside between the sense organ and its object.

The Buddha said: "As for what you say regarding being 'not deluded in the midst of the middle' (up to the point where) the essential substance [of the manifestation] is already confused and the mind is disordered.
(Gushan says: First he asks; below he discriminates.)

Wenling says: This section first distinguishes and determines the "middle" position with respect to the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). "Body" refers to the organ; "location" refers to the object.
Regarding the passage beginning "If it were in the body," this means that the body has two meanings: "extreme" and "middle. If it arises at an extreme, it cannot be the middle.

If it were in the middle, it would be the same as the previous case of being in the cause, and one should perceive the internal. Regarding the passage beginning "If it were in the location," this likewise analyzes [the matter].

The middle position has no fixed location. A "manifestation" (biao) is that which marks an object; it serves to reveal and display. If things are in confusion, there is nothing from which a middle can be taken.
Ānanda said: "As for what I have spoken of as the 'middle'... [up to] "...it is impossible that it should exist in the midst [of extremes]."
(Zhenji said: "What Ānanda calls 'the center' is not the center of the body; it is the center between the sense faculties and their objects.
(Zizhong said: "The four lines following the Buddha’s words open up this theme; what follows is the exposition of that principle.")
Wenling says: "If one combines both" and below, he refutes that combining both cannot constitute the Middle Way. "Objects" refers to the sense bases (*āyatana*) and their objects;

"essence" refers to the essence of the mind. "Objects are not the essence, yet they possess cognition" means that if objects are distinct from the essence yet possess cognition, then the sense bases/objects and the mind would stand as two separate entities, and there would be no middle position.
"If one does not combine both" and below, he refutes that not combining them cannot [constitute the Middle Way].
This refers to the "middle" [state]. If it does not encompass the faculties (*indriya*), it is not cognition; if it does not encompass the objects (*viṣaya*), it is not non-cognition.

Since both these meanings are untenable, how can the "middle" be definitively established? The Supplement states: When Master Huan explains that objects are not cognitive by nature, he says that the faculties and objects lack cognition while the substance of the mind possesses cognition;
yet when he explains what is neither cognition nor non-cognition, he again asserts that the faculties possess cognition.

The phrasing seems somewhat inconsistent. Now, one should still attribute "knowing" (*jñāna*) to the substance of the mind, while attributing "not-knowing" to the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
(Gushan says: "If it does not encompass both, it is neither mind nor organ-and-object; thus it would lack any essential nature. What characteristic could there be in the center?
An object is not the substance-knowledge. It is incorrect for the ancients to have taken "substance-knowledge" as the organ. This is because the Buddha...)
[This refers to] speaking of the essence of this mind.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One... [up to: ...is it not that my so-called 'mind' is characterized by non-attachment?
[Ziqing says: The Buddha’s intention was to reveal that the mind fundamentally has no location and should not have attachments; yet Ānanda again clings to non-existence.]
[This] attachment cannot avoid the persistence of objective phenomena—what is called the deluded mind that clings to conditions.
Ledu Tan said: "Since it is neither internal, external, nor in between, one knows that the mind has nothing to which it clings.

Yet he did not realize that the Buddha’s intent was to shatter the unreality of delusion so as to cause one to recognize the original truth. As it is said: "When sought throughout the three periods of time, the mind is not to be found; the mind..."
Because they do not exist, delusions are fundamentally non-existent. When the deluded mind has no locus, that is itself bodhi. Birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally equal.
Failing to understand this meaning, some erroneously cite the Buddha’s words and falsely establish the doctrine of non-attachment.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you said regarding 'awareness' (up to the point of) 'there being that which does not cling,' it cannot be called non-existent.
(Wenling says: "Regarding whether it exists or does not exist": this asks you, when your mind does not cling, does that objective phenomenon exist, or is it empty and non-existent?
If it were empty and non-existent, it would be like a tortoise's hair; how could it be clung to, such that you say it does not?)

[The Buddha] said: "If there were attachment, it would constitute a thing; if there were no attachment, it would likewise constitute a thing. Therefore, it cannot be called 'non-existent. (Gushan says:

When it conforms to conditions without attachment, it resembles causelessness (*ahetu*). Therefore, these two [extremes] are subsequently refuted.)
The supplementary note states: The text of the seven inquiries all serves to refute that deluded mind so that it has no place of dependence.
Ānanda previously stated, "Wherever there is contact, the mind immediately exists there.

Now, when all things are designated as "unattached" and called "mind," the Buddha then challenges the worldly void, water, land, flying creatures, and all material phenomena, asking whether they exist or do not exist, and so forth; this, too, is a refutation directed at their respective bases of dependence.

If there is no characteristic, then there is nothing that is not the characteristic itself; (up to: it is impossible for one to claim that the awakened mind knows this [characteristic]—there is no such place.

[This is] a hidden realization; it is merely for those of middling or inferior capacity that [the teaching] is explained more extensively.
Wēnlíng says: "If things truly have no marks, they would be like the hair of a tortoise. If things truly are not non-existent, then they must inherently possess marks."

At that time, Ānanda was among the great assembly... (until) causing all those icchantikas to destroy their Mleccha [delusions]. [Supplementary Note:

first, it is called 'able to extinguish' because it can extinguish afflictions; second, it is called 'able to discipline' because it can discipline the sense faculties; third, it is called 'quiescence.'"

It is called "tranquility" because it causes the three types of action (trikarma) to become still. It is called "separation" because it involves distancing oneself from the five desires (pañcakāmaguṇa).
It is called "purification" because it is capable of purifying the three turbidities, such as greed and the rest.

(Letang said: "Ananda, because I am without mind, I am like earth and wood; yet I do not know that the true self is no-self, that spiritual knowing is no-knowing—how could this wondrous, pure, and luminous mind not be present everywhere?")

At that time, the World-Honored One revealed to Ānanda that [the nature of] all minds has no inherent substance of its own.
(Gushan says: "That all dharmas arise as manifestations of mind means that because the mind is fundamentally present, it can create [phenomena] in accordance with conditions.")

Therefore, the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely capable of producing the mind. Since the environment (*bhājana-loka*) and its inhabitants (*sattva-loka*) are both of one mind, and this one mind is in reality devoid of subject and object, it is like water possessing the nature of waves:
only when it possesses this nature can it produce waves; thus, the waves that are produced are entirely the water that produces them.
Therefore, when observing the produced, one sees only what is originally inherent.

Wenling said: Because they were terrified by the notion of "no-mind," he cited what is commonly spoken to lead sentient beings toward realization and demonstrate that there is indeed a true mind, so that they might know where to apply themselves.
As for "the mind entering the patience of the non-arising of dharmas," this is intended to cause them to awaken to the true mark (dharmatā), not to extinguish the mind.
Since the three realms are but mind and the myriad phenomena are but consciousness, it is said: "The arising of all dharmas is but mind."
"All that is manifested" refers to the primary retributions (*vipāka*) of the ten realms; "the atoms of the world" refers to the secondary retributions (*niśraya*) of the ten realms.
Since there is nothing that does not take the mind as its constitutive essence, how can it be said that the mind is no different from earth or wood?
That which is inherently undefiled is called "pure"; that which is defiled yet remains undefiled is called "wondrously pure."
If you cling to and begrudge the discernment of vitarka and vicāra (up to the point where it is said): "it is still but a reflected image of the discrimination of dharma-objects" (Zizhong says:
"To be free from objects is the mind without foundation; one should not grasp or become attached to it").

Wenling says: This is based on the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) to demonstrate the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). "Discriminating between vitarka and vicāra" refers to the mind that performs such investigation.

This mind is devoid of nature when separated from the sense objects; one should not cling to it as true awakening. When one knows [the objects] have ceased, the mental faculty becomes tranquil and secluded;
yet even that which is tranquil and secluded is still a mere reflection of the dharma-objects (*dharmaviṣaya*), and thus lacks intrinsic nature as well.

[Zhendi said: "The various sensory activities refer to the six sense objects, such as form and so forth; all of these have the power to attract the mind and function as conditions for karmic activity.
I am not commanding you to hold that these are not the mind—[if they were not], who would cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
[Supplementary Note: "I do not command you to hold that it is not mind, etc."—this is a statement made for the sake of temporary concession.

For, above, I have already refuted their attachment and their discrimination of *vitarka* and *vicāra* as being not the true mind. It was done fearing that they might remain stubbornly attached and fail to attain fundamental awakening.
He then temporarily let him go and said: "What you have been grasping is certainly not the true mind.
You should now try to examine this mind minutely to verify for yourself whether it is true or false."

Gushan said: "The passage beginning with 'But you' below exhorts one to investigate and discern whether this mind has a substantial reality apart from objects, or whether it lacks such reality apart from objects.
If this deluded mind had a substantial reality apart from objects, it might be the true mind;
since it lacks reality apart from objects, how could it be anything other than deluded? You should know that this very mind is itself the true mind. This is also a temporary concession.
These words do not reveal the ultimate truth. For the six sense-objects are like forms, while discrimination is like a shadow. Since a shadow exists because of a form, it has no self-nature;
since the mind exists because of sense-objects, how could it have a self-nature?
(Changshui said: "To take the discrimination of conditioned objects as the mind is incorrect; for objects are not permanent, perishing immediately upon arising.
How could one take such a cause and expect to obtain a permanent fruit?")
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly—[up to the point where it is said] "though they have attained much learning, they do not achieve the fruit of sainthood.

(Supplementary Note: The preceding section refuted the deluded mind; from this point on, the deluded vision is refuted, leading to the convergence of vision within the mind and gradually revealing the true nature.
To begin with, the deluded mind originally has no self-nature; it manifests based upon the True [Nature], and its entire substance is identical to the True [Nature].)
What is called "destruction" has nothing to be destroyed. Ignorance is itself clarity; the true is not distinct from the true.
A single thought-moment is like an image appearing in a mirror: the entire image is the mirror. This is the perfect purport of the present sutra.

Changshui said: "The four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*) are called the nine meditative absorptions (*navasamāpatti*).

When it is now stated that one cannot become an arhat, this clarifies that one cannot become a Mahāyāna arhat. The cessation of perception and feeling is also called..."

Regarding the extinction samādhi (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the two vehicles, the World-Honored One previously stated that all sentient beings do not know the eternally abiding true mind and instead employ various deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).

One should know that in the Dharma there is neither gain nor loss; delusion and awakening depend on the person. If one's faculties are sharp...
Those whose delusions are thin understand the essence of false imagination: it is, in this very moment, the true mind. This is like realizing the mirror through its images;
then there is no image that is not the mirror. It is like realizing the images through the mirror; then there is no mirror that does not possess the images.
Now Ānanda manifests as if he were deluded, much like one who fails to recognize the substance of the mirror and instead identifies with [the reflections].
To take the images of the past and future and hold them up as a mirror—is this not an error?

Therefore, I have provisionally employed repeated refutations to sweep away these clinging attachments, so that right and wrong may become clear; only then can one realize the illusory to fully manifest the Real.

Ānanda’s erroneous fall into a house of prostitution was because the hindrance of phenomena had not yet been severed. His conceptual discrimination based on sensory objects was because the hindrance of principle had not yet been severed.
The "eye of the Way" is true vision; it is brought forth from the wondrously luminous mind.

"Thus, the true vision is gradually clarified.

This refers to the Tathāgata [speaking] within the great assembly... [until] "losing the true nature and acting in a perverted manner. (Changshui says:

This means that while the physical body and its objects are subject to movement, the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) is immovable. This serves as a critique directed at the great assembly for being deluded regarding the true permanence and instead perceiving impermanence.
(Gushan says: There are two kinds of impermanence: the destruction of continuous phenomena (*saṃtati-dharma*), and moment-to-moment arising and ceasing (*kṣaṇika-utpāda-vināśa*).
"From beginning to end" refers to the period from birth until death; this is the destruction of continuous phenomena. Having already lost the true nature, only...)
They create delusive karma; hence it is said that they act in a perverted manner.
The supplementary note states: It is simply that the conceptions regarding the body and its objects differ. Ordinary beings conceive of their bodies and objects as being truly existent;
this is to conceive of the impermanent as permanent. Although those of the Two Vehicles know that the body and its objects are impermanent...
Yet they have not yet awakened to the principle of true permanence; thus, regarding that which is truly permanent, they calculate it to be impermanent.
Therefore, the Buddha universally addressed the great assembly to collectively reprove them. The depth and shallowness of his words were understood by each according to their respective capacities.
"The fundamental nature and mind have lost their true essence; by identifying external objects as the self, one transmigrates within this cycle, taking upon oneself the flow of rebirth.
Wuxing said: "The previous statement, 'acting in a state of inversion,' merely refers to being turned by external objects, directly censuring the deluded mind.
The present statement, 'identifying objects as the self,' further censures the identification with the perceived objects of delusion as 'I' and 'mine.'"

If this is so, by what means can one escape from the realm of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*)? Therefore it is said: "Within this cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*), one takes up the flow for oneself. Zhenji said:

Although the preceding scriptural passages clarify that the nature of seeing is immovable, they have not yet discussed how this very seeing is also illusory, and that only by departing from seeing is there truth.
Zizhong said: This [passage] relies on coarse appearances to speak cryptically of the subtle.
The true vision and its analytical clarification are both found in the subsequent text.

(Gushan says: The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states, "To falsely take the four elements as the characteristic of one's own body, and the reflected images of the six sense-objects as the characteristic of one's own mind"—this is precisely the doctrine of identifying external objects as the self.)
