At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [continued] until they realized and knew this mind as the ground of neither-arising-nor-ceasing.

(Xie Li said: "Previously, you were reprimanded for taking movement as the self and movement as the environment; thus, the true and false aspects of body and mind have not yet been distinguished from their reality or unreality.

Furthermore, because you take the arising and ceasing of every thought-moment as real, you have lost sight of its nature. Consequently, even that which is non-arising and non-ceasing has not yet been distinguished.
Therefore, I ask these two questions. (Le Tan said: "The son of Śaṇḍaka Vairāṭīputra taught [that] among sentient beings..."
One attains the Way through ripening at the time of spontaneous occurrence, like a ball of thread thrown down that stops when it reaches its limit.

Furthermore, it is said that after eighty thousand kalpas have passed, one naturally attains the Way. Kāḷakaudika-Kātyāyana taught that regarding all phenomena, there is both existence and non-existence.
Thus, both of these individuals held the view of annihilationism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi). Therefore, King Bimbisāra cited Cāṇakya and Vaira as examples and questioned [the Buddha]. Wēnlíng says:
Previously, he was rebuked for taking movement to be the body and movement to be the environment; thus, he had not yet distinguished the reality from the falsity of body and mind.
Furthermore, he was rebuked for [claiming that] every thought-moment arises and perishes, thereby losing the true nature; yet even regarding that which arises and perishes, he had not yet...

This can be discerned. Therefore, I shall clarify these two meanings. As for the fact that this was initiated by King Ajātaśatru, it clarifies that the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing is fully present even while one is enmeshed in afflictions.
The Buddha told the Great King: "Your body exists now... [until] you must certainly know that this body shall eventually perish."

(Changshui said: "The Buddha raised this question desiring to reveal that within arising and ceasing there is non-arising and non-ceasing, just as previously [it was shown that] while the head itself moved, the vision remained unmoved.
(Wenling said: "Ānanda took the body and its objects to be moving; this characteristic is still coarse.")
This refers to the immovability of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*). Now, the Buddha questioned King Bimbisāra regarding the physical body, which undergoes decay and transformation;
the King replied that it cannot remain stationary even for a single moment (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*), its characteristics being exceedingly subtle. (This concludes the discussion on the nature of seeing.)
Wuxing said: "The former demonstration to Ānanda showed that seeing is without movement; the latter demonstration to King Nimi showed that the nature is without arising or ceasing.
At first glance these seem identical, yet their meanings must be distinguished. Why? Because there is a difference between coarse and subtle regarding the arising and ceasing that is being refuted."
The nature revealed through perception varies according to proximity and distance. When sages lead beings to enter the Tathāgatagarbha, their approach becomes progressively deeper;
let the reader examine this carefully.
The Buddha said, "It is so, Great King... (omitted)... therefore know that my body will ultimately undergo transformation and perish.
(Gushan says: The Buddha asked about two periods of time, while the answer provides three periods—namely, infancy, adulthood, and senility.)

Wenling says: "Hái" refers to one who has just become a child; "rú" refers to one who requires others for nourishment. "Pí" refers to the outer layer of skin; "fù" refers to the texture of the skin's grain.
"Máo" refers to senility and forgetfulness. To say "one or two *jì*" (twelve-year periods) is to observe with a broad and coarse perspective;
if one observes closely and minutely, in reality, every thought-moment (*nànniàn*) is incessant.
The Buddha told the Great King: "You see these transformations... how could you undergo birth and death therein? (Wenling says:
Makkhali Gosāla was a follower of Kātyāyanīputra. Since there is neither birth nor death, that is your true permanence;
you should not be deluded by his heterodox doctrine of annihilation.)
Gushan said: "The essence of seeing is the nature of seeing itself. That it wrinkles indicates change, which manifests the impermanence of birth and death;

that it does not wrinkle indicates non-change, which manifests the permanence of nirvana. Although birth and death and nirvana are divided into two streams, when one examines their essential nature, how could there be any duality?
The words are partial, but the meaning is complete: change is itself non-change. If this is so, how could there be..."
This merely refutes King Bimbisāra’s external views and also responds to Ānanda’s two requests. (Changshui says:

To describe his shallow realization, it is simply said that he "leaves one life to enter another. Yet, examining his profound intent, one must know that the source of extinction is itself unextinguished;
he understood according to what was appropriate for him, but did not yet speak explicitly.)
At that time, Ānanda joined his palms and knelt for a long time (until) he prayed, "May you arouse compassion and wash away my defilements.
[Xie Li said: This Ānanda, having fallen into a single inversion from birth, has lost the opportunity to pose his questions, which would have served to liberate sentient beings.]
Wenling says: Because of the dialogue between the King and [the Master], doubts were stirred up anew, leading him to think that if nature has birth and extinction, it can be said to be lost;
yet if there is no birth and extinction, how could it be lost?
At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm (until... and said, "I do not know who is upright and who is inverted.
(*Mudrā* means *hasta-mudrā*, which is one of the thirty-two marks.)
Wenling says: This clarifies that all Buddhas and sentient beings share the same essential nature; there is certainly no loss or omission.
It is only due to inverted views that one speaks of loss and omission. For example, having the arm hang down naturally is the correct state, yet one regards it as inverted;
having it turned upward against the grain is inverted, yet one regards it as correct. This is to lose the truth.
"Observe your own body and the Buddha’s body with careful attention... [until you] do not know where the inversion of body and mind resides.
(Xie Li said: "The World-Honored One’s intention was to censure Ānanda for recognizing delusion within enlightenment; this is precisely where the inversion resides.
At that time, the assembly had not yet attained realization, and so they were left in a state of bewilderment.")
The supplementary note says: Since you already know that your bodies are termed "perverted by nature," from where did this name "perversion" originate?
Out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, the Buddha [proceeded] until [the point where he said]: "Within the wondrous nature of jewel-like clarity, you mistake awakening for delusion."

(Changshui said: "This shows that inversion has no separate location; it is merely what is manifested by the mind. It causes one to awaken to the fact that [inversion] is none other than the mind itself.
(Xielü said: "All that you give rise to is manifested by the mind alone; this is the awakening to the fundamental substance.
To abandon this fundamental awakening and grasp at the physical body is to mistake delusion for awakening within awakening.)
Wenling says: "Form" (*rūpa*) collectively refers to the five sense organs and the six objects. "Mind" (*citta*) collectively refers to the six consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness.

"Various conditions" (*pratyaya*) refers to all phenomena that serve as the objects of the sense organs and consciousnesses. "What the mind is driven by" refers to the karmic actions of good and evil.

"Quietude and activity," "thoughts and reflections," and "all phenomena that serve as objects" broadly enumerate mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness—the true and the false.
The characteristics of nature, as well as the causes and effects of the heterodox and the orthodox, all lack intrinsic substance;

they are manifested solely by the mind, like images within a mirror, wherein the entire image is the mirror itself. Thus, your current illusory and deluded body and mind are both manifestations of the wondrously luminous mirror of the mind.

The whole is mind. To fail to awaken to the wondrous essence by directly realizing that it is not identical with illusory delusion, but instead to abandon the fundamental wondrousness and cling to illusory delusion—this is to mistake confusion for awakening; this is precisely where the inversion lies.
The wondrous mind is one, yet its designations differ so greatly because they follow the differences in their functions according to the teachings. This clarifies what is manifested by the mind.

Objects are like a mirror; therefore, it is called the "wondrously luminous true essence. Furthermore, because delusion involves abandoning the root to pursue the branches, it is called the "fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind.
As for what is termed "fundamentally wondrous," it is fundamentally and inherently wondrous, not requiring cultivation or effort.

"Mind" (*citta*) and "nature" (*prakṛti*) are mutually designated as the essence and its function. Mind arises luminosity from the wondrous, being perfectly integrated and clearly illuminating, just like [a mirror].

It is the light of the mirror; therefore, it is called the Perfectly Wondrous and Luminous Mind. Its nature is wondrous precisely because it is luminous, remaining unmoving, profoundly still, and serene like the substance of the mirror;
therefore, it is called the Treasure-like Luminous and Wondrous Nature.
Obscured darkness becomes emptiness; within this obscured darkness... (up to) "The Tathāgata calls them those who are to be pitied.
(Gushan says: "Obscured darkness becomes emptiness" means that because one is deluded regarding the luminosity of the nature, ignorance (*avidyā*) is produced. From this ignorance...)

It transforms into inert emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*). This transformed inert emptiness and the transforming ignorance (*avidyā*)—these two dharmas combine to transform and give rise to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which become the external forms of the mountain-rivers and the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*).

Thus, the land and its territory are established. Because the four great elements and their forms are combined with the mind of deluded thought (*vikalpa-citta*), they transform and give rise to the internal forms of sentient beings as their primary retribution (*upapatti-vipāka*). Therefore, it is said that "form is mixed with deluded thought," and "the characteristics of thought constitute [form]."
The body; "perception" refers to the deluded mind, and "characteristics" refers to deluded form. When form and mind combine, the five aggregates are complete;
thus one knows that sentience is precisely the sentient being.
Wenling says: This correctly traces the origin of delusion and inversion. Regarding "the accumulation of conditions agitates within," etc.:
there is a false accumulation of the breath of conditions; internally, it is tossed about by thoughts, while externally, it rushes away pursuing objects.
This is merely the appearance of being turbidly disturbed by various false conditions and sensory dust, yet people take this to be the essential nature of their own mind—is this not delusion?
Alas! Having once become deluded in this way, one will certainly regard the mind as existing within the illusory physical form.
One never realizes that the wondrously luminous true mind encompasses heaven and earth and contains all phenomena, yet instead identifies it within this tiny body.
How is this different from abandoning the boundless ocean of lands to identify a single bubble as the essence of the entire tide?
What a capacity it has, like that of the vast ocean!

(The supplementary note says: To turn one's back on the truth and pursue delusion is like discarding the sea to recognize a bubble; to grasp at delusion as truth is like recognizing a bubble as the sea.)
Ānanda said to the Buddha: [up to] "...I do not yet dare to recognize it as the fundamental source of the mind-ground.
(Wuxing says: Previously, the false mind was refuted, already demanding that the nature of discrimination based on sound be identified.

Now Ānanda again asks about the "conditioned mind" (*pratyaya-citta*) because he wishes to reveal that the true nature is devoid of the characteristics of subject and object. Since [the inquiry] concerns the conditioned mind...)
Free from coarse attachments, he therefore merely said, "I do not yet dare claim this as the fundamental original mind-ground.
Wénlǐng says: "Because of hearing the sound of the Dharma, one awakens to the wondrously luminous mind, which is fundamentally perfect and complete, with nothing lacking or lost."
Therefore, it is said that the mind-ground is eternally abiding. Yet, one's emotional state remains crude and superficial, and one's insight has not yet attained clarity;
one still takes the perceiving mind that hears as the fundamental nature realized. This is indeed the common delusion where the faculties are rooted in the mind and difficult to uproot;
thus, I pray that the Buddha will pull me out of it.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and the others still [regard things as real] because you have not yet realized that there is nothing to be understood; you are likewise so. (Zhenji said:
"Because one uses the mind that takes objects as a means to take the Buddha’s Dharma-sound as an object, one identifies it as self-nature, though it is not self-nature.
This Dharma-sound is merely the sound-teaching that serves as the object of cognition. (Wuxing said: "This is the metaphor of pointing at the moon. Although it dispels the finger..."
The pointing finger correctly singles out the cognizing mind as the object of refutation, because Ānanda had said, "I am currently using this cognizing mind to look up to you with devotion.
Therefore, it is for good reason that the scriptural text refutes only the nature of discursive discrimination.
Letan said: "That which discriminates due to sound is the conditioned mind; it is not the true nature of the mind. That which perceives delusively due to objects is the conditioned phenomena;
it is not the nature of phenomena. To falsely identify with objects due to conditions leads to a succession of delusions regarding those conditions, causing every matter to lose its true essence.
Gushan said: "The person is like the Tathāgata, and the finger is like the sound."

The teaching illustrates the True Principle, while the act of pointing it out to others illustrates the transformation of sentient beings. The teaching expounds the True Principle, and that Principle is the very mind of sentient beings.
Upon hearing the teaching, one should naturally turn to contemplate one's own mind; only by letting go of the finger can one recognize the moon.
If one discriminates that the sound of my Dharma-teachings—from [the mention of] Kuśinagara and other places—is the "Dark Principle" (mīngdì), [it is a mistake].
[Jielǐ says: "The mind that conditions sensory objects has no essence apart from those objects; therefore, it is called 'dark' (míng)."]
Wenling says: "The discriminating mind of conditions, being detached from sensory objects, has no inherent nature;
it is like a passing guest. The eternally abiding true mind, however, has nowhere to go; it is like the host of the pavilion. This is a further elaboration based on Ānanda’s underlying intent.
"The mind that discriminates sound" refers to the mind that takes sound as its object; it is that which awakens to the voice of the Buddha-dharma.
"Discriminating my own appearance" refers to the mind that takes form as its object; it is that which accords with what is gazed upon.

This means that not only does the mind that discriminates sound lack an intrinsic nature apart from sound, but the mind that discriminates form also lacks an intrinsic nature outside of the characteristics of form. It is as follows:
The phrase "this even extends to" and so forth refers collectively to the reflected images of the six sense objects; all of these lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because everything is entirely non-existent, they are not form (*rūpa*); because they falsely appear in dependence upon conditions, they are not emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Since they are neither form nor emptiness, they are indistinctly merged and impossible to discern.
Thus, the non-Buddhists take ignorance as the ultimate principle (*tattva*). This refers to Maskarī Gośālīputra.
Since all dharmas are free from conditions and lack a discriminative nature, how could the wondrously luminous primordial mind not be capable of returning [to its source]?
(Wenling says: This concludes the preceding section and introduces what follows. (Zhenji says:

Although the preceding text has already explained that such seeing of the nature is the mind and not the eye, the essence of seeing still contains a mixture of the true and the false. Therefore, the text extensively examines conditions and objects to distinguish and extract the true nature;
once the sand has been sifted away, the golden essence will naturally be pure.)

Wuxing said: "Regarding this question of why the nature of the mind has nothing to return to, the Buddha will later specifically point to the 'essence of seeing' (*darśana-viśuddha*) as that which does not return.
The Buddha told Ānanda: 'Furthermore, as for your seeing me... (until) now I shall show you the ground where there is nothing to return.'"
Wuxing said: "Regarding Ānanda’s question as to why the wondrously luminous primordial mind has no place from which it can return, the Buddha answered by means of the 'essence of seeing.
This was because the true mind leaves no trace and is difficult to awaken to; therefore, he relied upon the essence of seeing as a skillful means to provide instruction."
Although this belongs to the realm of delusion, it is closely proximate to the truth—like a second moon; while it is grasped as distinct, it is not far removed from reality.
One should know that this seeing is likewise the same seeing that previously perceived objects.
Gushan said: "Furthermore, when you say, 'I see,' you are referring to the fundamental essence of the clarity of seeing.
This fundamental essence of seeing emerges from the wondrous, luminous, and pure mind; therefore it is said that although it is not the wondrous mind itself, it is like a second moon.
This is because the second moon is in reality one body with the first, yet appears as different due to the pressure of the fingers—this serves as a metaphor for the essence of seeing."

The wondrous mind is fundamentally without dual characteristics; it is by people that duality is created. The reflection of the moon, however, inherently possesses two aspects, and for this reason it is said to be not [the true moon].
The true moon is a metaphor for the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind; the second moon is a metaphor for the fundamental essence of the clarity of seeing;
and the shadow in the water is a metaphor for the discrimination of objects.
"Ānanda, this great lecture hall... [is] clear and serene, with the air stilled; furthermore, observe its purity. (Wuxing says:
Among these eight conditions, seven are discussed in terms of their capacity to reflect upon the sense organs (*indriya*).
Only the condition of "discrimination" arises in relation to the seven objects (*viṣaya*); therefore, the scriptural text places it in the middle. This serves to connect the preceding [sections].)
[This is] the lower [view]. (Supplementary Note: As Master Yue previously stated that the nature of discriminating based on objects has a "return," he refuted it by saying it "has a return";
this is also evident here.)
The True Limit said: "In order to demonstrate the nature that cannot be returned, one first points to the characteristics that can be returned.
These eight [examples] merely set forth the essentials.
Ānanda, you have all observed these various changing phenomena... (up to)... for this reason, the Tathāgata calls himself 'one who is to be pitied.'"
(Zhenji said: "As for the fundamental causes: the sun is the cause of light; black is the cause of darkness; a crack is the cause of penetration; and a clear sky is the cause of purity. (Wuxing said:
"That the seeing-nature does not return is like the analogy of two moons. This seeing belongs to delusion and must also be returned.
Only the true moon, which serves as the metaphor for the true nature, truly does not return. As the following text says: 'There is but one moon.'"")
Truly. In the interim, there is inherently neither this "moon" nor "non-moon. Furthermore, it is said: "At the time of seeing the seer, the seeing is not the seer.
Is it not the case that this seeing can also be returned? Question: To what is this returned? Answer: It is returned to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because of ignorance, there is the capacity to see; if ignorance is shattered, this seeing is returned. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "If one is separated from karma..."
"Consciousness has no characteristic of seeing; its meaning is thus manifest. Wénlǐng says:
"Brightness and darkness, penetration and obstruction, the conditions of space, and the clarity and turbidity—each returns to its eight causes.

As for the nature of the clarity and brightness of the seeing faculty that can observe these eight kinds, to what place should it return? If one again gives rise to the mind of discrimination regarding the conditions of seeing, then seeing [arises]."

These are the various conditions of form and mind. If it were to return to the light below, this means that if there were something to which it returned, it would follow after the object and no longer be able to see.
While objects naturally differ from one another, the nature of seeing has no distinction; thus, seeing does not follow along with the objects.

"Regarding that which can be returned," and so forth, [the Buddha] concludes by demonstrating that there is nothing to be returned; this is your true nature, what is called "the body revealed alone amidst the myriad phenomena.
Ānanda said: "Although I recognize that this seeing-nature has nothing to be returned, how can I know it is my true nature?"
Wuxing said: "The intent of this question is as follows: although one recognizes two moons, why is it called the true moon? Xiali said:
"Although one knows that the essence of seeing has no place to return, it currently appears mixed with objects and has not yet been clearly distinguished."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "I now ask you... [up to] sentient beings who possess clear vision do not see beyond a few inches.
(Gushan says: Nalakūvara sees the trichiliocosm as if looking at a fruit in the palm of his hand; this refers to Jambudvīpa.)
Furthermore, let me illustrate this by way of something familiar. (Wuxing says: *Āmalaka* is difficult to distinguish;
its fruit resembles a peach but is not a peach, and resembles a crabapple but is not a crabapple.)
Lectan said: "This description has five parts: first, śrāvakas; second, arhats; third, bodhisattvas; fourth, Tathāgatas; and fifth, sentient beings.

The intent is to clarify that although the cognitive measures (*jñāna-pramāṇa*) of the four classes of noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings differ, the essence of seeing (*darśana-sāra*) is no different;

all can be resolved and discerned by means of their respective objects and forms. Because Ānanda’s vision had not yet departed from desire, it is said that he 'had not yet attained the state of non-'"* [The text here appears to be truncated].*
This is the purification of the outflows (*āsrava-viśuddhi*). The first dhyāna is the head of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the heaven of those free from desire.

Anuruddha was an Arhat free from outflows who had cultivated and attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), enabling him to see the great trichiliocosm; thus he beheld Jambudvīpa as if it were a single grain.
As for sentient beings not exceeding the size of a fraction of an inch, even a screen or curtain would obstruct his vision.
(Zhangshui said: "Not exceeding a fraction of an inch" means that one cannot see external objects through paper or film, nor can one see the five viscera through the skin.
Ānanda, all these natures of things, whether near or far, up to this subtle, wondrous, luminous, and sincere essence—this is your nature of seeing.
(Gushan said: "This [passage] relies upon the pervasiveness of the seeing-nature to manifest the pervasiveness of the true nature. (Wuxing said:

"The World-Honored One feared that Ānanda, having recognized this seeing-nature as already encompassing external objects, might still claim that those external objects possess the same capacity for seeing as he himself does.")
Therefore, the following passage refutes this).
Wuxing said: "Although Ānanda recognized the nature of seeing, he did not yet know the true nature. How could the Tathāgata’s answer not have revealed the truth?
It is simply that because the nature of seeing seems to reside within, one fails to realize that the true nature must pervade the outside as well."
The Buddha wished to demonstrate this to him; therefore, he pointed out that all objects and phenomena are what the essence of seeing perceives.
Since this perception is thus all-pervasive, how could its nature be limited?
If seeing were itself an object, then you [should likewise perceive my not-seeing]; why do you not see the place where I do not see?
(Zhenji said: "If you recognize seeing as a thing, then my seeing is likewise a thing; you should be able to see it. Wenglung said:
"That which is 'the same as seeing' is the trace of the thing; that which is 'not seeing' is the essence apart from the thing."
If you say that you and I see the same object, this is merely seeing my seeing; it is nothing more than a trace.
When I am detached from the object and do not see it, where is its substance? Since there is no place where it can be seen, it is certainly not an object.
If you see what is not seen, it is naturally not that characteristic of non-seeing.
(The supplementary note says: That characteristic of non-seeing is fundamentally without characteristics; how could it be something you are able to see?)
Wenling says: Even if one harbors the deluded thought that they can see my "not seeing," it ultimately remains nothing other than the characteristic of "not being seen" by them.
If one does not see the ground of my "not seeing," then naturally it is not a thing; how could it then not be you?
(Changshui said: "The meaning of this passage develops and converges through five successive stages. While the scriptural text preserves three, two meanings remain implicit)."
Zizhong said: "If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, you likewise do not see the place of my seeing.
Since you do not see the place of my seeing, my seeing is naturally not an object. If my seeing is not an object, then your seeing is also not an object.
Since your seeing is not an object, how could it not be your true seeing?"
Furthermore, at the very moment you now see an object—[up to] "and all things in the world would fail to be established" (Wenling says:
This further examines the confusion between object and self to demonstrate that seeing is not the object).
Lectan said: "If seeing were a thing, then that thing would possess the capacity for seeing; consequently, the natures of sentient and insentient beings would become confused and indistinguishable.
Therefore, it is said that [seeing] cannot be established as a fixed entity. Thus, it is clear that seeing is not a thing.
'All worlds' refers to both sentient beings and their environment, encompassing both the animate and the inanimate."
"Ānanda, when you see, it is you who see, not I. (Up to: "Your nature is not true; seek the reality from me. (Zhenji said:
"Although the seeing-nature is the same, each person experiences it individually. A thousand lamps in one room—how could their light be different?
Yet each illuminates itself, and they do not obstruct one another. (Gushan said: "Your nature is not true," etc., means that the True Nature resides...)
"You yourself cannot know its truth, yet you instead take my words to seek its reality. Your delusion is extreme;
your reproach is profound.
Wénlǐng says: "This restates the preceding [passage] to reveal the true nature. 'It is you, not me' clarifies the perception of the essence."

This is because [the seeing] is mixed with objects. If you awaken to the realization that the essence of seeing is not mixed with objects, then you will clearly know that the nature of seeing is vast, pure, and all-pervading throughout the Dharma-realm;
this is precisely your true nature. Why do you doubt its authenticity and seek a verification from me?
This concludes the answer to the question: "How can I know that this is my true nature?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One... (up to) I do not now know where this meaning resides. (Gushan says:
Since one observes the first heaven, one sees only a single set of four continents. To speak of 'Sahā' is to cite its general name;
it does not refer to the trichiliocosm. (Supplementary Note: The preceding text provides a general account of the application of vision, intending to reveal the Truth...)
The nature [of the visual faculty] is fundamentally all-pervasive; it is merely that the perceptions and capacities of the holy and the ordinary differ.
Now, because Ānanda suspects that the essence of the vision expands and contracts according to the breadth or narrowness of what is observed, he has raised this question.
Xie Li said: "This is because he has stepped upon the Buddha’s spiritual power and is thus able to see the events of the First Dhyāna;

it is based on the breadth or narrowness of what is seen that one suspects the substance of vision expands or contracts. This is because he has not yet attained direct realization and merely attempts to measure it with his conceptual mind.
The palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings are equal in height to the sun and moon; since the range of what they see is vast, it extends throughout the Sahā world."
The vihāra is narrow; the hall and its doors are likewise narrow. A single realm is this Sahā world.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All worlds... (down to)... the nature of their meaning is thus; how could they exist [within it]?"
(Gushan said: "Squareness and roundness depend on the vessel; they do not reside in empty space. Greatness and smallness arise from dust;

what concern does this have for the nature of seeing? Therefore, he questions: 'How can it be said to be located? Letan said: 'The vessel has squareness and roundness, but empty space undergoes no change.

Since there is no change, how could there be expansion or contraction? As for the question 'How can it be said to be located?', the essence of seeing is suchness (*tathatā*); it admits no emotional attachments, vessels, or delusions."')
(Du also). Wénlǐng says:
"All worlds" refers to categories such as the root-body and the vessel-world. "Large and small, internal and external" refers to categories such as a single realm or a single room.
"All activities" refers to categories such as expansion and contraction, or compression and separation. This is the general [classification].

All phenomena are merely objects of the external environment; they do not interact with my numinous awareness. Therefore, whether the objects before one are large or small, the seeing itself neither expands nor contracts.
To illustrate this: the vessel is a metaphor for the external environment, while the empty space within it is a metaphor for the essence of seeing.

"Ānanda, if you further wish to cause [the space] to enter into that which has neither square nor round [shape], you would have to further eliminate the location of the spatial characteristics of emptiness.

(Zizhong says: 'If you further wish to cause it to enter into that which has neither square nor round,' this means that the essence of emptiness has no direction; it serves as a metaphor for the fact that the nature of seeing is non-dual.

Since the spatial characteristics of emptiness can be eliminated because it has no squareness or roundness, how much more so can the nature of seeing—which has neither largeness nor smallness—be returned? This is why he speaks only thus.)"
"Square" (fang) means that the meaning subsumes the "round" (yuan); it is merely a brief expression of the Buddha’s words.

Gushan said: "The nature of emptiness is immovable; how could there be entering or exiting? It is only because of the movement or stillness of the vessel that one figuratively speaks of entering and exiting."
Wenling said: "To contemplate one's nature by departing from dust, one naturally attains the original truth without needing to exert effort.
As for your question regarding the time of entering the chamber—asking whether there is not a continuous trace of activity—this interpretation is incorrect."
(Wenling says: Since it cannot be pulled back, it certainly cannot be shortened; since it cannot be continued, it certainly cannot be severed.
Since this is not the case logically, there is no use for emotional calculations.)
All sentient beings, from time immemorial [until] they are able to universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
(The Supplemental Note states: Previously it was said that "one takes objects as oneself"; now it is said that "one is deluded and takes oneself as objects.

The former passage concerned the selection of the false from the true, speaking for the moment of the difference between objects and self; thus one's own body was disparaged and referred to entirely as "objects. Now, this shall use the True to integrate [all things].)
Delusion. One should know that all things are oneself. Although all things are oneself, one is deluded and takes them to be external objects;
thus, one loses the fundamental mind and is turned by objects, perceiving the distinction between internal and external, and the difference between the large and the small.
Gushan said: "To mistake oneself for objects means to lose one's true nature and follow after sensory dust. To be turned by objects means to become inverted and deluded because of them.
Being turned by objects is like space changing according to the shape of a vessel; thus, within this state, one perceives the large as small and ultimately remains a sentient being.
One who can turn objects is like removing the vessel to perceive the space itself; therefore, [one attains liberation].

The mind is perfectly luminous and pervades all lands, being identical to that of the Tathāgata. For the lands upon the tip of a hair are fundamentally not subject to the principle of smallness and greatness or containment;
they do not require supernatural transformations, but merely require the removal of emotional attachments and material vessels, whereupon they manifest before one in vast openness.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One... (up to the point where he) previously raised the objection that "objects can see me. (Xie Li says:
These are all objections based on deluded sentiments regarding the distinction [between self and object]. Wenling says:
To say "objects can see me" means that the seeing occurs in the objects and not in the body; thus, it is the objects that can see me.)
Gushan said: "It was previously stated that by mistaking oneself for objects, one loses the fundamental mind and is thus turned by objects.
If one can turn objects, then one is identical to the Tathāgata. Thus, the mountains and rivers perceived are all my wondrous nature;

therefore it is said, 'Now this wondrous nature is present before me. This is the comprehension of the essential meaning. Regarding the passage beginning with 'Seeing must be my true self,' Ānanda still..."
One still maintains the distinction between subject and object. This means that if what is seen is already the true nature, then what is this "I" that sees?

If you say the body lacks the nature of seeing, yet the present discernment is not false; or if you say that what appears before us is indeed seeing, then external objects would have no separate mental consciousness, whereas it is my own body that possesses it.
If those external objects truly were my mind, [how could they be perceived as such?]
That which can now be seen constitutes external objects; this internal body of mine is not-self.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said... [up to] the Buddha saying: "So it is, so it is."

(Xie Li said: "To thoroughly discern all phenomena without having any fixed views—whether regarding emptiness or material objects—is to provide a detailed analysis of all dharmas, both form and emptiness.
First it is called the 'essence of seeing,' next the 'source of seeing,' and finally 'refined seeing. This seeing is fundamentally rooted in the wondrous, refined, and luminous mind;
therefore, it is generally termed 'refined' (*jing*). Since it first emerges from the mind, it is called the 'source of seeing. It is designated according to its function...")

It is the essence; therefore, it is called "the essence of seeing. Relying on the essence to point to its function, it is called "the subtle seeing" (the characters *lin* and *qu* are equivalent to "forest springs").
Wénlǐng says: "Objects do not possess this seeing; therefore, even a Great Sage cannot discern it by analyzing objects directly.
The meaning must involve being detached from objects. Chángshuǐ says: "'Thus, thus' is a seal confirming that one cannot separate out the nature of seeing."
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda, [saying] as you have said... (up to) the Buddha saying, "So it is, so it is. [Xie Li said:
"Seeing is not itself an object; only when there is that which is seen does seeing exist. If the object were identical to seeing, then there would be nothing seen."
Among the myriad phenomena, there is nothing that is not seeing; this can be dissected and demonstrated.
Wēnlíng says: "If the tree were not seeing, how could one see the tree? If it were identical to seeing, then the tree itself should be named 'seeing'."

What is meant by "tree"? Now, as for the previous [position] that there is no such thing as a "view," since that does not accord with reason, one further contemplates that there is no "non-view" either.
Since neither of these two meanings is fixed, the Buddha permits both, because things such as form and emptiness are like flowers in the sky;
they fundamentally do not exist and cannot be definitively pointed out.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince... (up to) within this interval, there is neither "is" nor "is not.
(Ziqing says: "The two kinds" refer to the source of the refined and brilliant vision, and the preceding conditions of form and emptiness; these are the two meanings of "is" and "is not.")
Wenling says: The Buddha’s intention was to reveal that seeing and the conditions for seeing are like flowers in the sky; within them, there is fundamentally no such thing as "is" or "is not.

This is the direct answer to the question. "The faculty of seeing" refers to the sense organ; "seeing" refers to the objective realm. "The characteristics conceived" refers to consciousness.

"However, this is quite reckless. Mañjuśrī, I now ask you:

This is the second [point]. To be without Mañjuśrī is the third.

"If one says that what is called 'spontaneity' (*svabhāva*) today seems not to be the same as 'causes and conditions' (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the past, how is it distinguished from the 'spontaneity' of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)?

The meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is taught in order to refute the non-Buddhists' (*tīrthika*) attachment to spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

"It is not their realm" means that it is not the same as what the non-Buddhists perceive. Although the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* speaks of dependent origination to refute their false attachments, when one contemplates that the nature of awakening possesses a true essence of spontaneity, which is far removed from inversion and delusion, it appears as though it is not dependent origination.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If, as I have now [explained], the nature of seeing were to be annihilated, how could one see light?
(Gushan says: Taking light, darkness, form, and emptiness as the basis, one investigates the nature of spontaneity.

(All are known through the calculations of sentient beings).

If it were the original state of the self-substance, it would not change according to objects; yet now they all change according to objects, and thus are not natural."
Ānanda said: "This wondrous vision—whether it encounters light or darkness—is identical to emptiness or obstruction.
(Gushan says: Ānanda initially doubted that the wondrous nature was the same as external spontaneity;

having heard the successive refutations, he now believes that the meaning of the correct principle of causes and conditions is as the Buddha has taught, yet he does not yet know how the wondrous nature accords with this. (Zhenji says: ...).
Because the immediate cause is proximate while the contributing condition is remote, they are divided into two gates.
Wénlǐng says: "Your statement regarding causes and conditions" and below explains why they are not [true] causes and conditions.
Taking things as the cause and following things as the condition—since there is no fixed location, they are not [true] causes and conditions.
One should know that such a subtle, awakened, wondrous clarity (up to) being free from all marks yet identical with all dharmas.

(Wuxing says: Regarding the passage "not due to causes and conditions" and below, the phrase "not not due to causes and conditions" is not mentioned because this section primarily refutes [the notion of] causes and conditions;
therefore, it is set aside for now. "Neither non-being nor non-non-being, neither is-ness nor non-is-ness" reveals that the nature of awakening is fundamentally non-existent.)

Neither "is" nor "is not," and likewise neither "right" nor "wrong. To be detached from these is to manifest the True, as opposed to the conventional; to be immersed in them is to realize that all objects encountered are but the Mind. Wénlǐng says:

This repeatedly brushes away pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) to directly point toward essential awakening. As for causes and conditions, spontaneity, right and wrong, and calculation— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "是非筭".)

therefore, it is said that one "is identical with all phenomena. This is what the Patriarch meant when he said: "Simply by leaving behind delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā*). It is further stated: "This is..."

(Gushan said: "This further specifically explains the meaning of causes and conditions, so as to awaken sentient beings.

"To see seeing is not seeing. Wénlíng says:

Next, one should further understand this: when seeing the act of seeing, that seeing is not [the true] seeing. This is because one knows that light and darkness are not seeing;

When one knows that the seeing of seeing is not [true] seeing, then one awakens to the fact that the essence of seeing is free from characteristics, and truly sees the essence of seeing. Now, the sentiment of "seeing" belongs to delusion; how, then, can it be true?
To see again within seeing is indeed delusion. For the essence of seeing is the nature that reflects forms. Although seeing belongs to the realm of delusion, its nature is fundamentally true.
One should know that at the moment of "seeing-seeing," there is nothing else seen; it is merely seeing the nature within seeing itself.
Thus, if one has not yet seen this nature, the nature resides within seeing and is termed the "essence of seeing. If...

This is called the pure true mark (*dharmatā*), the wondrous path to Bodhi. Yet the śrāvakas are confined merely to names and marks and cannot penetrate it;

therefore, I urge you to contemplate it well and not be weary or indolent. The preceding text followed in its tracks to extensively clarify the truth and falsehood of body and mind, with the intent of giving rise to right knowledge and vision and revealing the Tathāgatagarbha. However, the student’s insight remains unclear.

thus, the Tathāgatagarbha exists within the very act of direct perception.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One... [his] mind is still not yet fully understood; you should now listen attentively. (Wuxing says:
Ānanda’s delusion concerns the subtleties of the mind and objects, whereas what the Tathāgata reveals is an ever-deeper contemplative illumination;

"Ānanda, all sentient beings transmigrate through the world... (up to) second, the deluded vision shared by sentient beings. (Wuxing says:
This is because Ānanda asked whether the seeing of seeing is itself seeing; therefore, [the Buddha] clarifies the doubts regarding these two types of karma.

(Supplementary Note: "Distinct karma" refers to the deluded vision of a single individual. "Shared karma" refers to the deluded vision of many people. Therefore, it is written with the radical for 'many' [彳*多].)

"'Distinct karma' refers to the differences in the arising of delusion; one falsely pursues the shadows of conditions and loses one's way."

Right View. Regarding "shared karma," it refers to what is experienced in common due to delusion; thus, delusion follows birth and death, causing the fundamental enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣājñāna*) to sink and decline.
Why is this called "deluded vision of separate karma"? [It is because] there are distinct circular shadows where the five colors overlap.

because there is the delusion of false illness, one gives rise to the confusion of differentiation regarding objects."
"What do you think? As for this lamp-light at night (up to) the one who sees the circular reflection, what is this called?

(Wenling says: "That which is seen by that person is produced by a cataract in the eye; it serves as a metaphor for the deluded perception of differentiation, which does not arise from the external object.")
Nor does it arise from the sense organs; it is entirely produced by the sickness of the sentient beings' vision. (Supplementary Note:
The five-colored circular shadows are neither the color of the lamp nor the color of the vision; they are produced solely by the cataract of the observer's eyes.

Regarding the observation of the cataract: this refers to the fact that only one who possesses a cataract sees it. What is its name?
If it were the seeing of color, then once the seeing has already become color, that person with the cataract who sees the circular shadow could not be said to be "seeing."
Form is precisely the shadow. Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular shadow [exists]... how can a person with cataracts see a circular shadow? (The supplementary note states:

"Form actually resides within the lamp" means the principle-body is fundamentally true. "Seeing" is the illness that becomes the shadow; the deluded mind constitutes the objective realm.]

Furthermore, the seeing of the reflection is a shared ailment; both the mind and its objects are illusory. To see the ailment is not itself a disease, for it implies the presence of a wise person who recognizes that the reflection arises due to an ocular disorder.
Such a person will never insist that the circular reflection truly exists; therefore, although the disorder is present, it does not constitute a disease of vision.
[The Buddha] perfected his initial resolve. Although ignorance still remained, he realized that ignorance was fundamentally non-existent from the beginning;
thus, there were no delusive objects to be apprehended. (Wuxing says: When the Tathāgata raised this to refute the attachment to intrinsic nature, he intended precisely to provide an example.

Seeing that the essence [of vision] is fundamentally free from disease, one realizes that the visual aberration of the shadow-vision is entirely a floating delusion; these two do not intersect at all.
Therefore, one should not insist on saying it is the lamp or it is the vision, nor should one insist on saying it is neither the lamp nor the vision.

This means that the circular reflection exists because of the lamp and the seeing; this is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The same applies to the meals of the various devas; they differ according to their respective merits. Letan said:

A halo (*yun*). A solar eclipse is called *shì*; this refers to what is known as the "manifestation of calamity" in the sun and moon.

When its rays and vapors radiate out in all directions, it is called a *bei*; it appears shimmering and diffuse. When it vanishes without leaving a trace, it is called a "flying" star; its light and traces remain connected.

"Ānanda, I now explain these two matters to you... (up to) 'thus, the one who perceives the visual defect ultimately has no fault of seeing'. [Xingfu said:
