Among these, the phrase "falsely taking it to be enlightened awareness" serves as a metaphor for this. It is then concluded with the statement: "Based on enlightenment, one establishes the objective.
These four characters constitute the essential answer. For "enlightenment" (ming) here refers to false enlightenment, and false enlightenment is precisely ignorance (avidyā).
"The objective" (suo) refers to the source from which all conditioned phenomena—such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth—manifest. To state the point briefly: based on enlightenment...
As for "establishing what exists," this refers to how, due to ignorance, the world, space, and the karmic fruits of sentient beings arise.
Thus, both the doubt regarding their manifestation according to karma and the question of how they suddenly come into being are simultaneously resolved by this single answer.

There is no need for further elaboration to establish this; therefore, although it was later hidden and revealed, or explained in both general and specific terms, it never went beyond setting forth the discourse on the world, sentient beings, karma, and its fruits to bring the teaching to its conclusion. Yet even this was merely a general manifestation.
Only after [discussing] the self-awakened clarity and the emptiness of delusion did he begin to separately open three sections, providing a detailed account of these three.
Having completed the detailed exposition on the continuity of these seeds, it further states:
"These three kinds of inverted continuities are all the nature of awakened clarity and luminous cognition. Because of this cognition, appearances arise; they are born from deluded vision.
The various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth undergo successive fluxes; because of this falsity, they end and then begin again. This, moreover—
This concludes the first chapter, summarizing the intended meaning by restating it for demonstration. The second question and answer will be explained separately in the subsequent text:
"The clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness interact to produce agitation... (up to)... by these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession."
(Gushan said: "The four wheels that support the world are, in reality, the earth wheel, the gold wheel, the water wheel, and the wind wheel.
The reason earth is not mentioned here is that earth and gold share the same nature of solidity and thus belong to the same category.

Since this refers to the 'four great elements' (mahābhūta), these already encompass the four wheels. Furthermore, among these four great elements, wind and gold arise from the deluded mind, while water and fire [arise from the same]. )

Furthermore, they arise from wind and metal. Some say that the essence of love externally encounters water; however, this contradicts the scriptural text. As for their acting as seeds for one another:

just as the clarity of awareness and the flavor of emptiness interact to form agitation, this becomes the seed of the wind-circle. Because of this agitation, obstruction is established, which becomes the seed of the metal-circle.
Wind and metal rubbing against each other become the seed of the fire-element. Metal and fire, in turn, become the seed of the water-element.
Fire and water further constitute the seeds of oceans and islands; earth and water further constitute the seeds of grasses and trees.

One should understand that all these delusive phenomena, within the single true nature, are like flowers in the sky. Where the flower is and where the sky is, there is fundamentally no difference. Therefore, when observing the delusive manifestations, one sees only the true manifestations.
As for the characteristics of manifestation and non-manifestation, who can name this "this" or "that"? Since the continuity of the world is thus, the following two [sections] are as follows.
The continuity [of this principle] is likewise so.
Wenling says: "The myriad dharmas arise from the transformations of the five elements; the five elements are produced by deluded awareness.
Thus, the beginning of the world originates in the clarity of awareness and depends upon wind, metal, water, and fire to generate and complete all things."

Furthermore, true awakening is wondrous emptiness; fundamentally, it is neither luminous nor obscure. Because of delusion, it is treated as luminous awareness, and thus there comes to be obscurity within emptiness.
When luminosity and obscurity oppose one another, the mind fails to realize its own movement; hence it is called "awakened luminosity" (*jue-ming*).

As luminosity and obscurity depend upon each other, they become agitated, giving rise to the world-system of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Since all that lies beneath rests supported by this wind-circle, it is called "that which upholds the world. This arises from emptiness.

Regarding "arising from shaking and so forth": due to the movement of thought within the obscurity of emptiness, one’s awakened clarity becomes rigidly attached, thereby establishing obstruction and sensation;

this is metal (*kāñcana*). It is at the very bottom of the great earth, arising in dependence upon the wheel of gold (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*); hence it is said to "sustain the lands. Regarding "the firm awakening accomplished as treasure and so forth":
due to the false shaking of firm awakening, contact gives rise to agitation and distress, which is experienced as fire. This transforms the two realms, internal and external.

The raw becomes cooked; the conditioned becomes unconditioned—all these are transformations produced by the fire element (tejas-mahābhūta); therefore, it is called the nature of transformation. Regarding the phrase "the brilliance of the jewel produces moisture" and so forth:
from the perception of solidity, consciousness arises, which then steams with afflictions (*kleśa*). Through the accumulation of mental states and the arousal of craving, water is evoked.
Since the world resides within the great ocean, it is said to "contain the realms of the ten directions. As the fire ascends, the water...

Regarding those of inferior grade: deluded awareness arises falsely, and deluded consciousness flows perversely. Through their mutual entanglement, obstructions are established and the soil is evoked.
Since the nature of earth is solidity and obstruction, it is called "establishing solidity. Its heights become mountains; its depths become seas—all are soil.
An island is a mound of water; a sandbar is a *tàn*. All these originate from delusive cognition and are stirred by the five elements.
Thus it is said: "Delusions arise in conjunction, mutually serving as seeds for one another. Earth and Water produce Wood; Wood and Earth produce Metal; Metal and Wood produce Fire;
Fire and Metal produce Water; Water and Fire produce Earth. The world initially arises from the consciousness manifested by awakened clarity.
Water arises [from darkness]. When emptiness and darkness congeal into form, it becomes earth. Their mutual dependence results in movement, which becomes wind and wood;

this is how earth and water give rise to wood. Furthermore, from the earth of empty darkness, movement arises to become wood; when solidity and clarity establish obstruction, wood and earth give rise to metal.
The remaining text is quite clear: earth is produced by water and fire. The gentleman receives his father’s...

Because the mother’s element is fire, fire arises from within the sea; because the father’s element is water, water pours forth from the sandbanks. According to the Five Elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*), when the "I" (the dominant element) overcomes [the other], it acts as the wife while the husband is inferior;
only then do yin and yang harmonize to produce offspring. Thus, when water is inferior and fire is dominant, it becomes a mountain. When earth is inferior and water is dominant, it becomes wood.

The blazing fusion and clarity represent the division of the elemental energies of fire and water; the burning and churning represent the clarity of the division between the elemental energies of earth and water. This...
This is the cause for the continuous succession of the world.
(Wuxing says: Through the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings, first, at the very bottom, supported by space, a wind-circle arises.
Above the wind-circle is a water-circle. Above the water-circle is gold [and so forth], due to the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings.)
This is the supreme merit. Great clouds and rain arise and pour down upon the wind-wheel, with droplets as large as chariot axles, accumulating to form a wheel of water.
Then, another distinct wind strikes this water, causing it to congeal above into gold.

The difference between this and that [previous description] is that the former concerns the establishment of the world, ascending from below to above to form its sequence; whereas this concerns the arising of the world, wherein the internal causes the external.
This completes the second section. However, as the meanings of "great" and "small" are distinct, there is no need to reconcile them.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa clarifies that delusion is not from another [source] (up to the point where): "mutually entangled by common karma, their union and separation form the transformations."
(Gushan said: "Now, it is merely stated that 'what is falsely established' exists. This refers to the preceding passage which says: 'Because of clarity, the object is established;

due to the nature of false clarity, what was not limited is made limited. Thus it is called 'the principle of clarity. Phrases such as 'not exceeding hearing' and 'not producing sound' demonstrate the characteristics of the inconceivable.
The subsequent passage states: 'Originally relying on one refined spirit, it divides into six harmonious combinations')."
Wuxing said: "To clarify delusion is to see that it is inherently luminous. 'Not something else' means that the substance of this delusory luminosity is not produced by any other dharma;
it is entirely true awakening. It arises as delusory luminosity and thus becomes a fault. 'The awareness of luminosity constitutes the fault.

Once what is delusory has been established, it subsequently results in obstruction. Therefore, the principle of luminosity does not transcend [itself], and thus hearing, seeing, and so forth [arise]. Six.
The faculties thus falsely become restricted; the six objects, such as form and fragrance, thus falsely become defiling; the six consciousnesses that perceive them thus falsely become differentiated.

Because these three—faculties, objects, and consciousness—constitute the nature of karma, they give rise to deluded karma. Thereupon, those with similar karma entwine one another, and through their union and separation, transformation occurs.
This is the beginning of the six paths and four modes of birth. Those with similar karma are the classes born from wombs and eggs.
Because the karma of the parents and oneself is identical, birth occurs through mutual entanglement. As for those born from moisture or by transformation, they are subject to union or separation;
they do not depend on parents but arise solely from one's own karma. Some take form by coalescing with moisture, such as crawling insects;
others are born by being separated and taking on a transformed existence, such as the classes of devas, hell-beings, and hungry ghosts.
"Seeing light and perceiving color, one gives rise to vision; the formation of perception constitutes a distinct view" (up to) "by these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.

(Gushan says: Because the deluded mind perceives a deluded object, it is said that "seeing light and perceiving color," which refers to seeing one's parents within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
"The formation of perception through clear vision" means giving rise to afflictions based on the deluded object. "Distinct view" means regarding the father as [the male principle]...)
Regarding the increase of the object and the identity of perception: the mother is the beloved object. When a daughter is conceived in the womb, the flow of craving reverses to become the seed;

that is, craving is directed toward the mother, and consciousness takes refuge therein. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that within the twelve links of dependent origination, ignorance is twofold:
first, the ignorance that moistens karma, which refers to the afflictions of the past; second, the ignorance that moistens birth, which is precisely the taking of rebirth in the womb.
At that time, one gives rise to feelings of aversion and attachment toward one's parents. Regarding the conception of the thought of the womb:
those with merit perceive their mother’s womb as a hall of flowering groves; those with little merit perceive it only as a thicket of thorns or a latrine.
"Conception through union" refers to the coming together of male and female; when the defiled mind is perfected, it draws in karma of a similar kind—meaning it draws in past karma of a similar kind.
[This refers to] entering the womb). Wēnlíng says:
That which is manifested by deluded vision and which brings forth deluded form is called "vision manifests as light and form.

This arises because the mind produces the objective realm. Because of light, vision arises; and because of vision, perception is produced. This is called "light, vision, and perception are formed. This...

Sentiment arises from the object. When one perceives difference, the object is contrary; thus, aversion is formed. When one conceives of similarity, the mind is compliant; thus, feeling (*vedanā*) is formed.
The mutual pouring of the three feelings is called "flowing" (*srotas*); the mutual meeting of the three perceptions (*saṃjñā*) is called "receiving" (*nāman*).

Feeling is the root of saṃsāra; therefore, flowing feeling constitutes the seed. Perception is the medium for transmitting life; therefore, the reception of perception forms the embryo. This relies upon union.
Through union, birth occurs; it is drawn forth by common karma (*sabhāga-karman*). This is the beginning of the entrustment of the physical basis for rebirth.
Within the womb, there are five stages, each changing every seven days: *kalala*—the Chinese term for which is "coagulated slime"—is the appearance of the first week.
*Arbuda*, meaning "bubble," is the appearance of the second week. This continues through *peśī*, *ghana*, and *praśākhā*.

Furthermore, among the four modes of birth, the egg-born corresponds to *saṃjñā* (perception), the womb-born corresponds to *sneha* (affection), the moisture-born corresponds to *saṃśleṣa* (adhesion), and the transformation-born corresponds to *viprayoga* (separation).

Thus it is said that they correspond according to what is appropriate. Disordered thought is called *saṃjñā*; the binding of craving is called *sneha*; the attachment of vital energy is called *saṃśleṣa*, for it arises through the adhesion of moisture;
and the evasion of form is called *viprayoga*, for it means departing from this life to be born elsewhere. Affection and perception are thus conjoined.
The [mode of] "leaving" (i.e., birth) is possessed by all who are born; this is stated merely in terms of the majority. As for why egg-birth is placed first:
it is because the movement of conceptual thought (saṃjñā) occurs first, while the reception of affective feeling (vedanā) arises later; furthermore, it includes both womb-birth and moisture-birth.

This text discusses "conceptualization," which refers to internal defiled conceptualization and not external pure conceptualization. Regarding "transformation" (nirmāṇa), it refers to transformation through the karma of molting or metamorphosis, and not the wondrous transformation produced by the mind (manomaya-nirmāṇa).

As for the mutual transformation and alternation of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), and of union and separation: sometimes feeling transforms into perception, and union transforms into separation;
thus, there is no fixed karma. An egg-born being may transform into a womb-born one, and a moisture-born being may transform into a transformation-born one;

thus, there is no fixed substance. Therefore, the karmic retribution one receives may involve ascent or descent; thus, there is no fixed realm of rebirth. This is the cause by which sentient beings continue their succession.
Pūrṇa, the conceptualization of craving and attachment forms a bond (extending to) these [beings], all of whom take theft and greed as their root.
(Wuxing says: "Desire-greed pervades the four modes of birth; here it refers specifically to the womb-born. Furthermore, the womb-born itself is pervasive;
here it is mostly distinguished by reference to human relations because they are easy to perceive. The strong kill the weak for the sake of food.")

It constitutes greed. If one does not nourish the mouth and belly [with such food], it belongs to the affliction of hatred (*dveṣa*). Regarding the question of why humans eat sheep and so forth: how does this differ from the greed for killing? The answer is:

setting aside the greed for killing for a moment, it concerns the repayment of prior debts. In terms of the past, they took [the lives of others] unrighteously regarding their bodies, lives, and wealth;
therefore, they come to devour one another in order to exact retribution for that theft.

Changshui said: "Parents and children do not gather together except through affection; they are not born except through desire. Among the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—the weak are preyed upon by the strong.
It is out of craving that the teachings were established. To take what is not given is called theft; furthermore, to take it secretly is also called theft."
Because humans eat sheep, it is taking what is not given. When the sheep dies and becomes a human, they come to devour one another; this is "taking.
That which is taken in the world is mutual devouring. This mutual devouring in the world is all theft and greed. Lust, killing, and theft—these three constitute the roots of karmic fruit.
"You owe me my life, and I shall repay you for your debt" (up to) "by these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue in succession.
(Supplementary Note: Regarding the two phrases "life-debt," the textual meanings are seen interchangeably; as in saying "you owe me my life" or "you repay my life," and "I owe you a debt.
The two phrases regarding "affection and pity" should likewise be seen interchangeably. This is precisely the mutual [conditioning]...)
[This is] the reason for its continuity). Wēn-líng says:
"The preceding [section] clarified the root of karmic results; this clarifies the reason for continuity. Debt is the reason for killing and stealing;
attachment and craving are the reasons. 'Only killing' below concludes by making it manifest."
Pūrṇa, these three kinds [of craving] (up to this point) thus proceed from this delusion, ending and beginning again. [Xie Li said:

"If one wishes to preserve the various objects, the attachment belongs to the mind. Because there are various desires, they assist attachment in manifesting its nature; therefore, they are able to cause death and birth to continue in succession."*] *Note: The bracketed portion is a commentary by Xie Li (攜李) on the preceding text.*

Wenling says: This summarizes the preceding text to conclude the answer regarding the karmic fruits of worlds and sentient beings—all of which have the "clarity of awareness" (*jue-ming*) as their fault.
"Clarity of awareness" refers to the nature of clear knowing; it is that which falsely constitutes "luminous awareness.

"The manifestation of characteristics" refers to establishing the objective world based on that luminosity. "Deluded seeing" refers to the production of your deluded subjectivity. This points to what is empty and false.
This refers to "Awakened Clarity. The previous question asked how the great earth suddenly arose and, at its end, begins again;
this passage fully restates those words and answers by pointing to Awakened Clarity.
Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous awakening [is thus], how could the outflows of conditioned phenomena ever arise again? (Wenling says:

The essence of awakening in sentient beings is no different from that of the Buddha. If, without cause, the various marks of conditioned existence were suddenly to arise, then since the Tathāgata has already realized the awakening of emptiness, when would he ever again give rise to conditioned existence? This is indeed a point that deludes ordinary minds; therefore—)
(Pūrṇa, *tèfǎnnàn*. (Gushan says: "Without cause" (*wúzhuàng*) means "without reason" (*wúgù*). Zizhong says:

"Subtle enlightenment" (*miàojiào*) refers to the essence that is neither true nor false. "Fundamentally subtle, enlightened, and luminous" refers to that which arises as delusion based upon the True.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "It is like a person who has lost their way... [until] awakening; when delusion is extinguished through awakening, delusion no longer arises.

(Xie Li said: "That sentient beings and Tathāgatas differ in their delusion and awakening, that habitual outflows exist or do not exist according to priority, that worlds arise and perish through beginning and end, and that purity and sudden arising are opposites—this is truly because false doubt acts as a tether, giving rise to erroneous confusion.")
Because of this cause, the views of extremes—namely, the views of annihilationism and eternalism—suddenly arise. Within this essence of awakening, one must inquire into the subtle delusions).

Wuxing said: "A 'village' (púluó) refers to a market town. The village serves as a metaphor for the nature-portion (xìngfèn), while north and south serve as metaphors for delusion and inversion. However..."
Since north and south have never been easily changed from the beginning, the nature of things is fundamentally without inversion. Therefore it is said: "Delusion originally has no root;
awakening does not give rise to delusion. The supplementary note says: "In the past, there was originally no delusion, yet there seems to be the awareness of delusion.
This means that originally there is neither delusion nor awareness; 'awareness' is precisely awakening. However, since one now attains awakening by means of delusion, there seems to be awareness."
Delusion is awakened; awakening is initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*). When awakening reaches its consummation, the initial and the fundamental are not different;
there is only the single wondrous awakening (*ekam adbhuta-bodhi*), and delusion no longer arises. This reveals that once one has awakened, one is no longer deluded.
It is also like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky (up to: when will the mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever appear again?
(Lectan said: "Once the deluded person has awakened, awakening does not give rise to further delusion. All such metaphors are raised to demonstrate the ultimate realization:
that awakening is devoid of the false mountains and rivers.")

Wenling says: "The cataract is a metaphor for deluded vision; the flowers are a metaphor for mountains and rivers; the extinction of the flowers in space is a metaphor for the wondrous emptiness of luminous awareness.
Regarding the passage beginning with 'The Buddha said,' it means that since one has already understood the metaphors, why persist in the previous doubts?"
Furthermore, just as gold ore may be mixed with refined gold (up to: so it is with bodhi and nirvāṇa).
[Ziqing says: Once it has already become gold, it no longer remains ore; the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is also like this.]
Wenling says: Gold is a metaphor for the fruit of Bodhi, whose awakening is unchanging; ashes are a metaphor for the fruit of Nirvana, whose virtue is non-arising.
When the fruit reaches the state of being unchanging and non-arising, it can be known that habitual outflows no longer arise. Previously, the village was used as a metaphor for not being deluded;
furthermore, the flowers in the sky were used as a metaphor for wondrous emptiness having no habitual tendencies. Thus, regarding the meaning of these four metaphors, the first two...

Clear understanding and practice are fundamentally free from delusion; delusion arises from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). The subsequent two metaphors of gold and ash clarify that habitual outflows and false conditions must be realized and then permanently severed.
If one were to cite only the former two [metaphors], there might be the fear that false conceptualization does not obstruct the True, and that afflictions can extinguish themselves spontaneously.

This establishes the refutation of nihilistic attachments; however, only the latter two [analogies] are cited here. Fearing that one might think awakening is fundamentally not pure and that its nature is inherently subject to the production of defiled views, four analogies are presented together, so that one may understand that although delusion and awakening are both illusory, this does not preclude cultivation and realization.
(An added note states: At the beginning of this fascicle, Pūrṇa had two questions. The first asked how various phenomena arise from that which is fundamentally pure;
the second asked how the four great elements, each being all-pervasive, can coexist within one another. What follows is the answer to the second question.)
Pūrṇa, as for what you asked [up to] "yet it does not reject those various manifestations":
Wuxing says, "This is like how the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha is fundamentally not the seven elements, yet it does not reject their manifestation.
Xiali says, "All manner of illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment; this is the substance."
"Although marks are empty, this does not preclude the manifestation of illusory marks.
Zhenji said: "Empty space is not the various marks, yet the various marks arise in dependence upon emptiness.

The true essence is not the four great elements, yet the four great elements are formed by means of the true essence. Since it was originally neither water nor fire, they do not obstruct one another."
Why is this? Pūrṇa (up to) why do you further ask about those that are not mutually compatible?
[The True Limit] says: "If illumination were produced by the sun, then it would be of the same color as the eye and should not be seen within empty space as a round sun.
If illumination were produced by empty space, then at midnight when there is no sun, that empty space should be luminous. [Supplementary Note: Regarding the various marks...]
"Delusion. Since there is nothing to point to, how much less can one interrogate it regarding the meaning of mutual sublation? This is like seeking flowers in the sky to produce fruit from the void.
Wēnlíng says: "The phrase 'therefore' indicates the various marks; the phrase 'in the mind' clarifies their mutual containment. Contemplating the fundamental nature of the marks..."
Delusion is false; even the subduing and extinguishing of it is false. When one contemplates that the nature of things is uniformly true, there is nothing that is not embraced.
Since this manifests everywhere, it is called "different regions"—referring to such things as the sun and clouds mentioned therein.
The true, wondrous, enlightened clarity is also like this... (up to) "if both are manifested through illumination, then both appear.
(Zizhong says: Because True Suchness does not cling to its own nature, it manifests various appearances according to conditions.
(Wenling says: This is like empty space, which has no form, yet does not refuse to be brought forth.)
Lectan said: "As for 'you take emptiness as clarity' and so forth: in terms of phenomena, it is like digging a well to bring forth empty space, or striking a fire-drill to produce fire.
In terms of karma, it is like movement forming the world and stillness becoming empty space;
when wind and metal rub against each other, there is light and fire. In terms of the mind, when deluded views of emptiness arise, then [there is...]"
Space appears; earth, water, fire, and wind are likewise. Therefore it is said: "Each individually brings forth illumination, and thus each individually appears.
"Individually" refers to before and after; "together" refers to simultaneity.
"How is it that they both appear together? Pūrṇa [said]... (up to) "they revolve in delusion and falsehood, having nothing upon which to rely.

(Gushan says: The sun is a metaphor for true nature; the water is a metaphor for the deluded mind; the sun within the water is a metaphor for the deluded environment; the two people are metaphors for deluded karma.
When they walk separately, they each proceed according to their karma and both set out together; when they follow along, the deluded environment appears to both. To observe them together is...)
First: Knowing that both are empty. Since the two [reflections] each move separately, one verifies that the one is illusory; thus it is said, "winding and turning in emptiness and falsity.

Wēnlíng says: This explains the phenomenon of simultaneous manifestation. Just as the shadow of the sun varies according to the person, so too do the seven great elements (mahābhūta) arise in accordance with conditions.
They differ from what existed previously and have no fixed standard; therefore, they should not be subject to censure or difficulty.
"Pūrṇa, because you take form to be empty (up to this point), you give rise to weariness and the appearance of the world.

(Wuxing says: Form comprises the four great elements; together with space, they constitute five. Previously, when Pūrṇa asked about the nature of earth, water, fire, and wind being perfectly interfused, he doubted that the natures of water and fire would not mutually overcome or extinguish one another—that is, their characteristics would conflict. [He did not doubt] empty space and the great earth...)
"Uniting with appearances" (meaning that appearances immediately usurp one's capacity).
Wēnlíng says: "To lose the true essence and differentiate conditioned reflections is called 'turning away from awakening and uniting with dust.
To realize that appearances are fundamentally illusory and to contemplate that nature is fundamentally real is called 'extinguishing dust and uniting with awakening.'"
"By means of this wondrous clarity, which neither perishes nor arises... (omitted)... I have thus brought forth the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous nature of True Suchness.
(Ziqing says: "Form and emptiness are the delusive appearances of the world; wondrous clarity is the wondrous and true nature.

Both are manifested from the Tathāgatagarbha and are originally one in perfect fusion. It is only because sentient beings turn their backs on the truth and unite with delusion that they become confined within worldly appearances.)"

Within this, the Buddhas extinguish delusion and merge with the Real; thus they wondrously attain the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, the one and the many respond to one another, and the small and the large contain one another.
They manifest jewel-adorned lands upon the tip of a hair and turn the wheel of Dharma within a speck of dust. Every phenomenon is unimpeded, and every dharma is as it truly is.
This is because when one contemplates appearances, one perceives delusion, which cannot be pointed out or described; yet when one contemplates the nature, it is fundamentally real. Thus...
"There is nothing that is not embraced.
Wuxing said: "Wondrous clarity" refers to the wisdom of tranquil illumination; "neither extinguished nor born" refers to the essence of wisdom being truly eternal.
These all are able to harmonize with the Tathāgatagarbha, which is that which is harmonized. As for the Tathāgatagarbha, it restates that which is harmonized.
"Principle is solely wondrous awakening and clarity" refers to the wisdom that is capable of unifying; "perfectly illuminating the dharma-realm" demonstrates its function of reflecting all things.

To illustrate this by analogy: the *tathāgatagarbha* is like the substance of a mirror, wondrous awakening and clarity are like the light of the mirror, and perfectly illuminating the dharma-realm is like the mirror manifesting images.
Though three, they are one; though one, they are three. As for their unity, they are equal in measure.
All of these clarify this meaning: that the one is the immeasurable, and the immeasurable is the one; that the large appears within the small, and the small appears within the large.

These constitute the four meanings of the general and the particular. "Without moving from the site of enlightenment, he pervades the worlds of the ten directions" refers to the one being the immeasurable.
"His body contains the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions" refers to the immeasurable... [the one].
The measure is one. To manifest a Jewel-King Land upon a single hair-tip, and to turn the Great Dharma-Wheel within a mote of dust, is to manifest the great within the small.
Manifesting a land on a hair-tip is to manifest the primary within the secondary; turning the wheel within a mote of dust is to manifest the primary based upon the secondary.
"Extinguishing the dust and merging with awakening," etc., summarizes the preceding meanings.

And the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and complete mind (up to: it is neither permanence, nor bliss, nor self, nor purity. (Guishan says: From "neither mind" up to "neither the realm of mental consciousness," this collectively negates the six realms of ordinary beings. "Neither clarity nor ignorance," etc., negates the realm of the pratyekabuddhas. "Neither suffering nor its origin," etc., negates the realm of the śrāvakas. "Neither knowing nor attaining," etc.)... [text continues] ...negates the realm of the bodhisattvas. "Neither the Buddha-nature nor the Buddha-realm," etc., negates the realm of the Buddhas. This is called the negation of the ten realms. It is neither knowledge nor attainment. It is neither the Buddha-nature nor the Buddha-realm. It is neither the Dharma-nature nor the Dharma-realm. It is neither the Sangha-nature nor the Sangha-realm. It is neither the nature of nirvana nor the realm of nirvana. It is neither the nature of liberation nor the realm of liberation. It is neither the nature of the path nor the realm of the path. It is neither the nature of cessation nor the realm of cessation. It is neither the nature of the fruit nor the realm of the fruit. It is neither the nature of the cause nor the realm of the cause. It is neither the nature of the effect nor the realm of the effect. It is neither the nature of the condition nor the realm of the condition. It is neither the nature of the support nor the realm of the support. It is neither the nature of the supported nor the realm of the supported. It is neither the nature of the subject nor the realm of the subject. It is neither the nature of the object nor the realm of the object. It is neither the nature of the perceiver nor the realm of the perceiver. It is neither the nature of the perceived nor the realm of the perceived. It is neither the nature of the knower nor the realm of the knower. It is neither the nature of the known nor the realm of the known. It is neither the nature of the seer nor the realm of the seer. It is neither the nature of the seen nor the realm of the seen. It is neither the nature of the hearer nor the realm of the hearer. It is neither the nature of the heard nor the realm of the heard. It is neither the nature of the smeller nor the realm of the smeller. It is neither the nature of the smelled nor the realm of the smelled. It is neither the nature of the taster nor the realm of the taster. It is neither the nature of the tasted nor the realm of the tasted. It is neither the nature of the toucher nor the realm of the toucher. It is neither the nature of the touched nor the realm of the touched. It is neither the nature of the thinker nor the realm of the thinker. It is neither the nature of the thought nor the realm of the thought. It is neither the nature of the cognizer nor the realm of the cognizer. It is neither the nature of the cognized nor the realm of the cognized. It is neither the nature of the mind nor the realm of the mind. It is neither the nature of the mental consciousness nor the realm of the mental consciousness. It is neither the nature of the eye nor the realm of the eye. It is neither the nature of the visible nor the realm of the visible. It is neither the nature of the ear nor the realm of the ear. It is neither the nature of the audible nor the realm of the audible. It is neither the nature of the nose nor the realm of the nose. It is neither the nature of the olfactory nor the realm of the olfactory. It is neither the nature of the tongue nor the realm of the tongue. It is neither the nature of the gustatory nor the realm of the gustatory. It is neither the nature of the body nor the realm of the body. It is neither the nature of the tactile nor the realm of the tactile. It is neither the nature of the intellect nor the realm of the intellect. It is neither the nature of the mental consciousness nor the realm of the mental consciousness. It is neither the nature of the sense-base nor the realm of the sense-base. It is neither the nature of the element nor the realm of the element. It is neither the nature of the aggregate nor the realm of the aggregate. It is neither the nature of the sense-field nor the realm of the sense-field. It is neither the nature of the dependent origination nor the realm of dependent origination. It is neither the nature of the emptiness nor the realm of emptiness. It is neither the nature of the provisional nor the realm of the provisional. It is neither the nature of the conventional nor the realm of the conventional. It is neither the nature of the ultimate nor the realm of the ultimate. It is neither the nature of the worldly nor the realm of the worldly. It is neither the nature of the supramundane nor the realm of the supramundane. It is neither the nature of the conditioned nor the realm of the conditioned. It is neither the nature of the unconditioned nor the realm of the unconditioned. It is neither the nature of the tainted nor the realm of the tainted. It is neither the nature of the untainted nor the realm of the untainted. It is neither the nature of the outflowing nor the realm of the outflowing. It is neither the nature of the non-outflowing nor the realm of the non-outflowing. It is neither the nature of the defiled nor the realm of the defiled. It is neither the nature of the pure nor the realm of the pure. It is neither the nature of the mundane nor the realm of the mundane. It is neither the nature of the transmundane nor the realm of the transmundane. It is neither the nature of the past nor the realm of the past. It is neither the nature of the future nor the realm of the future. It is neither the nature of the present nor the realm of the present. It is neither the nature of the internal nor the realm of the internal. It is neither the nature of the external nor the realm of the external. It is neither the nature of the near nor the realm of the near. It is neither the nature of the far nor the realm of the far. It is neither the nature of the coarse nor the realm of the coarse. It is neither the nature of the subtle nor the realm of the subtle. It is neither the nature of the small nor the realm of the small. It is neither the nature of the great nor the realm of the great. It is neither the nature of the limited nor the realm of the limited. It is neither the nature of the infinite nor the realm of the infinite. It is neither the nature of the one nor the realm of the one. It is neither the nature of the many nor the realm of the many. It is neither the nature of the same nor the realm of the same. It is neither the nature of the different nor the realm of the different. It is neither the nature of existence nor the realm of existence. It is neither the nature of non-existence nor the realm of non-existence. It is neither the nature of birth nor the realm of birth. It is neither the nature of death nor the realm of death. It is neither the nature of life nor the realm of life. It is neither the nature of extinction nor the realm of extinction. It is neither the nature of arising nor the realm of arising. It is neither the nature of ceasing nor the realm of ceasing. It is neither the nature of coming nor the realm of coming. It is neither the nature of going nor the realm of going. It is neither the nature of staying nor the realm of staying. It is neither the nature of abiding nor the realm of abiding. It is neither the nature of motion nor the realm of motion. It is neither the nature of stillness nor the realm of stillness. It is neither the nature of light nor the realm of light. It is neither the nature of darkness nor the realm of darkness. It is neither the nature of form nor the realm of form. It is neither the nature of formlessness nor the realm of formlessness. It is neither the nature of desire nor the realm of desire. It is neither the nature of form nor the realm of form. It is neither the nature of formlessness nor the realm of formlessness. It is neither the nature of the three realms nor the realm of the three realms. It is neither the nature of the four modes of birth nor the realm of the four modes of birth. It is neither the nature of the five destinies nor the realm of the five destinies. It is neither the nature of the six consciousnesses nor the realm of the six consciousnesses. It is neither the nature of the seven elements nor the realm of the seven elements. It is neither the nature of the eight consciousnesses nor the realm of the eight consciousnesses. It is neither the nature of the nine dwellings nor the realm of the nine dwellings. It is neither the nature of the ten stages nor the realm of the ten stages. It is neither the nature of the eleven sense-bases nor the realm of the eleven sense-bases. It is neither the nature of the twelve links of dependent origination nor the realm of the twelve links of dependent origination. It is neither the nature of the eighteen elements nor the realm of the eighteen elements. It is neither the nature of the twenty-two faculties nor the realm of the twenty-two faculties. It is neither the nature of the twenty-four conditions nor the realm of the twenty-four conditions. It is
"Those who [attain] it": it is not the principle attained by the wisdom of the two vehicles; it is not the *dāna* (generosity) and so forth; it is not the realm of the bodhisattvas.
"That which is not first the practice capable of approaching it" refers to that which is not the *pāramitās*; this collectively refers to that which is not the principle to be approached.

"Not the *Tathāgata*" (referring to the section below): it is not the realm of the Buddha; it is not first the person capable of realizing it—the three titles refer to this. Next, it is not the dharma realized: *nirvāṇa*.
These are the four virtues. *Tathāgata* means "Thus-Come One"; *Arhat* means "Worthy of Offerings"; *Samyaksaṃbuddha* means "Perfectly All-Knowing.
These constitute three of the ten titles [of a Buddha]. *Nirvāṇa* is the general term, while the four virtues are the specific ones.

Wenling says: Although one extinguishes the dust and manifests the truth, such that the one and the many, the small and the large, are all able to be as they are, the fundamentally wondrous and perfect essence has from the beginning undergone no change or variation;
therefore, it is "neither mind nor emptiness," and so on, up to "neither worldly nor world-transcending dharmas.
From "neither mind" to "neither fire" means it is not the seven elements or the five aggregates. Mind refers to the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), which subsumes [the others].
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). From "neither eye nor ear" up to "neither the sphere of mental consciousness," this refers to the eighteen spheres (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).

It also encompasses the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). These above constitute mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*). From "neither clarity nor ignorance" up to "neither the exhaustion of old age and death."

This refers to that which is not the dharma of the pratyekabuddhas. Pratyekabuddhas contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination; there is the characteristic of arising and the characteristic of cultivation and abandonment.
These are mentioned here together. From the stage of the pratyekabuddha up to nirvana, all are supramundane dharmas.
This is because it is neither mundane nor supramundane.
(Wenling says: This concludes the preceding and introduces what follows.
Gushan says: "Mundane" refers to the six realms of ordinary beings; "supramundane" refers to the four classes of noble ones. The principle of the *ālaya* is emptiness itself.
There are ten realms; therefore, [the preceding] was not [the case].
That is to say, the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamental luminosity of the mind, wondrous (up to) "it is permanence, it is bliss, it is self, and it is purity.

(Gushan says: The previous passage was entirely "not," which, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), reveals the Tathāgatagarbha; this passage is entirely "is," which, according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), [reveals it].)
[The text] elucidates the Tathāgatagarbha. This is because the principle of the Garbha is "non-existent yet existent," for the ten realms are completely non-existent [within it].
Wénlǐng says: "Although its essence is unchanging, its function is suchness; thus, mind is identical to dharmas, and dharmas are identical to mind."
Because these are both identical to and distinct from the mundane and the supramundane... they are neither identical nor non-identical, and thus neither identical nor non-identical. (Ziqing says:
Furthermore, the Dharma-realm is a single suchness, fundamentally devoid of names and marks. Due to delusion, there is the false; in opposition to the false, the "true" is spoken.
Once the false marks are contrasted, names and words do not cease. Following names to grasp at marks, how can one's inversions ever end? Therefore, based on words...)

Regarding the act of sending forth words: beginning with the non-sending of the characteristic of "not sending," proceeding to the sending of "not" itself, and finally remaining bound by names and phrases—none of these reach the ultimate principle of the One True [Dharma].

Only when one transcends both "is" and "is not," and reaches the state where there is neither "not" nor "not-not," such that the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases, does one manifest the One True Dharma-realm, the Tathāgatagarbha.
Wenling says: "Since it is 'not' yet 'immediate,' and 'immediate' yet 'not,' it is wondrous beyond thought and speech, and cannot be fathomed.
This passage may seem contradictory, yet each statement has its own intended meaning. The first says, 'The fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind,' which refers to its self-substance.
The second says, 'The originally luminous, wondrous mind,' which refers to its function. The final one says, 'The wondrously luminous, original mind.'"
This is spoken in terms of the synthesis of essence and function. The fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind is the source rather than the derivative;
it is perfect rather than pervasive; it is mind rather than matter; it is the truly pure and wondrous essence, and therefore it is not any phenomenon.

Original luminosity is the wondrousness of the mind: it is the origin rather than the source, it is luminosity rather than essence; it is the wondrous function of suchness, and therefore it is identical with all phenomena.

The wondrously luminous source of the mind is the luminosity of the wondrous; it is the source of this mind. When the provisional and the wondrous are observed together, one is thus free from both "is" and "is not," and is both "is" and "is not.
When the wondrous reaches this state, essence and function are perfectly merged, and the dust of sensory afflictions is utterly severed.
Yet the wondrous nature of the hidden mind is vast and free from flaw or blemish. Changshui said:
"The fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind—'neither mind nor emptiness,' etc.—clarifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by way of non-phenomena.

'Originally luminous, the mind is wondrous'—'just mind and just emptiness,' etc.—clarifies the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by way of phenomena. The wondrously luminous source of the mind transcends both 'just' and 'not just'; it is precisely [this]."
"Neither identical" refers to elucidating the Middle Way Truth by means of simultaneous negation and illumination. This concerns the non-duality of these two gates;

it is solely the one mind. Because it simultaneously negates both the ultimate and the conventional, it is said to be "neither identical nor non-identical. Because it simultaneously illuminates both the ultimate and the conventional, it is said to be "both identical and non-identical.
Since the three truths are of one essence, they are all said to be the Tathāgatagarbha.
[Supplementary Note: Regarding "this is neither identical nor not identical," it is further explained as "not separate from identity and not separate from non-identity"].
How do the sentient beings of the three realms of existence in the world [until] use worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
(Gushan says: "It merely refutes ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, but does not mention Bodhisattvas because [Śāriputra] Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra represents the Two Vehicles.
In reality, even Bodhisattvas of the partial teachings cannot fathom it; as the *Lotus Sūtra* states: 'Even non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas cannot know it.'"")

Letan said: "To bind the wondrous and cut off mind and speech is to rebuke their false conjectures; this is because as soon as one directs the mind or stirs a thought, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma.
It is like the lute, the harp, the *konghou*, and the *pipa*... [up to] ...clinging to and cherishing the Lesser Vehicle, considering a small attainment to be sufficient."

[Changshui said: "The lute and so forth metaphorize sentient beings; the exquisite sound metaphorizes the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; the skillful fingers metaphorize true wisdom; and 'producing' metaphorizes the manifestation of function.
You and sentient beings correspond to the aforementioned lute and so forth; the precious awakened true mind corresponds to the aforementioned exquisite sound.

Pressing the fingers is wisdom accords with principle; producing light is the great function manifesting before one. Your 'momentarily raising the mind,' etc., corresponds to the aforementioned [absence of sound]."
(Exquisite fingers). (Zizhong said: Regarding "Ocean Seal" (*Sāgara-mudrā*), the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states: "All forms and images existing in Jambudvīpa have their seals within the great ocean.
This metaphor illustrates how the nature-ocean of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body universally manifests all phenomena of the world.)
Zhendi said: "Though the sound of the lute is complete within it, it does not emerge without the fingers; though the human mind is perfect, it is not realized without a teacher.
The various methods mentioned previously were to reveal the Tathāgatagarbha—this is the Buddha pressing his fingers upon the strings.

That body, mind, and the myriad dharmas are, in their very place, radiantly clear—this is the Sea-Seal manifesting its light. Yet Pūrṇa and the others gave rise to interpretations based on the words and remained in doubt."

This confusion is the initial arising of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). It stems from the fault of failing to seek the unsurpassed path of enlightenment and instead cherishing the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Now, when the Master strikes [the student] with a direct blow, the truth is immediately manifest; yet scholars, following this, compete to give rise to wild interpretations.
This is all because the dust of the emotions is easily stirred up, causing one’s movements to involve doubt and delusion. Let it be known that this is the path to unsurpassed enlightenment.
In the Way, a single call and a single response are sufficient to clear and purify heaven and earth; how, then, could there be any further defilement or toil?
The myriad phenomena of Jambudvīpa all appear within the ocean; therefore, it is named the "Ocean-Seal" (Sāgaramudrā).
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata... [have] obscured our own wondrous clarity; this is what constitutes drowning. (The supplementary note states:

"In terms of proximity, this refers back to the preceding passage; in terms of distance, it refers back to the earlier section. This is because the previous text had not yet reached the meaning of 'manifesting according to karma,' and thus there arose the question:
'How could it suddenly arise? The Tathāgata then [responded] that taking delusion as the cause for luminous awareness... [the text continues with the phrase] "...because of luminosity.")
Śāriputra and the others answered him accordingly. Since Pūrṇa already knew that [the answer] was false, yet did not know for what reason there could be falsehood, he asked this question.
Wēnlíng says: "This question is raised by following the previous statement that each is 'perfectly complete. Once one has realized non-duality, it is further [clarified]."
This reveals the descent into delusion; yet, because they do not know the source from which this delusion arises, I ask that you exhaustively investigate its cause.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts... [up to] ...this person’s mind has become deranged, and there is no other cause."

(Gushan said: "The metaphor of looking in a mirror represents the deluded mind that speculates, delineates, and discriminates. The head in the mirror represents the grasping for deluded objects and deluded phenomena;
it is easy to become attached to them, just as eyebrows and eyes are easily seen. True principle is difficult to know, like scolding one's own head [for not being visible].

To turn away from awakening and toward delusion is like running madly without cause. As for the four realms of existence, they involve turning away from good and heading toward evil; as for humans and devas,")

Turning one's back on suffering and facing toward pleasure—both the Two Vehicles do this by turning toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while Bodhisattvas turn their backs on the extremes and face toward the Middle Way.
All these are termed "the mind of frantic wandering. "Frantic" is a metaphor for the nine realms of existence, wherein all grasping and rejecting arise solely from the deluded mind.
Wenling says: "Yajñadatta" means "Sacrificial Bestowal," as he was obtained by praying to a deity.

His love for his head in the mirror and his consequent frantic running represent how, due to grasping at a reflected image, one becomes deluded regarding the original reality and falsely follows the cycle of transmigration. The Supplemental Note says:
By citing Yajñadatta’s reflection in the mirror as a metaphor, it is stated that he ran frantically because [the head] was not there; this is intended to make known the nature of madness.
Since they arise without cause, one knows that delusion fundamentally has no origin.
The Buddha said: "The wondrous enlightenment is bright and perfect; it is fundamentally perfect, bright, and wondrous" (up to) "...the nature of delusion is thus; for what reason would it exist?"

(Zizhong said: "That various deluded thoughts arise through successive mutual causation is like one person suddenly speaking falsely, which is then passed down in succession until it reaches many people;
yet when one traces back to its origin, nothing real is found at all. (Xiali said:
"Birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday; they are what a person who has awakened describes as events within a dream.")
Wenling says: "The wondrous enlightenment is bright and perfect" refers to the fact that I and the Tathāgata are identical in our perfect fulfillment.
"Originally perfect, bright, and wondrous" means that fundamentally there is no deficiency and fundamentally there is no delusion; this is the original face of every person.
How can one allow the two types of delusion to cause such impairment? Consequently, one distinguishes between self and others, forcibly giving rise to hatred and attachment;

these various delusions become causes for one another, and the wheel of confusion turns without end. At the end of the section on "The Delusion of Consciousness," Fu-na regrets his past encounter with false thoughts and addresses the World-Honored One regarding all such delusions.
He seems to suggest that delusion has a cause from which it arises and that there is something within delusion that can be extinguished. Therefore, [the Buddha] tells him:
This is as explained below in the section on "The City. By restating the parable to clarify it further, it is shown that delusion has no cause and nothing can be extinguished.
You need only refrain from following the conceptualization of worldly karma and its fruits; what need is there for the arduous labor of cultivating and realizing through painful effort?
(Wu Xing said: "The three conditions refer to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct within the fruits of karma. The three causes refer to the three types of greed, such as killing, and so forth.
This very cause is what is termed 'the nature of madness. The Supplemental Note says:

'If you simply do not follow after the discrimination of worldly karma and its fruits, because the continuity of the three groups of sentient beings and the three conditions are severed, the three causes will not arise. The character "three" [is repeated here].)
"Conditioned by three causes" refers to the causal conditions for the three types of continuity. The causal conditions for continuity consist of ignorance, its objects, and so forth.
Ignorance, its objects, and so forth are the subtle fetters of affliction; they are what is meant by the term "sinews and gristle.
Once these causal conditions are severed, the mind of Bodhi is attained.
Wenling says: "The karmic fruits of sentient beings in the world are all reflections of the wondrous mind, like a head in a mirror.
To engage in discrimination is delusion; therefore, by not following discrimination, the nature of madness naturally subsides.

To take the karmic fruits of sentient beings in the world as the 'three conditions' means that the deluded mind arises by taking them as its objects. To take killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the 'three'..."
"Causes" means that it exists because of the deluded mind. That is to say, from various false thoughts, they mutually cause one another in succession;

therefore, when they are severed and do not arise, the nature of madness naturally subsides. "Subsiding is itself Bodhi," etc., means that by merely departing from delusive conditions, one is the Tathāgata.
"Ken" refers to the meat between the bones; "qing" refers to the sinews at the internal joints. (From the *Zhuangzi*)...
The son [Dian] had never encountered the "ken-king" (the tough sinews and joints) in his carving. Now, "ken-king" is used as a metaphor for subtle, minute delusions and fetters.

Indeed, the diligent cultivation and realization are undertaken solely because of false delusions; once the causes of falsehood have ceased, the knots of delusion naturally dissolve. Therefore, there is no need for the laborious cultivation and realization that would involve such "ken-king."
It is like a person who, within his own clothing (until) finally realizes that the divine pearl was not obtained from without.
(Wenling says: The metaphor of obtaining the pearl also illustrates that when delusion ceases, the truth manifests; there is no need for arduous cultivation or realization.)
Wuxing said: "The robe is a metaphor for the five aggregates; the pearl is a metaphor for the nature of the treasury. Due to ignorance, one fails to awaken;
because its wondrous function is lacking, one remains impoverished and exposed. The Buddha-realm is like one's own native land, while the nine realms are like other regions.

To seek the pleasures of humans and devas or to grasp at the benefits of the partial and small vehicles is like wandering about begging for food. When deluded sentiments are momentarily lost, true nature is fundamentally perfect—just as one may be poor [yet possess the treasure]."
The jewel is present. The Buddha is like the wise person; the teaching is like pointing out the jewel. When one realizes the principle and gives rise to its function, one attains great abundance;
only then does one know that true nature is not obtained from without.
At that moment, Ānanda was among the great assembly... (up to) "...I have attained awakening through causes and conditions.
[Lectan said: After Pūrṇa, Ānanda was again made to pose questions and challenges because, once all dharmas are clarified, one's cultivation will proceed without obstruction.
Furthermore, it was to demonstrate the gateway for cultivation and realization; thus, he was also the person suited to the occasion who initiated the inquiry.]
Wenling says: This successively builds upon the preceding text to raise a difficulty, resolving doubts for later students.
Above, it was stated that "when conditions cease, causes do not arise"—this is the principle of direct causes and conditions. Why then would the previous statement be suddenly discarded?
If one now discards causes and conditions, then the heterodox doctrine of spontaneous existence (*svabhāva*) would be correct.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just as within the city... (up to) "...the principle of natural causality is exhausted herein.

[Xie Li said: "To mistake the head for the reflection is entirely due to the causal conditions of a deluded nature. If the reflection were extinguished and the agitation vanished, then the original nature of bodhi—how could it be obtained from without?"]
Wenling said: "Once the cause of madness has been extinguished, the original nature naturally emerges. Prior to the state of madness, both were fundamentally non-existent.
Viewed from this perspective, all that is called 'causality' or 'spontaneity' was originally non-existent; they all arise based on the delusion of madness.
Therefore, it is said that the ultimate principle is exhausted here."
Ānanda, the head of Yan-ruo-da-duo (Śaṇḍha) was originally natural; for what reason did he become terrified of his own head and run about in a frenzy?
(Wenling says: This uses causes and conditions to refute the notion of "naturalness.")
Letan said: "That which is 'spontaneous' (ziran) is inherently natural; it does not depend on causes and conditions.
If it were inherently spontaneous, then whether one is mad or not mad would have nothing to cause it, and thus it would not be self-originated.
Why, then, must one depend on the causes and conditions of looking into a mirror before one runs mad? This calculation of spontaneity has fallen into error."
If one goes mad due to the causal conditions of one's own head, [and yet] it has never undergone any change, why rely upon causal conditions?
(Supplementary Note: Upatiṣya did not see his own head and, believing he had lost it, ran about in a frenzy.
Yet his head was originally there; it was never lost simply because he looked in a mirror. This is true even more so for others; moreover, looking in a mirror does not cause one to go mad.)
"In that case, your madness is spontaneous and has nothing to do with causes and conditions.

Wēnlíng says: "This uses spontaneity to refute causes and conditions. If one was originally not mad and became mad only because of causes and conditions, then since one was originally not lost, why would one become lost because of causes and conditions? Since the head is not lost, it is simply due to..."
If one is deluded and arrogant, then the calculation of causes and conditions falls away.
Fundamentally, madness is natural; fundamentally, there is innate madness and fear. (Up to: Since the head is fundamentally without delusion, why run about in a frenzy?
(Xie Li said: "This is the doctrine of the spontaneous nature of the destruction of causal conditions.
Wenling said: "If madness and fear were based on spontaneity, then madness and fear would be inherently present.
However, since there is nothing hidden [within them], they are not inherently mad. If madness and fear were not based on spontaneity, then the head would originally have no delusion."
Why do you run about in such a frenzy? It is not that you were originally not mad; yet, since you were not originally mad, it is also not the case that you were not originally mad.
From this, one can know for certain that all theories concerning natural causes and conditions are merely false constructs.
"If one awakens to the original head and recognizes the deluded running" (up to this point) is only then called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
(Gushan says: "If one awakens to the original reality, then one knows that all delusions are fundamentally unrelated.
For one who has truly seen their nature, all delusive conditions are suddenly and utterly severed; it is by means of this that one attains great liberation.")

(Zizhong said: "In the preceding text, the Buddha stated that when conditions are severed, madness ceases, and this cessation is itself Bodhi. Ānanda suspected that Bodhi is obtained through causes and conditions;

he feared that if one were to abandon causes and conditions, it would instead belong to the realm of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the Buddha again raised the analogy of madness to refute [this view] repeatedly.
Furthermore, if one awakens to one's original head and recognizes the deluded running about, then both causes and conditions and spontaneity are [seen for what they are]."

Conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, I say that because the three conditions are severed, it is the bodhicitta; as it is said, "Because conceptual proliferation is severed, it is the bodhicitta.
[The section on] bodhicitta follows below, where it will again be explained in detail as the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
Wenling said: Within the mind of bodhi, there is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing, nor is there anything that is "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*).
If one claims that the mind of bodhi arises while the mind of arising and ceasing ceases, this is merely arising and ceasing, not bodhi.

If one claims that both arising and ceasing are exhausted and that there is a state of spontaneity within the path of non-exertion (*anābhoga*), then by reason of this, one will clarify that the spontaneous mind gives rise to arising and ceasing.

The extinction of the mind—this too is arising and ceasing, and is not Bodhi. Furthermore, to point back toward that which is without arising or ceasing and call it "spontaneous" (svabhāva) is entirely conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It is like saying there is "conjunction" because of the mixing of various elements, yet pointing back to that which is not a conjunction and calling it "original nature.
All such things are falsely established through duality as conceptual proliferations.
The Dharma is simply to remain far removed from both "thus" and "not thus," as well as from "conjoined" and "not conjoined. Furthermore, there is no mind that intends such distancing;
this is the truly effortless path (*anābhoga-mārga*), the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
"Bodhi and Nirvana still lie far away" (up to) "...like the sands of the Ganges, they only increase frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Letan said: "This passage reprimands their false conceptualizations and frivolous proliferations. As long as frivolous proliferation is not severed, the deluded mind has not ceased;
thus it is difficult to accord with Bodhi. Therefore it is said that 'Bodhi and Nirvana still lie far away. If one does not pass through..."
"Though one has cultivated and realized [the truth] for kalpas, and though one upholds many sutras and subtle principles, it only serves to increase frivolous proliferation.
(The supplementary note states: "This rebukes Ānanda’s false conceptualization.")
"Although you speak of causes and conditions and spontaneity (up to) being far removed from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love.

(Gushan says: "This means to cause you to attain liberation and leave behind the chamber of lust. (Gushan says: "To cultivate the karma of the outflow-free [anāsrava] is to perfectly cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
thus one does not fall into the two kinds of birth-and-death, nor does one lose the meaning of the Three Truths. This is the principle.")

Since the untainted (*anāsrava*) is profound, the aversion to and attachment to [conditioned] reception are not shallow. To abandon the false is to realize the true; to leave behind phenomena and conform to principle—these are all termed "aversion and love. Lektam said:
"Whether through causes and conditions or spontaneously, this may be beneficial for discrimination, but it is of no benefit to the Way. Extensive learning is foremost [in its application]."

This is beneficial for reputation but not beneficial for reality; therefore, even if one cultivates and maintains it through the accumulation of kalpas, it is not equal to practicing untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) for a single day.
Untainted karma is the *Śūraṅgama* Samādhi. One who attains this samādhi eternally extinguishes all outflows (*āsrava*), and thus becomes free from the suffering of hatred and attachment.
"Such as Mātanga, who was formerly a courtesan... (down to) how can you deceive yourself and still linger in watching and listening?
(Zizhong said: "To employ wisdom to dispel emotion, yet one still sinks into the sea of desire; to use cessation to extinguish [the mind], yet one remains stuck in the function of that cessation.
Even until there is nothing left to dispel—when the Way accords with non-action, the essence is settled and the principle is exhausted—this is the ultimate return to the source. (Wuxing...)

It is said: Relying on various masters, the Sūtra has been divided into the stages of understanding and practice; the preceding section concludes with the opening of understanding, while the subsequent section demonstrates practice.
Thus, for those of superior faculties and sharp instruments who attain realization upon hearing [the teaching], the general essence of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is already complete.

However, for those of middling or inferior capacities, they must further await the discussion of practice, contemplating it and cultivating it accordingly. Therefore, [the Buddha] provisionally employs Ānanda and others to request entry into the jeweled chamber; thus it begins:
Extensively demonstrating the path of samādhi. Wénlíng says:
"As in the case of Mātanga below," this clarifies the swift efficacy of perfuming untainted karma.

"Past causes" refers to the causes of suffering from craving throughout successive lifetimes. "Emerging from the entanglements" refers to Mātanga; "receiving a prediction" refers to Yaśodharā. As it is said:

Why this reproach? It is to rebuke Ānanda, causing him to abandon the root of suffering and cultivate the path free from outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*), so that he does not allow craving and attachment to remain within his mind and eyes.

From the initial discernment of the true and the false and the illumination of the nature of awakening, up until the profound investigation of the myriad dharmas and the resolution of all doubts and obstructions, it is intended that his faith and understanding become authentic as the "mind of the causal ground. Once the causal mind is truly authentic...

This is because it enables the complete realization of the fruits of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). The preceding sutra, which constitutes the section on the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), concludes here;

the following text begins separately as the section on the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). For although one may perceive the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it cannot be realized without cultivation.
Therefore, immediately following the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the previous section, the gateway to the gates of practice is now revealed.
When Ānanda and the great assembly heard the Buddha’s instruction—[extending] to "leading those who are submerged in darkness out of the sea of suffering"—Wuxing remarked:
"Regarding 'doubts are eliminated and the mind awakens to the true reality,' this was stated in a verse at the end of the third fascicle to describe the benefits.

If it refers to realization through awakening (*pratyakṣa-bodha*), then this constitutes the increase of the Path (*mārga-vardhana*). Even if it refers to understanding through comprehension (*avabodha*), how could there not be realization here? Thus we know [this]."
"Please exercise skillful means to initiate this [work]. Wuxing said:

"The delusions have been dispelled and the mind has attained awakening; body and mind are light and at ease. This is the benefit of revealing the luminous nature of awareness and decisively resolving doubts and obstructions.
To provide instruction through manifold methods is the unsurpassed great compassion; it washes away my defilements and brings about purification."
"O King of Pure Jewels, World-Honored One, although I have now received such a Dharma-sound (up to: attained the dhāraṇī for entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision)," [Guishan says:
"The *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies three dhāraṇīs, which correspond to the three meanings of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way. Now, I request one..."]

The three contemplations of the mind encompass the gate of subduing thought and formation. Desiring to enter the first stage (*bhūmi*), one simultaneously develops the three wisdoms; hence it is called "the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Wēnlíng says:

"Losing one's nature is like being a traveler in a lodging; seeing one's nature is like finding a magnificent mansion. To see one's nature and not cultivate it is like having obtained [a treasure]..."
The house cannot be entered; therefore, I request the path of the Tathāgata’s original aspiration for the mind, hoping thereby to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Nirvana without remainder is the perfect fruit; the path of the original aspiration for the mind is the perfect cause.
Since one has already seen one's nature, yet still seeks to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it is because seeing provides the opening and cultivation leads to awakening and entry.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those in the assembly... (up to)... because from beginning to end there is no destruction or extinction.
(Changshui says: "The wondrous samādhi" refers to the *Śūraṅgama* Samādhi; the "two determinate meanings" refer to the fundamental nature of the karma of the causal mind.
(Wuxing says: Within emptiness and detachment, all are termed "arising and ceasing"; within arising and ceasing are emptiness and the provisional—this is called the Buddha...)

Vehicle. The *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that while Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom, it is precisely because all phenomena are subject to transformation and extinction that this is so;
this serves as a metaphor for the impermanence of the essence of delusion. That emptiness does not decay or perish serves as a metaphor for the eternal abiding of true nature. (Xielü said:
Previously, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it was shown that the stage of arising and ceasing is taken as the foundation for the initial aspiration toward awakening; [the state of] neither ceasing nor...)
"Birth" [is used] to harmonize with the Tathāgatagarbha as being the same; "birth-and-death mind" is used to seek the fruit of eternal abiding, which constitutes the difference).
Regarding the passage "You should illuminate all vessels below," it means you should first examine that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are none other than illusory and false.

Taking your own body as the example, it is the very source of illusion and falsehood; there is only the profoundly still and perfect true essence, which ultimately never perishes or decays. This is...

It serves as the true foundation. The substance of the delusory is impermanent and will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction; the true nature is eternally abiding—how could it ever suffer decay or ruin?
Thus, the solid characteristics within your body constitute earth (and so on, up to) your five turbid layers, which are likewise thus.

(Gushan said: "From these four entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) to the five turbidities (*kaṣāya*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are bound together to form the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

By means of the four great elements, the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) are formed, with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) situated in their midst. It enables the eye to see, the ear to hear, and the nose, tongue, and body to perceive;
the mind then examines causes and follows forms and sounds, whereby there arise sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Thus, the five [aggregates] are established.)

The colors of the *skandhas* constitute consciousness and mark the end. Because the five *skandhas* obscure that profound, perfect [nature], there are the five layers of turbidity, such as the kalpas and so forth.
Wénlǐng says: "The four great elements form a body of false and illusory delusion; they bind the nature and entangle it. The five [elements] are woven together to produce views and perceptions."
This delusion muddies the limpid clarity into turbidity and entangles one in the root of birth and death. Turbidity constitutes the root of afflictions and karma;

therefore, one should examine and clarify this thoroughly. It is like clear water: the clear water represents the nature of limpid, luminous awareness, while the dust and sand represent afflictions, delusions, and karma.
These natures do not follow one another, for the true and the false, and the pure and the defiled, are distinct. Worldly people lack the wisdom that transcends the world.
Thus, delusions arise and turbid the clarity, causing the nature to become muddled.

(Xingfu said: "Clear water" is a metaphor for the perfectly湛 (zhan) and wondrous mind; "dust, soil, ash, and sand" are metaphors for the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and the phenomena of birth—the five layers that confuse the truth. Therefore, the five aggregates are singled out.)
"Ānanda, you see empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions... this is the first layer, called the *kalpa-turbidity* (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

(Gushan says: This turbidity depends upon the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Now, the four great elements, the five sense organs, and the five sense objects are all collectively termed the aggregate of form.)"
