Now, although the visual faculty perceives the dust of space, the speaker explains this by means of the meaning of turbidity. Why is it called the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (age-turbidity)?
Because all four phases—formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness—are termed "ages" (*kalpa*), the perception of space is designated as the age-turbidity.
Wenling says: Awareness is not empty form; it is through a single thought of non-awakening that one falsely perceives the appearance of emptiness.

Because this gives rise to pervasive delusion, the seeing and the emptiness are not distinguished. Because they are not distinguished, there is "emptiness" that lacks substance, as it is mixed with seeing.
There is "existence" (form) that lacks awareness, as it is mixed with emptiness. This is the initial arising of clarity—the appearance of the primordial chaos.
Therefore, this constitutes the first layer. Nirvāṇa is called "without weaving. Weaving refers to the intermingling of two things, the sense of constructing through warp and woof.
The essence of nirvāṇa is intrinsically pure; it does not involve various conditions and is free from the act of weaving.
Now, one weaves the view of non-awakening with the essence of non-emptiness, and with that view of non-awakening, one weaves [the essence].

The essence of space is such that one falsely perceives it as empty while both [space and its perceived object] lack actual reality. Thus, when the earth loses its obstructive nature, does this not cloud the true nature?
Your body currently manifests with the four great elements as its substance; this is the second layer, called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*).

(Xie Li said: "The true nature is vast and limpid; fundamentally, there is neither seeing nor cognition. Because the four great elements coalesce and form obstructions as sense organs, seeing and cognition arise.
Thus, the vast limpidity is blocked and the four great elements revolve, whereby awareness and knowledge are produced. This is what is called 'mutual entanglement'. )
Gushan said: "This turbidity depends upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Now, that which experiences an object is called sensation, and it is of six kinds;
that is to say, the six sensations arise based on the conditions of the six contacts (*sparśa*). These six sensations are then obstructed by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)."

Therefore, they cause obstruction and hindrance. This is why seeing does not transcend form and hearing does not go beyond sound. The four great elements are whirled about by the six sensations, which causes the arising of cognitive awareness.
When these two factors interweave, they falsely constitute the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Because perceiving objects leads to the reception that turbidly obscures the true nature, it is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
Furthermore, within your mind, there is the recollection, cognition, and rehearsal [of objects]—this is the third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
(Changshui says: "Recollection refers to past objects; cognition refers to present sensory realms; rehearsal refers to future objects. (Xielü says:)
The consciousness of cognition recites; its habitual practice consists of wisdom and continuity, which grasp and conceptualize named phenomena.

From this, within the internal divisions of the nature, the six faculties of cognition arise; externally, within the divisions of the environment, the six objective realms manifest. The faculties and objects entangle one another, thereby vexing the profound nature—this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

Gushan said: This turbidity depends upon the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception). The characteristics of the objects perceived by the perceiving subject are called "perception" (*saṃjñā*), and there are six kinds.
That is to say, grasping the characteristics of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) that are perceived constitutes the six perceptions. Their nature manifests as seeing;
that is, they are able to grasp the six perceptions, while allowing the six sense-objects to appear—this refers to the characteristics of the six sense-objects that are grasped. By means of this...
These characteristics interweave, falsely forming the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Once one becomes attached to what is perceived, the agitation becomes even more severe than before.
Since this muddies the true nature, it is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Furthermore, that your arising and ceasing continue without rest from morning until evening—this is the fourth layer, called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
(Gushan says: This turbidity relies upon the mind of fabrication within the *saṃskāra-skandha* [aggregate of formations], which is able to lead toward the realms;

it is thus called the "activity of formations. There are six types of these. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, they are described as the "six volitions" (*ṣaḍ-cetanā*). Volition is itself karma; that is to say, regarding the six perceptions...)
Thereafter, each gives rise to unwholesome karma, wholesome karma, and immovable karma.
Wēnlíng says: "Arising and ceasing without pause constitutes *saṃskāra* (formative activity). Because the characteristics of these activities shift and flow, they are called the 'movement of karma.

Deluded thoughts and cognitive views are the very substance of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, the realms of existence constantly change; accordingly, one undergoes birth within the various destinies."
This is why they are called sentient beings.
Your seeing and hearing fundamentally possess no distinct natures (up to: "this is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of life"). [Xie Li said:

Seeing and hearing are originally tranquil and perfect, yet they become differentiated; therefore, they fundamentally have no distinct natures. The various sensory objects obstruct the perfect fusion.]
Because its substance is thus, it forms differences without a beginning; because its self-nature is observed as the same true permanence, it is called "form" (*xiàng*).
When observing through its own function, one knows that arising and ceasing occur alternately; therefore, it is said they are "opposed. (Wuxing says:
The five turbidities, from the subtle to the coarse, are possessed by all that has birth—namely, the root of birth and death, which is false and extinguishes birth.)
Gushan said: "This turbidity depends upon consciousness (*vijñāna*). That which discerns the objects of perception is called consciousness.
There are six kinds of consciousness; these are the six consciousnesses. 'Fundamentally there is no difference in nature' means that the mind of discernment is one and the same.

'The various cities are separated and distinct' means that because the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are not identical, they draw forth the production of the six consciousnesses; hence it is said, 'without form.'"

"Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) know each other within their nature," which explains that fundamentally there is no differentiated nature. "In their functioning they turn away from one another," which explains that there is no manifest form of being ordinary.
The eye does not distinguish sound, and the ear does not distinguish form; this is what is meant by turning away from one another. Regarding the loss of the standard for sameness and difference:
when one speaks of their sameness, their functions turn away from one another; when one speaks of their difference, their natures are known to each other.

Therefore, there is no fixed standard. By means of this interweaving, one falsely constructs the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*), wherein consciousness dwells and life-force (*jīva*) exists; when consciousness departs, life-force fades away, and the true nature becomes turbid.
Hence, it is called the turbidity of life-force (*jīva-kaṣāya*).
"Ānanda, you now wish to cause seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition (up to) all to accord with the pure and wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*.

(Wuxing says: By means of the nature of perfect stillness, one turns back the deluded mind; this refers to practicing the three types of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), illuminating the realms of the two truths, subduing and severing birth-and-death, and realizing non-birth-and-death.
'Subduing' refers to the preceding stage of causes, which encompasses the ten stages of faith.)"

Subsequently, the lower fruits are attained through both partial and full realization. The "vessel of stillness" refers to the mind of śamatha and vipaśyanā. Prior to this, faith is still shallow; as one enters into faith, it gradually deepens.
The sand and soil settle of their own accord, for coarse impurities fall away first. When clear water appears before one, the Three Truths seem to manifest.
(Xie Li said: "The minds of sentient beings are fundamentally pure, like the clarity of water; they are merely turbid because they are defiled by adventitious dust. Therefore it is said:
'If this were not subject to defilement and confusion, all would naturally be liberated. If this were not subject to purification, spiritual effort would bear no fruit.
It is neither defiled nor non-defiled; it is neither pure nor non-pure. The nature of the mind is originally pure.")
"Therefore, it is defiled by adventitious afflictions. (Gushan says: "All transformations and manifestations are responses to the capacities of sentient beings;

the manifestation of forms across the ten realms are all pure functions. Thus it is said that they do not constitute afflictions. Since function is identical to essence, it is said that they are all in accord with nirvana.)"

Wenling said: "Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing are the six faculties of sensory reception (*ṣaḍ-āyatanāni*). Permanence, bliss, self, and purity are the wondrous virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
Birth-and-death and its fundamental source are the karmic functions of the five turbidities (*pañca-kāṣāya*).

Now, one who wishes to turn back from delusion and accord with reality must first select and eliminate the deluded root of birth-and-death, and rely upon the nature of non-arising, non-ceasing, perfect, and profound stillness to accomplish this task. As it is said:

To clarify turbid water, one must use a still vessel; by causing the water to settle and revolve, its false delusions are suppressed so that the original awakening returns, just as stillness causes sand and soil to sink, allowing the clear water to manifest before one. This, however, merely suppresses adventitious afflictions.
For while the water is being caused to revolve and settle, it is not yet the true nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. And when that [nature] is attained...
When the awakening of the original, fundamental, true luminosity possesses the nature of being without birth or extinction, then the root of ignorance is forever severed.

Consequently, the aspect of the awakening’s profound clarity becomes pure and refined; all transformations and manifestations no longer constitute afflictions. It is like pure water from which the mud has been removed:
no matter how much it is stirred, it can never again become turbid. Only then can it serve as the mind for the causal ground. This is the causal mind.
Thus, the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition will be without exception perfect, and the wondrous virtue of nirvana will be without exception attained.
Therefore, one must not fail to examine the causal mind with care.
The second meaning is: "If you all truly desire [to reach]... how shall you subdue [them] and attain the rank of a Tathāgata? (Supplementary Note:

The first meaning examines the arousal of the mind at the causal stage; therefore, it points to the karmic functions of the five turbidities as the root of birth-and-death—that is, the extinction and arising of the false.
It instructs one to select and revolve them, thereby relying on the perfect and profound stillness so that no further birth occurs.)

The nature of cessation is established to complete its function. Next, following the command to examine the root of afflictions, the text also incorporates the intent of selecting the perfect faculty (*indriya*).
Therefore, it subsequently identifies the six faculties—the thieves and robbers who plunder the house—as the root of afflictions.

This is followed by the principle of the mutual interpenetration of the worlds, which fully reveals the quantitative measures of the merits of the six faculties and determines their relative superiority and inferiority. Next—
This is merely to clarify and enable one to understand what is to be discerned).
Lektan said: "Ignorance initiates karma; craving and grasping moisten rebirth; the six consciousnesses perform the action, while the ālayavijñāna receives it."
Latent, they constitute the root of afflictions; manifesting, they become the false roots of sense organs and objects.

Only by knowing them can one subdue them; only by subduing them can one attain the fruit. "The arising of karma moistens rebirth" refers to the afflictions. "Who acts and who receives? investigates the root.
This implies that the six sense organs act and receive the results themselves.
"Ānanda, observe those in the world who understand how to untie the knots... [yet] they cannot transcend the vessel-world. (Wu-xing says:

The six external sense-objects and the six internal consciousnesses are all induced and brought together by the eyes and other faculties; therefore it is said that "the six are the intermediaries for thieves.
The afflictions they give rise to harm the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore it is said that "they plunder the family treasure themselves. Because of this...
Because afflictions arise from the six sense organs, they initiate karma and moisten rebirth, resulting in the world of sentient beings that has no beginning.

Wénlǐng says: "Observe this below" explains that one must know the locus [of these phenomena]. To cite the meaning of emptiness is to say that if there were no bondage (*saṃyojana*), there would be no liberation;
yet who is able to be without bondage? "Then you... and so forth indicates the false nature of the sense organs and their objects.
This is perversion. The six media, such as the eyes, are the false faculties. The six thieves, which they attract, are the false objects.
To plunder one's own true nature is perversion.
Ānanda, why is it called the world of sentient beings? (Up to: each possesses twelve hundred merits.
(Zizhong said: "This is based on the fact that the nature of the six faculties' capacity for discernment is identical; therefore it is said that each possesses twelve hundred merits.
Below, this is contrasted with the function of discerning the six sense-objects, which differs; thus, the merits are entirely unequal. Does this not accord with what was stated in the preceding text:
'In their nature they know one another, and in their functions they respond to one another'? Master Kuò [explains] this in terms of the three [natures]... )

In the four directions of the world, there are five faculties and five objects, totaling one hundred and twenty-one. When each faculty and object is permeated by [the seeds of] cultivation, they form ten categories;
thus, sentient beings constitute one thousand two hundred. Master Yuan criticized this, while Master Jie approved it. Furthermore, Master Min said:
within each of the twelve [links], all ten wholesome deeds are present, forming one hundred and twenty; within each of these wholesome deeds, the ten "thusnesses" (yǒurúshì) are complete.
There are twelve hundred [verses]. However, the Buddha’s intent is difficult to fathom, and human sentiments diverge; furthermore, there is no definitive evidence as to who is most correct.
As for Zizhong, Gushan, and Changshui, they merely calculate the totals, yet their methods of transformation and repetition differ.

Although I have provided my own interpretation, I also do not dare to equate it with their specific doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). May future sages remain impartial and follow only that which is good. (Supplementary Note)
It is said: "Up and down have no fixed positions" means that what we designate as up and down are simply the upper and lower directions among the four cardinal points.
Apart from these, there is no other up or down; therefore, it is said they have no fixed position. "The center has no fixed direction" refers to the middle of the four intermediate corners (*koṇa*).
A corner is named by the intersection of two directions; since it belongs to both directions simultaneously, it is said to have no fixed direction.
(Wenling says: The world of sentient beings also possesses four directions, namely left, right, front, and back.

"World" (*loka*) refers to the successive transition through the three time periods; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to each abiding in its own fixed position. There are ten realms and three temporal periods.)
That which is possessed by a single body naturally involves mutual interpenetration; thus it is said that within the body, worlds trade with and interpenetrate one another.

Although the directions of the realms are ten, the constant numbers are only four. Because these three and four mutually interpenetrate, it is said that they revolve through the transformations of the three periods of time.
Thus, there are three layers: from one layer to ten, ten layers to a hundred, and a hundred layers to a thousand; these form twelve hundred [layers], each of the six sense-faculties possessing them.
However, this is merely a provisional reliance on worldly discourse to manifest the general outline of its wondrous function.

As for the state where the six are liberated and the one is extinguished, such that they are used interchangeably in perfect illumination—how could such a thing be reached by any calculation or quantity? Wuxing said: "This is based on..."

The twelve transmigrations and transformations together constitute three layers. As for the "ten, hundred, thousand," this is merely a general enumeration of the method of increasing numerical values—meaning that one increases to ten, ten increases to a hundred, and so forth.
Now, taking the engagement with the world as a model to clarify these three layers: first, regarding the four directions, each is discussed in terms of the three periods of time, thus forming twelve.
Second, in the three times of the eastern direction, one transforms into ten, becoming thirty. The same applies to the south, west, and north.
Thus, with thirty in each of the four directions, they become one hundred and twenty. Third, in the thirty [units] of the eastern direction, ten transform into a hundred, becoming three hundred.
The same occurs for the other three directions. Thus, with three hundred in each of the four directions, they become...
One thousand two hundred [verses]. By applying this to the world’s engagement with the directions, the analogy can be understood.

This is likely because the Tathāgata merely pointed to the world where the six sense faculties of ordinary beings and their objects are interwoven and the worlds themselves intersect. From the coarse to the subtle, he proceeded up to three layers to manifest his virtue.
The general intent is to let it be known that what is presently seen, heard, sensed, and cognized occurs moment by moment.
All these involve the coarse and subtle characteristics of the phenomenal world.
Ānanda, you should further determine the relative superiority and inferiority among them... (up to) you should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits.
(Zizhong said: "Each of the four cardinal directions is two hundred [units], and each of the four corners is one hundred.
What is currently seen by the eyes—the front, left, and right—constitutes three sides totaling six hundred. Adding the two preceding corners, which total two hundred, makes eight hundred in all.
Only the rear side of two hundred and the two rear corners of two hundred are not seen; therefore, it is said to be 'two-thirds'").
Wenling says: First, he reveals the falsity of the weaving [of the six sense organs] in order to clarify the origin of the knots of the faculties;
next, he distinguishes their relative superiority and inferiority in order to clarify the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, so that one may know what to choose.
Just as the ear listens all around to the ten directions without omission, [it reaches] the fulfillment of one thousand two hundred merits.
(Letam said: "The previous statement that the nature of the six faculties' discernment is the same is why their merits are each one thousand two hundred;
this present statement that the nature of the six objects' discernment is different is why their merits are incomplete and unequal.")
Wenling says: Because it can hear all-pervasively, its function is complete. As for "moving as they do," when one follows their movement, there appears to be near and far;
yet in one's own stillness, all-pervasive hearing is boundless.
Just as the nose smells while the inhalation and exhalation pass through, one should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits.

(Changshui says: When the inhalation and exhalation intersect within, they together form three parts; each part consists of four hundred [merits]. Because the intersection is missing, there are only eight hundred.)

Wenling says: "When it goes out, it can grasp fragrances; when it comes in, it can smell fragrances. Within this going and coming, there is no capacity [of its own]; thus, it lacks the middle function.
It is like the tongue proclaiming and exhausting all the worlds... (up to) perfecting one thousand two hundred merits."
(Gushan said: "To grasp it is to depart from speech; do not deliberate upon its flavor. If one grasps its flavor, its efficacy is inferior, because it involves cognition through synthesis.")
Wenling says: "The objects known by mundane and supramundane wisdom can only be fully expressed through the tongue. Although these words are limited, the principles they convey are inexhaustible.
For example, when the body perceives touch and recognizes what is adverse or favorable—[one should know that] the body possesses only eight hundred merits."
(Gushan says: "To be separated from the one and united with the two" means that in separation, the lack of one part is not known;
in union, it depends upon the cognizing faculty to perceive whether there is opposition or conformity; therefore, both parts must be present).
Wenling says: "To depart from one part is to unite the two full parts; this is called 'departing from the one and uniting the pair.
As it is said, 'The mind-king silently accommodates the ten directions and the three periods of time,' up to 'perfectly complete with one thousand two hundred merits.'"
Wuxing said: "The mental faculty (*manas*) perceives objects throughout the three periods of time—namely, the past, present, and future. Zhenjì said:
"The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises alone and universally conditions all phenomena; therefore, it is called 'silent containment' (*mo-róng*)."

Ānanda, if you now wish to reverse the cycle of birth and death, [the time required] will be many times greater than that for those with incomplete faculties—increasing by factors of ten and a hundred.
(The True Limit says: The eyes and ears perceive objects through separation; the nose and other senses know phenomena through contact.
When separated, the object is distant and thus profound; when in contact, the object is near and thus shallow.)

Wenling says: "The flowing roots are precisely that which is wondrously profound and unmoving. When they are directed outward, they flow and escape, rushing toward objects; this is called the 'flow of birth and death.
When they are turned inward, they reverse the flow and become one with the whole; this is called 'non-arising and non-extinction. The six faculties of sensory reception are those explained above:
if they follow the perfect [nature], they accord with the fundamental nature and are profound; if they do not follow the perfect, they depart from the nature."

Yet they are shallow; the distance between the shallow and the deep is vast. Therefore, the merit of their progress—whether slow or swift—differs by multiples as great as those between a day and a kalpa.
Those who wish to return swiftly must select a faculty that is complete and perfect.
I shall now fully manifest the six profound, perfect, and luminous [faculties], until those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified.
(Wenling says: When one attains the wisdom of perfect mastery, then the eighteen realms are all without exception perfectly penetrating.
However, for those of inferior capacity and beginners who have not yet attained perfection, they must enter through a single gate. If one faculty is free from delusion, then all six will be pure.)
"Only upon awakening does one realize that within the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), every particle of dust and every world-system is perfectly penetrating.
Wuxing said: "The 'six profound, perfect luminosities' and so forth refer to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). The merit of deluded luminosity is entirely true luminosity."
It is inherently possessed; because it is truly possessed, it is thus falsely possessed.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [up to] ...the divisions, measures, and numerical counts of arising, abiding, change, and cessation."
(Gushan said: "The afflictions severed by the vision of the Truths are the eighty-eight *kleśas*.
The afflictions severed through the Path of Cultivation are the eighty-one *cetanās*. Birth, abiding, change, and extinction are the *avidyā* of identical substance.
'Quantitative divisions' refers to the forty-two stages from the First Abode up to the Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*). 'Empty practice' is what is meant by 'delusion' [or *mṛṣā*].")
...delusion). Wēnlíng says:

"The profound perfection is differentiated due to delusion, and the 'one' and 'six' arise because of delusion. Therefore, before explaining the meaning of the 'one' and 'six,' he first distinguishes delusion for him.
In the Small Vehicle’s gateway of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), one cuts off the anger, ignorance, and so forth of the three realms."
By thoroughly discerning the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), one realizes the first fruit. Hence it is said: "Having attained *srotāpanna*, one has already extinguished the delusions of views.

Regarding the gateway of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one abandons the greed, anger, ignorance, and pride of the three realms, as well as the four innate delusions, which are also called the "delusions of thought" (*vicikitsā-kleśa*).
These are the accumulated habits from beginningless time that reside within the faculties; they are severed by the third fruit. This is why Ānanda was unaware of them.
Moreover, within this faculty, there further exist the various subtle afflictions of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;
when these are each divided into their respective portions and these six afflictions are exhausted, the state becomes profoundly still and perfect.
(Furthermore, that which is not known by Ānanda has been severed).
Now, you should observe the six faculties present before you... (up to) although the six have dissolved, one still remains undissolved.
(Gushan said: The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "The Srotāpanna is called 'one who has entered the stream,' yet there is nothing entered;
they do not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. This refers to the dissolution of the six [sense objects].

Yet, they have not yet extinguished the one [remaining] attachment, which is the grasping at the existence of nirvana, because this is what is realized by the Hīnayāna. It is, therefore, ignorance. (Zizhong said: Not due to the six sense objects...)
When one creates new karma, it is called "attaining the six and dissolving them. Yet, one is still deluded regarding the six sense organs as being a single entity;
thus, they have not yet perished. Ledu Tan said: "The ear does not see, and the feet do not speak; therefore, they cannot be considered one.

The ear hears the Dharma, yet the body and mouth act in accord with it; therefore, they cannot be said to lack the six. Since there is no fixed direction [of identity], the meaning of 'one' and 'six' is not [fixed]."
The fundamental origin arises from inversion. The *srotāpanna* has already severed the coarse delusions and does not enter into form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas;

thus, the six [sense objects] are dissolved. Yet, they still linger in the dharma, and their attachment to it remains undestroyed—this is the first [point]. To prove this by means of the subsequent text:

at this stage, one has merely attained the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), but has not yet achieved liberation through the dharma (*dharma-vimukti*). This continues until both [person and dharma] are empty.

If [the one] does not arise, then one is lost. However, in the Hīnayāna, one must first dissolve the six before one is lost; in the Mahāyāna, one simply loses the one, causing the six to dissolve of their own accord.
In these degenerate times, those who exhaustively pursue the Way may claim to have attained the subtle, yet they ultimately remain within the realm of separation and subtlety (*liwei*).
Those who can truly lose the one are not easily found. Re-examining the sacred words of the Buddha, I am deeply inspired by what they reveal.
(Wu Xing said: "The meaning of 'one essence' as explained by Master Yuan differs from that of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; it is simply that the meaning of 'one' has not yet been clarified.
One should know that from the 'seeing-essence' down to the 'knowing-essence' mentioned in the following text, they are fundamentally one essence.")
"Just as the great void of space merges with various vessels" (up to) "the six functions of the faculties are also like this. [Ziqing says:

The passage from 'The great void of space' below serves as a metaphor for the arising of the meanings of 'one' and 'six. The passage from 'That great void of space' below serves as a metaphor for the fact that, fundamentally, there is neither one nor six.
This pattern applies to the subsequent text, from 'due to brightness and darkness,' up to 'the seeing-essence reflects color and binds with color to form the faculties.']

This refers to the arising of the "one" and the "six. You need only not follow [the delusions] below—up until the point where you have pulled out one root and the five adhesions are completely liberated—and then the "one" and the "six" were never there in the first place.
This is the direct explanation for Ānanda’s doubt regarding the "one entrance" and the "purity of the six."
Wenling says: "Empty space is fundamentally neither identical nor different; this is a metaphor for how the perfectly湛 (zhàn) [luminous-still] state is fundamentally neither one nor six.
The removal of the vessel serves as a metaphor for the origin by which the meanings of 'one' and 'six' arise.

If one knows that the identity and difference of empty space are not established by the subject, then both 'one' and 'six' vanish together, and the perfectly湛 state is undivided. Once 'one' and 'six' no longer exist, then [the world] manifests..."

The existence of the six sense organs arises from the false manifestation of that which is inherently still and clear. Therefore, the following traces the source of this false manifestation to demonstrate it:
from the mutual conditioning of the two types of phenomena, light and darkness, [up to] the floating root-faculties and the four sensory objects, which flow away and rush toward forms.
Wu Xing says: "The manifestation of clarity through adhesion arises from the defilement of objects such as light and darkness, giving rise to the pure nature.
[The same applies to all other cases. Wenling says: "The essence of seeing is the eye-consciousness; form is the object of the eye. These two falsely conjoin to form the eye."
The sense-faculties (*indriya*). This is the root of these faculties; they agitate the four great elements to form a physical body.
Because they have not yet rushed toward external objects, they are called "pure. At this stage, it is like a grape; for although the physical body is complete, consciousness has not yet flowed out.
This is what is meant by the statement that there is simply nothing known apart from what is within a mirror. When consciousness flows outward and rushes toward objects, it becomes defiled.
Therefore, they are renamed the "floating faculties" (*bhūta-indriya*) consisting of the four sense-objects, rather than being called the pure *mahābhūtas*.
Due to the mutual impact of the two types of characteristics—movement and stillness—the floating faculties consisting of the four sense-objects flow outward and rush toward their respective objects.

(Xiali said: "The new leaves have merely holes in them. (Zhenji said: "Externally uprooting the six sense-faculties and internally merging with the true nature, one causes hearing and seeing to unite into a single, perfectly clear and profound state;
when this opens, it responds universally. Thus, the various faculties function interchangeably, and all delusions are completely eliminated.
What is called 'the non-interchangeability of your six faculties'—this opening and closing is merely a false thought that can never cease.")
The meaning lies in the cessation of delusions; only then does one know the uprooting [of afflictions]. The meaning lies in severing what gives rise to retribution.
(Zizhong said: "The constant nature is tranquility; rushing toward flavors is change. The moon at its first appearance is flat upon the surface of the tongue.

These are all metaphors for insentient things, clarifying that although the substance is complete, consciousness has not yet flowed forth. (Changshui said: "Awakened essence is the body-consciousness. A waist-drum...")
The skull has only the substance of touch, but not yet the function of touching; this is a metaphor for the pure source of the sense organs.

The skull represents the source of the organs, while the drum represents the floating organ (the physical faculty). Only because the source depends on the floating organ does the flow proceed like the skull, and only because the cause becomes the drum does touching occur.
(Xielü said: "Even the vision in a dark room possesses only substance; consciousness has not yet flowed forth.")
Gushan said: "That which adheres to the profound stillness and gives rise to cognition" refers to deluded conceptual cognition.

Regarding the phrase "the root-source," this refers to the physical mass of the eye, which serves as the locus upon which the mind-root rests for its conceptual cognitions. Therefore, the ultimate sense-faculty (*paramārtha-indriya*) is itself the pure four great elements.
It is like seeing within a dark chamber; that is, the physical sense organ (*bu-chén-gēn*) serves as the basis upon which the mental faculty (*yì*) relies, just as one dwells within a dark chamber.
As the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* says: "It is like the opening and closing of a lotus flower. This refers to that very point.
Ānanda, these six faculties arise from that awakened clarity (up to) the realization that they neither perish nor arise, and thus find their secure resting place.
(Wenling says: Therefore, from "you now" downward, because one falsely gives rise to superior causes based on the deluded, all six are illusory;
when separated from the six sense-objects, they all lack inherent substance.)
Gushan said: "That which arises from the awakening-illumination is true illumination; that which possesses illumination and is illuminated is deluded illumination.

Because one is deluded regarding that true illumination, it is said that 'one loses that essential clarity' and 'produces this deluded illumination. Therefore, it is said that 'clinging to delusion, light is emitted.'"
If you simply do not follow after movement and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and change—[and so forth]—then these six faculties will function as one for one another.
(Wu-xing says: "By means of these two kinds of faculties, the clarity of awareness is developed; therefore, each of the twelve hundred merits allows the faculties to function interchangeably.
(Gu-shan says: "Functioning may be either true or semblance; semblance is like the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *True Thusness* of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.")
Wenling says: Those twelve marks can adhere to the six sense organs and obstruct the profound clarity. Therefore, by uprooting even one organ, the fundamental clarity is revealed.
Once the fundamental clarity is revealed, all false attachments are shed and perfected. Adherence to delusion occurs because one follows external objects through the floating roots;
thus, obstructions arise. To shed this adherence, one does not follow nor does one pursue; it simply rests upon the roots.
It is simply this. Therefore, they can be used interchangeably.
Ānanda, do you not know that within this assembly [from "up to"] there is a perfect, clear, and knowing awareness that does not depend on mental thought?
(Xie Li said: "The function of 'extracting the root by citing evidence' involves mentioning all six individuals together to clarify that all six delusions can be completely uprooted;
thus, the true essence may become pure and shine alone—what is called 'that which the ears and eyes know, yet the mind has never died.
(Gu Shan said: "Gaṅgā is the name of a river; here it is translated as 'Coming from Heaven,' because it originates from the Snow Mountains...")

This is because they flow from the Lake Without Heat (Anavatapta) at the summit. As for the six individuals such as Aniruddha, some are ordinary beings experiencing the retribution of karma, while others are minor sages who have attained these through cultivation;
these are all powers of delusion that do not even rely upon the physical sense organs, let alone the state of perfect liberation—how could there not be mutual functioning among them?
Wenling says: Venerable Aniruddha was able to see despite losing his sight through excessive diligence; the Dragon King Bhadrika could hear without ears;
the deity of the Ganges smelled fragrances without a nose; and Gavāmpati received the retribution of a cow’s snout, hence he is called "Different Tongue.
Śūnyatāra is the deity who presides over space; his substance is like wind, yet he is capable of perceiving touch.

One who cultivates the meditative attainment of cessation and attains emptiness and stillness has the faculty of mind extinguished; yet, like Mahākāśyapa, although the faculty of mind is extinguished, they are still able to cognize.
"Ānanda, if your faculties were now to be completely uprooted [from their objects]... how could your awakened clarity fail to become perfectly wondrous?
(Ziqing says: When one loses that essential lucidity and perceives through the arising of sensory objects, then the faculties and their environments become obstructive.

Therefore, when one detaches from the "glue" and uproots them completely, the true light shines forth with brilliance; then the floating dust and illusory appearances are like ice melting in hot water, becoming one unified, pure, and harmonious state.)
The Jewel-Awareness is like boiling water, while deluded thoughts are like the water itself. When the perception gathers at the eye, it is perfectly luminous; this is the moment when seeing exists.

If one suddenly closes the eyes and it becomes dark, then darkness arises; this is the moment when seeing is absent. Once the six sense organs—head and feet alike—are shrouded in gloom, [the true nature is obscured].

Yet, even without seeing, one can touch and discern each thing exactly as when it is bright. From this we may verify that the capacity for clarity to manifest spontaneously and darkness to fail to obscure it is possessed by every person;
it is simply a matter of shedding attachment and dissolving the dust of sensory objects, whereby one naturally achieves perfect wonder.

Wuxing said: "True wisdom is like boiling water, while delusory objects are like ice. When delusion is thoroughly understood, it becomes true; thus, the transformation results in cognitive awareness (*jñāna*).
Previously, it was explained that cognitive awareness does not depend on the sense organs, which is why the case of Nalakalīra—who could see despite having no eyes—was cited.

Now, it is shown that true awakening does not rely on external conditions, which is why the ability of ordinary people to discern within darkness is pointed out. The person referred to there is... [the text ends here].
A person with eyes closed follows along the body; that is, they perceive the body of another as their own. This shows that perception is the same [in both states].

It means that perception in the dark is no different from what is seen in the light. If even ordinary people can still discern things without depending on the condition of light, how much more so for the true awakening of a sage—what need would it have to be triggered by conditions? The phrase "perception depends on conditions" below points to delusion; it does not clarify [the truth].
The following clarifies this briefly by illustrating light and darkness; all conditions are likewise so.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...desiring to attain the seven fruits of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding."
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. There is the empty Tathāgatagarbha, and there is the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "The empty Tathāgatagarbha is free from all afflictions that are not yet liberated."
The non-empty Tathāgatagarbha possesses the inconceivable dharmas of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha manifests as form or emptiness according to circumstances, universally responding to all things; the latter two receive their names according to their respective functions.

The solitary-empty Tathāgatagarbha constitutes its essence, and thus it is designated by the name of the "fruit. (Xielü says: Bodhi is the nature of perfect enlightenment; Nirvāṇa is the essence of the virtue of cessation.)

Because it is without change, it is called *tathatā* (Suchness). As the fundamental substance of awakening, it is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature). Its substance is fundamentally pure, thus it is called *amala* (the stainless).

Because afflictions do not dwell within it, it is called the *śūnya-tathāgatagarbha* (empty womb of the Tathāgata). Because it is pure and luminously manifest, it is called the *mahādarśana-jñāna* (Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom).

Binding the mind is a metaphor for contemplating the Middle Way, whereby both extremes are simultaneously released.
Wuxing said: "Pulling and tugging from either side, neither can untie it; this is a metaphor for observing the two extremes, which both fail to destroy fundamental ignorance.
Ordinary people and non-Buddhists take annihilationism and eternalism as the two extremes; the followers of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas take emptiness and existence as the two extremes.
Although they are said to suppress or sever them, the knots in the cloth still remain. If one wishes to remove the knots, one must attend to..."
Regarding "tying the mind": when one perceives the establishment of knowledge, this is called "tying. To contemplate that knowledge within the Middle Way is what is meant by "tying the mind.
The knot does not exist apart from the cloth; once untied, it is one. Knowledge is not different from the Way; once lost, there is the Center.
"Ānanda, I say that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions... (until) all delusions have been extinguished; what need is there for anything that is not true?
(Wuxing says: Since he has already instructed him on how to untie the knots, he now intends to lead him to select the faculty and cultivate the perfect practice.
Therefore, he shows that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions, conversely demonstrating that if there were no causes and conditions, the Buddha-dharma would have no way to arise.)
As the preceding text states: "For example, although a lute or a zither possesses exquisite sounds, if there are no skillful fingers, they can never produce them.

This is precisely the principle of the simultaneous cultivation of samādhi and prajñā, which serves as the present causal condition. If one were to rely on the Tripiṭaka, the practice of the six pāramitās and so forth would all be mundane, compounded, and coarse characteristics.
(Letam said: "Knowing that causes arise from conditions, up to the point where one knows even a falling drop of rain—this is [the meaning].")

The Tathāgata’s awakening is the complete realization of all dharmas; that which he speaks are all words of sincere admonition. Regarding the selection of the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), the preceding text states:
"If one can, within this, awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-indriya*) as opposed to the non-perfect faculty, then a day and an eon will differ by a factor of ten million.

Wenling says: This means to rely on supramundane right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) to discern the fundamental cause of the root-fetters (*mūla-saṃyojana*) and thereby resolve them.

If one attains right wisdom, not only can one know the fundamental cause of the root-fetters, but even the myriad species throughout the sands of worlds will all have their original source fully understood.

The world refers to the six classes of ordinary beings, while the supramundane refers to the four types of noble ones; it is by knowing this that the ten realms are all seen to be rooted in [this same principle].
The mind follows the defiled conditions of ignorance and thus emerges from the nine realms; it follows the pure conditions of teaching and practice and thus emerges from the Buddha-realm.

Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says, "The seeds of the Buddha arise from conditions," and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "There are also causes and conditions by which, through the cessation [of ignorance], the lamp of perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) blazes forth. The Buddha possesses two types of wisdom, provisional and real; the real wisdom...
The profound principle is that expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna) discerns all things, illuminating both mundane and supramundane dharmas, even to the point of knowing their various origins;

all of these are what expedient wisdom discerns. Since it clearly perceives both the sentient and the insentient without confusion, the method for untangling the knots and the meaning of selecting the faculties as explained here are entirely appropriate according to the discernment of things; indeed, there is no doubt of this.
This is erroneous. Ānanda, I now ask you: when this *karpāsa* cloth is knotted [and later] the knots are untied, how could they be removed simultaneously? (Ziqing says:
This shows that the six [sense organs] are not liberated all at once, but must follow their proper sequence. Master Ke says: The meaning clarifies the six sense faculties.)
They cannot be viewed as being equal; one enters into realization by relying on only a single faculty, whereupon the other six naturally accord with this principle.
Wuxing said: "While there is a sequence in tying a cloth to form knots, there is necessarily no such order in how the clarity of stillness adheres to form the faculties."

Therefore, it is not possible to challenge the Dharma by means of analogies. This refers to the distinctions among the six functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, which arise sequentially like the tying of knots.
One selects from among the six sense organs and develops contemplation according to any single one, thereby attaining liberation in sequence.
The Buddha said: "The liberation of the six sense faculties is also like this" (up to) "attaining the patience of non-arising from samādhi.

(Wu-xing says: In the Small Vehicle, analytical contemplation involves deliberate mental effort; first one breaks the attachment to a person, then one breaks the attachment to phenomena, and only thereafter does one realize entry into the principle of the equality of emptiness.

The statement that "this faculty first understands and first attains the emptiness of persons" is also like the preceding passage, which compared it to turbid water being clarified:
the sand and silt settle of their own accord, as it were spontaneously.

Wenling said: "To understand the fetters of affliction is to realize that they all arise from attachment to the self; thus, by having no attachment to the self, one leaves behind the obstacle of affliction—this is the realization of the emptiness of persons.
To understand the fetters of the knowable is to realize that they all arise from attachment to phenomena; thus, by having no attachment to phenomena..."

Being free from the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is the attainment of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which is termed "liberation through phenomena" (*dharma-vimukti*). When both person and phenomena are simultaneously liberated, this is termed "universal emptiness" (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*).

When even universal emptiness is extinguished and the mind has no further arisings, one emerges from meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When Avalokiteśvara first, within the faculty of hearing, entered the stream and lost the objective field, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly ceased to arise;

this was his initial attainment of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Thus he gradually increased [his realization] until both hearing and that which is heard were exhausted. When hearing was exhausted, he did not dwell therein;

when the awareness of what is perceived became empty, he attained liberation through phenomena (*dharma-vimukti*). When the emptiness of awareness reached ultimate perfection, the very emptiness of that which is emptied was extinguished; this is the simultaneous emptiness of both person and phenomenon (*pudgala-dharma-ubhaya-śūnyatā*).
There is no arising. When both arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa) manifests before one;
thus, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). (Xie Li said: "These three kinds of emptiness all take the Middle Way as the essence of contemplation.
If it were not for this, how would they differ from those who remove their headbands and are pulled and tugged from left to right?")
Ānanda and the great assembly addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "May you deign to bestow upon me your great compassionate wisdom and secret adornment.

Each realized their own perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). Thus we know that the fundamental source is darkly identical with the myriad dharmas. The Buddha did not proclaim it explicitly, but rather unfolded it through the various [disciples];
this is what is called "dark transmission" (*ming-shou*). To withdraw and conceal the secret mechanism is precisely to still the thoughts and concentrate the mind.
Wenling said: "The perfect penetration of wisdom and awakening resides in the single mind. Having already received this instruction, my body and mind are now radiant and clear.

"Esoteric words (*mantra*) are the very words that clarify and manifest the awakening of wisdom. Secret Adornment (*guhyavibhūṣaṇa*) refers to the secret essentials of the fundamental source of perfect penetration.
Since the awakening of wisdom and perfect penetration are inherently possessed by me, even though I rely on esoteric words, I am restored to my original enlightenment.
However, if the secret adornment is not opened, it would be no different from never having heard them at all; therefore, one seeks a separate revelation."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the entire assembly... (up to) "By what skillful means does one enter samādhi?
(Gushan says: The five aggregates, six sense bases, and eighteen elements are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness.

Ultimately, it perfects the true and pervasive penetration. It transforms the Hīnayāna at the final stage of the mind and expands the Mahāyāna from the first assembly. It is further said:
"The twenty-five sages below this contemplate the eighteen realms as well as the seven great elements; these are merely differences in the expansion and contraction [of the categories]."
Lectan said: "The twenty-five gates of universal penetration are precisely the eighteen realms and the seven elements.

Since the seven elements are opened from within the eighteen realms, these [twenty-five gates] do not speak of the myriad dharmas of the faculties and vessels; rather, they are fully encompassed by the eighteen realms and the seven elements.
Therefore, these are presented in detail, desiring to lead practitioners, upon the various phenomena of the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world,"
In moments of distress or haste, one attains true perfect penetration without the slightest obstruction.
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, immediately rose from their seats... [until] "...as I have realized, sound is supreme."
(Xie Li said: "To silently awaken to the perfect principle through sounds and traces—this relies on internal realization, and is therefore called 'Esoteric' (*mi*).

(Gushan says: "The subtle sound is secretly perfect" means that one secretly awakens to the principle of perfection.

Furthermore, the meaning is the same for these twenty-five gates. Regarding the initial designation of "sound" (*śabda*) as the object-field (*viṣaya*):

this first refers to the teaching-body (*deha*) of this region. King Aśoka of the Aśoka Garden built it to welcome the Buddha. Wuxing said: "The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is wondrous in its beginning, middle, and end;

It further states that Mahābrahmā’s body and mind were "wondrously perfect" and his "wondrous vision was perfectly clear. Could this "wondrous perfection" be the same as the nature of the "wondrous clarity" of Perfect Enlightenment?
One should know that the Tathāgata first had the various sages speak in succession until they had finished, and only afterward did he address Mañjuśrī.
He said: "These twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training, as well as the Arhats, each spoke of the expedient means by which they first attained the Way;

all of them declared that they practiced the true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). In their cultivation, there was in reality no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or posteriority.
This is the authentic text for opening up the provisional and returning to the real."
Upāliṣada immediately rose from his seat... [as far as] "...as I have realized, form (*rūpa*) is the primary cause. (The Master of Nanyue said:

"Contemplating the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is called the 'foundations of mindfulness of nature' (*dharmatā-smṛtyupasthāna*). Therefore, a verse in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* says:
'This body has the characteristic of impurity; its true nature is eternally fixed. The same is said for all feelings (*vedanā*), mind (*citta*), and mental factors (*dharma*').")

From the impure, through the white bones and subtle particles, they return to empty space. Because of excessive desire, one cultivates the remedial dharmas and accomplishes the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*).

When true insight arises and delusions are shattered, one is a *dharmavibhūta-arhat*. Upon the accomplishment of the nine contemplations, one attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*) and realizes the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state regarding all forms and appearances; therefore, it is said that "wondrous form is secretly perfect."
Wenling says: *Upāniṣad* is translated here as "near" or "slight," and also as "the nature of dust. This means that subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) are a minute portion of form (*rūpa*).
Because he attained awakening through the dust, he received this name. Formerly, he was full of lustful desires;

the Buddha had him practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Changshui says: Because he contemplated the dust of form as being fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, it is said that he "attained awakening."

Regarding "the nature of all forms" (*sarvarūpa-svabhāva*), Wuxing says: "Not so. Since it speaks of contemplating the Buddha's initial attainment of enlightenment, this is precisely the untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*) of the Hīnayāna.

The youth Aromakṣema rose from his seat... [up to] "...as I have realized, the fragrance is supreme.

refers to contemplating the emptiness of nature. (Wuxing says: Whenever one speaks of the emptiness of nature, one must first trace it back to the four [elements].)

This resembles the Mahāyāna method of contemplating that what exists as an illusion is itself emptiness.

Although the various Śrāvakas below mostly follow the Hīnayāna, which contemplates the cessation of real existence as emptiness—despite the differences between the Small and Great Vehicles—the perfect realization they attain is one and the same True Truth (*tattva*).
Wenling says: He contemplates conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and, through the perfect realization of fragrance, attains the stage of the "Pure Youth" (*kumārabhūta*);

thus he is named "The Youth. Regarding his "leaving the Buddha to sit in quietude": this means sitting in silent seclusion to conceal his traces, purifying his mind to engage in contemplation. Both wood and smoke are non-existent.
Since past and future do not exist and the mind has no object of perception, the mind is thereby dissolved and the untainted (anāsrava) is revealed;
because the dust-like vapors have been extinguished, the wondrous fragrance is subtle and perfect.
The two Dharma-Princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata... (up to) "...as I have realized, the cause of taste is supreme. (Wuxing says:

Because one serves the Buddha, one necessarily hears the True Dharma; thus, regarding the nature of taste, one realizes that arising is non-arising and that emptiness and existence are one—this refers to the sense-object of taste.
"Body and mind" refers to the tongue-consciousness. Since taste is known through contact, they are relative.)
To speak of it: because flavor is not empty, it is not separate from body and mind; because flavor does not exist [as a substantial entity], it is not identical to body and mind.
Thus, the nature of the Middle Way is revealed.
Wenling said: "His merit in skillfully saving others was perfected, making him worthy to succeed to the Buddha’s position; thus he was named the Son of Dharma-rectitude (*Dharmasubhūti*).

For kalpas on end he has served as a physician, always skillfully saving people. To speak of 'discerning the cause of flavor' means to thoroughly understand the nature of flavor and thereby realize that it is neither empty nor existent, transcending both.

This is the entry [into the explanation]. As previously stated regarding the cause of form (*rūpa*), the subsequent explanations of the causes of water and phenomena (*dharma*) are the same. Regarding the six tastes, such as sourness and so forth:
when various tastes combine to produce a single flavor, it is called a "conjoined taste" (*saṃyukta-rasa*). When used in its natural state, it is called an "innate taste" (*sahaja-rasa*).
When processed through refinement, roasting, or baking, it is called a "transformed taste" (*vikṛta-rasa*).
Bhadrapāla and his companions... [up to] "...as I have realized, the cause of touch is supreme. (Wuxing says:

The mind is peacefully in accord with its nature. (Lectan said: "Contact involves the threefold harmony; 'gold' is transformed into the three virtues.

All are false touchings and false awakenings; therefore, when one attains non-existence, wondrous touch is proclaimed and clarified, and one becomes a true child of the Buddha, which is called the Stage of the Buddha’s Child.
Because one is well able to guard [the mind], causing delusion not to arise and awakening not to be disturbed, it is named the Stage of Worthy Guarding (Bhadrapāla).
Mahākāśyapa and the Purple-Gold Light... (up to) "knowing that the cause of the Dharma I have realized is supreme.

seeing with half his head, he beheld the trichiliocosm as clearly as a fruit in the palm of his hand. This is now called the Vajra-samādhi, by which one perceives the ten directions.
