As for the subsequent passage, "profoundly penetrating the true mark," this is all based on the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) school;
there is no fault in making such distinctions. Wēn-líng says: Subhūti has understood emptiness throughout vast kalpas, not merely in a single lifetime.

Because he realizes that the body is empty and quiescent, his mind attains non-obstruction. Because he thoroughly penetrates past lives and realizes that objects are empty and quiescent, the ten directions become empty. This is self-awakening.

To awaken others, he likewise causes sentient beings to realize emptiness; however, this is merely the emptiness realized by the Hīnayāna, which has not yet fully clarified the true emptiness of the awakened nature.
Therefore, up to the present, I have elucidated the true emptiness of the awakened nature.

Thus one is able to enter suddenly into the ocean of true emptiness, the wondrous nature of precious luminosity. Departing from the views of the two vehicles, one attains the same knowledge and vision as the Buddha.
All phenomena enter into non-existence; both subject and object are exhausted, for they are all integrated within the ocean of precious luminous emptiness.
All existing phenomena revolve and return once more to non-existence; they ultimately return to the ocean of jewel-luminous emptiness.
(Zizhong says: "First, by means of single emptiness, one empties all marks, hence it is said that 'all marks enter the non-existent.
Next, by means of double emptiness, one empties the mark of emptiness itself, hence it is said that 'that which was non-existent is exhausted.'"")
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat... [until] "...this supreme knowledge and vision of light is foremost.
(Wuxing says: This refers to the realm of the Four Truths, both mundane and supramundane; it refers to the various marks of transformation, arising, and ceasing.)
Changshan said: "The mind sees; this is eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Because consciousness is pure, all things are penetrating and sharp.

Because the mind is boundless, the seeing-awakening is perfectly luminous. When the mind’s seeing emits light, and that light reaches the ultimate limit of knowing and seeing, it is because the mind’s seeing has brought forth illumination."

Yet it perfectly illumines the myriad dharmas. As for the brothers Kāśyapa—namely Uruvilvākāśyapa and his companions, or as some say, those who encountered the horse and spoke the verses—that pertains to the causal conditions of the Hīnayāna and is not what is grasped by Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong).
Śāriputra possessed the foremost wisdom, and since his reputation for voice and virtue was preeminent, he is called the "eldest son."
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva then rose from his seat... [up to] ...this mastery of discernment is the foremost. (Wenling says:

Generally, those who possess great roots and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva are all said to perform the conduct of Samantabhadra. "Hearing with the mind" refers to the consciousness of the ear.
"Discerning the knowledge and views of sentient beings" means selecting the practices of Samantabhadra and bringing them to fulfillment. (Gushan...)
It is said: "The mind-hearing that brings forth illumination is internal realization; the discernment of mastery is external function. Xie Li said:

"To practice pervasively throughout the Dharma-realm is called 'Universal' (Pu); to have a rank adjacent to the ultimate sage is called 'Worthy' (Xian). This is not the 'Worthy' prior to the [ten] stages;
rather, it refers to the Vajropama-samādhi (Diamond-like Samādhi), which dwells at the summit of all Buddhas and is thus named 'Worthy.'"
Sundarananda immediately rose from his seat... [up to] ...that Mingyuan’s extinction of outflows is foremost.
(Wuxing says: Counting the breath is for the purpose of developing consciousness; contemplating the breath is for the purpose of stabilizing consciousness.)
Gushan said: "Sundarī means 'lovely'; it is the name of the Buddha's wife. Nanda means 'joyful splendor'; he was the Buddha’s own younger brother.
The former [practice of] counting breaths relies on the sense faculties (*indriya*) to collect the mind; this contemplation of white [light] relies on consciousness (*vijñāna*) to settle the mind.
Breath arises from wind and fire, and because it stirs up the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa*), its appearance is like smoke. Those who are deluded..."
One does not perceive it. Only through diligent contemplation can one see the six lines (*ṣaḍ-yoga*). One sees fire burning the breath, which produces black smoke and purple flames;
these are all manifestations of turbid afflictions (*kleśa*). When one strives in contemplation to bring forth illumination, the turbid afflictions gradually dissipate.

Thus, the interior becomes luminous and the exterior becomes empty; as the smoke vanishes, it turns white. Upon the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), there are no further afflictions; the inner clarity emits light. Therefore...
The inhalation and exhalation transform into radiant light. The "dissolving of breath" refers to the smoke dissipating and becoming white.
The "extinguishing of outflows" refers to the mind opening and the outflows being exhausted. All of these are the illumination produced by the nose-consciousness.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra... [is] foremost among those who have extinguished all outflows (*āsrava*). (Wuxing says:
"The passage beginning with 'proclaiming' refers to the teachings of the Hīnayāna; the passage beginning with 'in this way' demonstrates the meaning of the Mahāyāna; it begins with the Āgamas.")

This concludes the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, it says "up to and including" (*yāvat*). In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is praised as being foremost among those who preach the Dharma.

The fact that he, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (the *Mohebanruo*), turns the teaching over to the various bodhisattvas is precisely what this refers to. This is a retrospective account of his attainment of the Way, whether by means of skillful means (*upāya*) or ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), as has been analyzed previously.

The Ultimate Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) says: "To be foremost in preaching the Dharma and to possess unimpeded eloquence, thereby subduing Māra and extinguishing outflows—all these are due to the power of the faculty of tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*).
As for the true mark of suffering and emptiness: all worldly phenomena are impermanent, all are suffering, and all are empty;
yet within them there is that which is truly permanent, neither suffering nor empty, such as the four virtues of *nirvāṇa*."
This is precisely the true mark (*dharmatā*). Through the three wheels of body, speech, and mind, the Buddha responds to sentient beings without obstruction. "Voice" refers to the wheel of speech.
Upāli then rose from his seat... [until] ...he was foremost among all those who master the Vinaya.
(Gushan said: "Upāli" is translated here as "Foremost," because he upholds the Vinaya as the guiding principle for the assembly. (Xielü said:
"Because consciousness depends upon the body, one first grasps the body, and subsequently grasps the mind. (Gushan said: "Grasping both body and mind.")
From the coarse to the subtle, this serves to guard against the subtlety of body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*). Once body-consciousness has ceased, true wisdom manifests.
This is what is meant by "purity of precepts and the possession of wisdom," whereby one attains the foremost path.
Zhenjì said: "Upāli speaks of 'near-attachment,' which means to draw near to and rely upon the Buddha.

To say 'intimate following' and 'intimate observation,' and even 'liberating oneself from desire to receive the teaching,' all clarify the reverence and submission of the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*).

Regarding the ethical discipline (*vinaya*) for walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, there are two hundred and fifty rules for each; these, when paired with the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*), constitute three thousand. Furthermore, these three thousand are assigned..."
The seven branches of body and speech are further correlated with the four categories of afflictions to form eighty-four thousand [types of karma].

Those rooted in the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) are the primary karmas, such as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Those arising from the secondary factors (*mūla*) are the prohibitive karmas, namely the transgressions of the minor branches. These arise because of the faults that exceed the prohibitions.
The precepts serve as the governing framework for the assembly; "personally sealed by my heart" means they are approved by the community.

Regarding the phrase "I take hold of the body and so forth," it means that through the observance of the precepts, both the body and the consciousness of the body are fully and universally penetrating.
In attaining deliverance according to the Vinaya, Upāli was foremost; in attaining deliverance within the Saṃgha, Kauṇḍinya was the first. Therefore, Kauṇḍinya is now enshrined in this hall.
In the Chen period, Upāli was enshrined upon the altar; each was established according to its original basis.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat [and departed]... having long since attained crystalline purity, he is considered the foremost.

(Xie Li said: "The 'intention' (*manas*) serves as the generative cause for all phenomena; the myriad dharmas pass through it by means of conditions. Therefore, upon hearing the internal condition, one suddenly manifests supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

(Wu Xing said: "The name 'spirit' (*shen*) refers to the mind of Heaven (*tianxin*); the name 'penetration' (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom (*huixing*). This nature of mind is precisely the manifestation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
In the Mahayana, this is the manifestation of the *tathāgatagarbha*; in the Hinayana, it is the manifestation of fundamental dhyāna. Among the six supernatural powers...")
The supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is its internal realization; the remaining five supernormal powers all belong to external application).
Guishan said: "Uruvilvā" means "papaya tumor" in this language, because there was a tumor on his chest like a papaya fruit.
"Mount Gayā" is the name of Elephant Head Mountain (*Gajapṛṣṭha-parvata*). It is also called "City," because a city is near this mountain. Na... [text ends]
The name of the river is the Ganges. There were two younger brothers to one elder brother; thus Śāriputra said, "Those we encountered were the Kāśyapa brothers.
Wēnlíng says: The profound meaning of these causal conditions refers not to the coarse appearances of worldly conjunction, but to the elucidation of both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, by means of this, they gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and attained great penetration, with supernormal powers as they pleased.

"Revolve the stillness" means to revolve the mental consciousness so as to restore its wondrous stillness; thus, after a long time, it becomes clear and translucent, and one’s supernormal powers become perfectly luminous, pure, and autonomous.
Among those from the presence of the Tathāgata [down to] those who have ascended to unsurpassed enlightenment, Ucchuṣma is the foremost.
(Zizhong said: "The subtle and coarse aspects of the Dharma-gates are non-dual; therefore, even the fires of worldly afflictions and desire can both realize perfect penetration. (Wuxing said:
"If one observes the four great elements everywhere, they are all objects of the sense-field of touch. The hundred bones and four limbs are the element of earth;

the various sensations of cold and warmth are the elements of water, fire, and wind. Once samādhi is established, it is said that 'divine light condenses within,' especially for those who have many desires.")

Because the fire element was predominant, his lustful fire was transformed into the fire of wisdom. After he became an Arhat—which refers to attaining the lesser fruit—he subsequently made a great vow:
"Will I not manifest in various forms as a Vajrapāṇi spirit to assist the Buddha and propagate his transformation?"
Xie Li said: "Ucchuṣma means 'Fire-Head,' which refers to the Vajra Fire-Head. Those who indulge excessively in lust are fundamentally impelled by the sensation of warmth;
while alive they are driven by the fire of desire, and at death they are consumed by the fire of karma. Thus, the power of karma blazes ever more fiercely."
Thus, it becomes a mass of fierce fire. To observe the pervasive warmth everywhere is to cause one to realize that the fire element flows unimpededly.
Once all obstructions have dissolved, the divine light coalesces within, forming the fire of wisdom which issues forth from the crown of the head;
hence it is called the "fire-head. The production of great jewel-flames is precisely the Fire-Light Samādhi (*Jvalana-prabhā-samādhi*).
The Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara rose from his seat... [until] attaining the unsurpassed path; this is the foremost. (Changshui said:
"The essential nature of the atoms does not touch one another; they are identical to space. Therefore, by awakening to this true nature, weapons have no place to touch. Wuxing said:
"From the atoms of the body and the elements, even up to weapons—because these are all...")
This is the form produced by the great element of earth; it is a phenomenon born of causes and conditions. It is the emptiness of atoms without differentiation.
It is the non-contact with self-nature within the center. It is the complete fulfillment of the three truths. Is this not the Tathāgatagarbha?

Having awakened to non-arising and so forth, one provisionally attains the lesser fruit through the partial realization of the Dharmakāya; therefore, it is distinguished by means of the "patience regarding non-arising. First, one liberates oneself, and afterwards...
"Transforming others" refers to what is called "turning the mind.

Ledanting said: "Leveling the steep and preventing damage; acting on behalf of others to save the oxen, without the notions of 'other' or 'self,' this manifests the leveling of the mind-ground, wherein there is no high or low.
Vipaśyin (Vishvabhū) means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All," which also arises from leveling [the mind].
Because the mind is thus, all things are sovereign. From "I am the opening of the mind" below, everything is based on the perfect enlightenment of the earth-element (mahābhūta).
The two objects of the body and the realm are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha; from "vainly arising" above, they do not rub or touch one another.
To realize that they are fundamentally vain and false is to awaken to non-arising. The wondrous lotus flower is the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is the mind-ground of all Buddhas.
This is the Dharma-gate. When practice is truly perfected and in accord with reality, defilement and purity are both forgotten; this is called the "Flower of Sublime Study.

Transcending the three vehicles and attaining profound realization of the single reality is called the "Ground of the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision. That which is held by the Ground of Holding is found herein alone.
Thus, one attains the dissolution of the body and the sensory realms, and the perfection of supreme wisdom.
The youth Candraprabha immediately rose from his seat... [up to] "to bring the Bodhi of perfect enlightenment to full completion—this is the foremost. (Ziqing says:
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the Flower Treasury Ocean there is a great lotus flower. Within that lotus flower are various fragrant waters.
Each and every fragrant water ocean serves as the seed for the worlds of the Buddha-fields. This is the Flower Treasury World.)

It floats within the fragrant waters; therefore, it is called the Floating Banner King Land (*Puṇḍarīka-rāja-kṣetra*). The Flower Treasury (*Kusuma-alaṃkāra*) consists of twenty layers, heaped high like a banner and being the most magnificent and lofty;
thus it is termed "King. Now, observing the water within one's own body, it is identical to that ocean; hence it is said: "The various fragrant water-oceans of the Floating Banner King Land.
When first cultivating this visualization and seeing only the water, this is the "form resulting from meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), which follows the mind.

That which is transformed is like the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*). It exists when one enters meditative absorption, but does not exist when one emerges from it. This differs from the matter that is the fruit of karma;

for while the latter is collectively induced by shared karma, one must refrain from creating worldly karma to attain purity. As for the ten universal bases, they are blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
All these ten universal bases are present [in the mind]; for instance, when one forms the perception of blue, then all places [appear as blue].
[All are blue. (Wuxing says: "Having attained arhatship, one has long been separated from the conditions of illness," etc.
Examining the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it clarifies that all sages possess bodily suffering, such as Śāriputra’s wind-disease and Pindola Bharadvāja’s eye pain.

The current statement that "having already attained arhatship, one has long been separated from the conditions of illness" is truly difficult to reconcile. This likely refers to having previously attained the lesser fruits [of the path] in the past.]

Since there are no longer the matters of the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) or of karma, this is the condition for departing from the suffering of the illness of the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence).
(Zizhong said: "Only then does one attain the 'extinction of the body' and so forth. Initially, one realizes the portion of the Dharma-body; the changing body is extinguished.

The nature of the water within the body becomes identical with the nature of the ocean of fragrant water, merging with the nature of the treasury of emptiness of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Letan said: "Having first accomplished the contemplation of water, one again encounters...")

"Only after immeasurable time can one attain the dissolution of the body; it is through the long and distant path of the holy Way that this is possible. (Xielü said: "The Venerable Shuiguan of Mianzhu County, Hanzhou, was a trace-manifestation of Candraprabha Buddha.

His primary biography states that the Master entered the fire-light samādhi."*) *Note: The parenthetical remark and the final sentence appear to be editorial notes or commentary appended to the main text.*
"His chamber was as if on fire; this is of the same category. Wēnlíng says:
"The moon is the Yin principle, the essence of water. In the past, he took Water-Deity (Varuṇa) as his teacher and practiced the contemplation of water (*āp-kasiṇa*).
Because the nature of water is perfectly luminous, he was named Moonlight. 'Practicing the water-essence' refers to contemplating the nature of the water-essence. The nature of water is without..."

As for "seizing," it refers to the internal fluids and blood and the external oceans of lands (*kṣetra-samudra*). Although their watery appearances differ, their nature does not conflict or exclude one another;
this is precisely awakening to the perfection [of reality] through water. "The Floating Banner King Land" is the general designation for the various fragrant water-oceans beyond the worlds.
At that time, my physical body returned to its original state; this describes the conditions for practicing the contemplation.

One merely perceives that water, meaning one is focused exclusively on a single contemplation; because the four great elements have not yet been integrated, one has not yet attained the state of being bodiless.
When Śāriputra entered meditative absorption on the banks of the Ganges and was struck by a malevolent ghost, he emerged from concentration with a headache;
this was also because he had not yet attained the state of being bodiless. As for the King of Sovereign Penetration of Mountains and Seas, [he does so] immediately within the earth, water, and all...
"Great! This is one who has attained wondrous, perfect penetration. When the Moonlight Samādhi reaches this stage, it dissolves the four great elements;
only then does one attain bodilessness, such that one's nature merges with true emptiness. It initially proceeded from the nature of water, flowing through as a single flavor."
The Dharma Prince Vairocanaraśmiprabha immediately rose from his seat... [up to] ...transmitting this one wondrous mind; this is the foremost. (Wenling says:

Because he attained great, perfect enlightenment through the element of wind, his body and mind emitted light, penetrating all things without obstruction. He was named the Buddha Vairocanaraśmiprabha Anantaghoṣa.
Furthermore, relying on the element of wind, he revealed the teaching to the Bodhisattvas, enabling them to know that fundamental awakening is immovable, yet the body...)
The movement of the realms is entirely driven by the power of wind. Vairocana-prabha, through this, contemplates the realms, contemplates the world, contemplates the body, and contemplates the mind;
he sees that their shifting, flowing, moving, and ceasing are all solely due to the power of wind. Therefore it is said: "All movements are non-dual.

From this, he realizes that the myriad movements within the great trichiliocosm are all merely frantic toil—like a hundred mosquitoes buzzing within a square inch. Having realized this frantic toil, [he attains liberation].
Thereupon, one beholds Akṣobhya Buddha. The East is the source of all movement, yet the Buddha’s name is "Immovable";
this signifies that he is stillness within movement itself. Because he can be still within movement, his body and mind are unimpeded. This is the transmission of the single wondrous mind.
[The text states: "One knows that the power of wind has no basis and that all myriad movements are illusory, thereby alone realizing the unmoving primordial enlightenment (*amala-vijñāna*).
Wuxing said: "The 'elements' (*dhātu*) constitute spatial directions, and thus they are established; the 'worlds' (*loka*) constitute temporal flux, and thus they move through time.
Time refers precisely to the past, present, and future. Gushan said: "'Not long after meeting the Buddha' means not for many [years]."
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja immediately rose from his seat... [up to] "...this perfect clarity of wondrous power is foremost.
(Wuxing says: Because one contemplates the material substance of the four great elements, there is immediately the boundless Dharmakāya.

To manifest that this body universally permeates and fuses with all things, he grasps a precious jewel to illuminate the ten directions and so forth, thereby representing it. Since the jewel represents form...)
Furthermore, the mirror symbolizes the mind. Form is created from the mind; its entire substance is the mind. Thus, it emits jewel-light to consecrate the ten directions and so forth.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serenely responsive to all things. This body is identical to space; such is the nature of phenomena (*dharma*).

Entering the dust-like lands with the body is the response (*anurūpa*). Preaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles constitutes the Buddha-work (*buddhakārya*). Adapting to the capacities of the four *siddhārtha* (the four types of audiences) is called "conformity" (*anuloma*).
Regarding the "Limit of Reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*): because one realizes the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), everything within that nature is empty;
thus, the body and the ocean of lands interpenetrate without obstruction, and this is termed the "Treasury of Space" (*ākāśagarbha*). "Dingguang" is the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. At Dingguang...
As for the attainment of the Boundless Body (*anantakāya*): the Dharma-body is like space, having no boundaries or limits;
it must be revealed through the tranquil illumination of the lamp of the mind. As for those who grasp the four precious jewels and so forth:

by contemplating that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) have no basis, their wondrous power becomes perfectly luminous, thereby illuminating and comprehending the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein all things are empty. This is what is meant by "emptiness is non-dual," O Buddha.
The fundamental substance of the realms is the same. Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and so forth within one's own mind:

this is also due to the four great elements being without support; through their wondrous power of perfect luminosity, they shine forth from within the perfectly hollow mind, mutually penetrating and harmoniously integrating.
The "Dhvajendra-buddhakṣetra" (Crown-King Buddha-field) is the name of a buddha-field within the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm.
Maitreya Bodhisattva then rose from his seat... [up to] ...attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is the foremost.
(Gushan said: "The cessation and disappearance of the mind that seeks worldly fame" refers to the stage of semblance.
"Attaining the unsurpassed, wondrous, perfect Samādhi of the cognitive mind" refers to the stage of partial realization. (Zhenji said:

"If the nature of consciousness does not maintain its stillness, but externally discriminates names and marks according to the *tathatā*, this is to wander among the noble clans in pursuit of fame. (Wuxing said: "'Exhausting all of space'...")
This refers to all Buddha-lands throughout the entirety of space, which are manifested solely by the mind. To speak in terms of the four lands:

the mind itself is the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), while the transformation land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*) corresponds to the Land of Real Reward (*vipākaphala-bhūmi*), the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kṣetra*), and the Land of Shared Dwelling (*sahā-vāsa*).

Purity and defilement are merely the characteristics of these three lands, which arise and cease in alternation. Thus, it is said that "existence and non-existence flow forth from the Tathāgata," meaning they emerge from the consciousness of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
[This refers to] the nature [which flows forth as the bodies of the *vipāka* and *nairmāṇika* Buddhas].
Xielǐ said: "Maitreya is here translated as 'The Compassionate One' (*Cishi*). This is because his compassion flourishes within this very world, rather than waiting for a future kalpa.

Out of pity for sentient beings who are deluded regarding consciousness, he manifests the brilliance of his awakening. Those whose minds value worldly fame and who delight in frequenting the families of the noble are deluded."

Because consciousness clings to objects, it externally craves and falsely seeks. One who follows the teaching of the Lamp-Light and suddenly brings the mind to rest realizes that consciousness depends upon wisdom;
thus, delusion and falsehood are naturally eliminated. When the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appears, one then achieves wondrous perfection.
Once delusion is removed, the lamp of the mind immediately appears. Once the lamp of the mind appears, then the myriad objects are wondrously perfect.

Having attained this wondrous perfection, samādhi is thereby realized. The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Within the entirety of emptiness, all Tathāgatas are my own mind.
The transformation of lands into purity or defilement is likewise the transformation of my own mind. From this, the immeasurable Buddha-nature [is revealed].
This is called "flowing forth.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with his peers, has attained samādhi; he is foremost among them.

Wuxing said: "The mother’s longing for her son is like a person who focuses intently on remembering; the son’s flight is like a person who focuses intently on forgetting. Question: Previously it was asked whether one meets [the Buddha] or not;
why here do you say only, "even though she remembers, what can be done"? Answer: Even if she were to meet and see him, she would not receive the benefit of the Dharma;

this is no different from his having fled. Is it not so with the nine hundred million households in Śrāvastī? This applies to those who have entered the realization of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When practicing through verification, the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha cannot be understood solely in terms of phenomenal characteristics.

Mindfulness must encompass the three contemplations (*san guan*), the Buddha possesses the three bodies (*trisambhava*), and the mind must shatter the three delusions (*san huo*) before one can enter the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Zizhong cites the *Amitābha Sūtra*—specifically the passage "this mind is the Buddha," etc.—to explain this; this is also a crucial point. As for "Pure Land" (*jìngtǔ*), it specifically refers to the Ultimate [Land].

This refers to the Land of Bliss and the Land of Quiescent Light. Regarding "completely gathering the six sense faculties": mindfulness belongs to the mental faculty (*manas*). If the mental faculty is pure, the other faculties are naturally gathered;
therefore, there is no need for selective effort.
Wenling says: The *Amitābha Sūtra* states, "With the light of wisdom, he universally illumines all, causing them to leave the three miserable realms and attain supreme power;
thus he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. It further states, "Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha must not allow even a single snap of the fingers' duration [to pass without it]."
To be mindful of the five worldly desires is called "binding the mind. It is like a person who must first bind their attention before they can achieve correspondence with the object.
If one does not single-mindedly recollect the Buddha, then even when encountering him one does not encounter him, and even when seeing him one does not see him.

Just as one who is smeared with fragrance is permeated by that fragrance, so too, by recollecting the Buddha, one sees the Buddha. Therefore, through the wondrous perfuming of mindfulness of the Buddha, it is called the "Adornment of Fragrance and Light."
The Sixth Chapter of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva... enters samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

(Wu Xing said: According to the following passage, it says: "Because I do not contemplate sound through contemplation, but rather contemplate the contemplator, I cause those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions to contemplate its sounds, whereby they immediately attain liberation.
This also accords with the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding the explanation of the name [Avalokiteśvara].
"Teaching" refers to worldly sound, and "hearing" refers to the faculty of the ear; both are the objects of contemplation. [This concerns] the cultivation of reflection.)

All of these are indeed contemplations. Thus, while contemplation enters through its objects and those objects truly pervade all things, the specific selection of sound as the object of hearing is the essential method for accommodating the capacities of sentient beings.
Wenling says: "Guanyin" means observing the sounds of the world; it is a title for perfect awakening and perfect response.
One speaks of "observing" (guan) regarding sound because one illuminates it with the wisdom of observation, rather than hearing it with the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*).

That the Buddha whom he takes as his teacher is also named Guanyin demonstrates that cause and effect correspond; the Way is one and the same throughout past and present. To reach the ear is what is called "hearing" (wen).

The application of the mind is called *cintā* (reflection); the cultivation of habituation is called *bhāvanā* (meditative development). When these three are perfectly clear and bright, they are termed the "three wisdoms.
First, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object; (continuing until: when birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
Wuxing said: "In the previous [text], the three kinds of wisdom were explained in successive order; now it is not so. The sections are divided into four.

First, 'losing the external objects' refers to the passage from 'first, within hearing' up to 'clearly non-arising. 'Entering the stream and losing the object': 'stream' refers to the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature).
This 'entering' and 'losing' of sounds and objects pertains to the stages of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) and semblance-realization (*xiangsi-wei*)."
As for the nature of the dharmas entered, since its essence is eternally quiescent, the external objects before one are fundamentally unmoving; now, there is likewise no stillness.

Thus it is said that "the two marks clearly do not arise. When the two [marks] are exhausted, the internal faculty is likewise gradually increased until what is heard and the hearing itself are both exhausted.
External objects are easy to eliminate, but the internal faculty is difficult to exhaust; this is because the wisdom of elimination has degrees of distance and intimacy.
"Clouds gradually increase" refers to the cessation of what is heard. "The hearing and that which is heard are exhausted" means that the faculty of hearing and the object heard likewise do not arise.

This cites the object to reveal the subject. The subsequent passages—"the perceiver and the perceived are empty," and "emptiness and that which is emptied are extinguished"—are to be understood by the same principle.
Lectan said: "The Śākya [Buddha] entered perfect penetration through the three types of wisdom.

'Entering the stream and losing the object' means not following after the dust of sound, suddenly entering the flow of the Dharma, and thereby losing the very object one has entered. The nature of sound is manifested through movement and stillness."
Therefore, once that which enters [the ears] has become tranquil, then movement and stillness do not arise; this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Having reached the ears, it further adheres to the mind, like water gradually filling a vessel or soil accumulating by degrees, such that both the faculty of hearing and the object heard vanish together.
When even the mind that exhausts hearing no longer abides, it unites with true awakening; this is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Once...

It is applied to the mind. One then uses it to treat habitual tendencies, enabling one to realize that both the subject of cognition and the object of cognition are entirely in accord with wondrous emptiness.

Thus, emptiness and awareness are non-dual; this is called ultimate perfection. When neither the capacity to empty nor the object to be emptied is established, this constitutes the path of exhaustion.
This is the cultivation of wisdom. Only then do birth-and-death and cessation mutually extinguish one another; subject and object are both exhausted, resulting in true stillness and true extinction.
The essence of perfect penetration thus manifests before one; this is what is called "entering samādhi.
Correlating this with the *Awakening of Faith*, the passage beginning with "entering the stream and losing the object" means that one should distance oneself from illusory and false realms.

The passage beginning with "thus gradually increasing" means that even the mind that perceives things as illusory must likewise be distanced. "The emptiness of the perceiver and the perceived" refers to distancing oneself [from these].
"Detachment is like an illusion; it is also a state of further distancing. When that which is empty and that which empties it both cease, this is detachment from distance as an illusion;
it is also a state of further distancing. Once birth and cessation have been extinguished, one attains that which has nothing to be detached from—this is the elimination of all illusions.
When quiescent extinction manifests before one, it is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the clarity appears. Reaching this point is perfect penetration."

This is the ultimate essence [of the teaching]. Wēn-líng says: "The wisdom of the contemplation of the three voids" refers to "exhausting hearing and not abiding," which is "the realization that the realized is void.

The former phrase eliminates the preceding mark of exhaustion; the latter phrase correctly establishes the wisdom of contemplation. "Realization" (jué) means illuminating awareness; it is the very substance of wisdom. Four.
The principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the ultimate perfection of the awakening to emptiness; it is the cessation of both emptiness and that which is emptied.
The preceding phrase reveals the wisdom of profound emptiness, while the latter correctly demonstrates the principle of the cessation of profound emptiness.
(Su Ziyou said: "The passage beginning with 'At first, within hearing' describes how, in the space of a single finger-snap, one traverses the three voids;
at that moment, one is no different from all Buddhas.")
Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane [realms]... [up to] being of one sorrow and longing with all sentient beings. (Xie Li said:

One should know that because sentient beings possess compassion (*karuṇā*), they are able to evoke the power to pull them from suffering; because Bodhisattvas possess loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they are able to respond to the capacity for longing for bliss.
The resonance between stimulus and response is ever-hidden, while the act of pulling [from suffering] is ever-manifest. If one understands this principle, then...)
Regarding the thirty-two manifestations mentioned in the following text, up to the four inconceivable powers—would one not forget their fundamental basis?
Wuxing said: "As for what was stated above regarding 'the power of compassion' (*maitrī-bala*), since compassion bestows happiness, it must also be able to extract suffering;

thus the character 'power' (*bala*) should encompass the meaning of 'compassion' (*karuṇā*). As for what is stated below regarding 'sorrowful yearning,' 'sorrow' refers to grieving over suffering, while 'yearning' refers to looking up toward happiness."
This does not refer to a formal correspondence; rather, it speaks of their spiritual capacity (*mūla*).

Therefore, those who feel weary of and afflicted by the path of suffering take compassion as their capacity, while those who rejoice in and aspire to the fruit of bliss take veneration as their response. The principle of universal penetration realized by the Bodhisattva is omnipresent within the compassion and veneration of sentient beings;
hence it is said that they are "with" [the beings] and "identical to" them.
World-Honored One, having received [the empowerment] from that Tathāgata... [up to]... it causes my body to manifest thirty-two transformations to enter all lands.
(Xie Li says: "The illusion" metaphorizes the essence of the three types of wisdom, which is ungraspable; "vajra" metaphorizes the power to crush what is solid.)
Wenling said: "The activities of the illusory person are rooted in non-action; therefore, this refers to the Illusory Samādhi, while the subsequent reference is to the wondrous power of non-action.
This samādhi begins with habitual cultivation and concludes with neither cultivation nor realization;
it takes decisive wisdom and severance as its ultimate firmness, serving as the true reception (*samāpatti*). As for the thirty-two manifestations, ten [are shown]..."

The Dharma-realm body universally responds to all capacities; when opened, it manifests in thirty-two forms, encompassing all categories of beings from the four types of noble ones to the six classes of ordinary beings.
World-Honored One, if various bodhisattvas enter samādhi... [and so forth] ...the Buddha speaks the Dharma for them to bring about their liberation.

(Gushan said: "The Bodhisattva possesses the capacities of both the Separate and Perfect Teachings. If they enter the semblance *samādhi* and advance in the cultivation of the untainted Middle Way, then their partial realization (*fenzhen*) of superior understanding will become manifest and perfect.
Furthermore, if they advance in the cultivation of the adamantine (*vajra*) untainted state, then their ultimate (*jiu*) superior understanding will become manifest and perfect.
In all such cases, the Great Being manifests the Buddha-body and preaches the Sudden Dharma, causing them to attain partial realization and ultimate realization. )
[Regarding] liberation from objects:
the Ultimate Reality (bhūtakoṭi) says that cultivating right concentration and attaining the right fruit is called "advancing in the cultivation of the untainted" (anāsrava).

When both object and wisdom are forgotten and both emotional attachments and intellectual understandings are extinguished, it is named "the perfection of the manifestation of resolute belief" (adhimukti). By this, one may attain Buddhahood; therefore, he manifests the Buddha-body to preach for them.
This refers to the dharmas of fruition.
If there are those in training (*śaikṣa*) who possess tranquil, wondrous, and luminous [wisdom]... [the Buddha] preaches the Dharma for them so that they may attain liberation.

[Xie Li says: "Those in training" refers to the lesser *śrāvakas*. "Luminous" means being able to wondrously transform all things; because they take this luminosity as their own nature, it is so called.]
"Exquisite and sublime.
Wénlǐng says: "The Pratyekabuddha appears in an age when no Buddha is present; by observing the transformation of phenomena, he personally realizes non-arising, and is thus called 'Solitary Realizer.
Delighting in solitary tranquility and seeking natural wisdom, he is therefore termed 'Tranquil, Sublime, and Luminous. This refers to the Pratyekabuddha."

This means that by receiving the Buddha’s teaching, one contemplates conditions (*pratyaya*) to awaken to the Way. One realizes that the delusion of the supreme nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) arises through the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), and thus severs them.
From the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) up to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, the conditions are severed and the supreme nature manifests.
Because the nature manifests due to the severance of conditions, it is called "the supreme nature through the severance of conditions."
Xie Li said: "To realize the Way through the observation of conditions is called the Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. Xie Li said:
"'The Victorious Subtlety Manifests Perfection' refers to each [vehicle] attaining this name as their respective fundamental wisdom and principle are about to manifest before them."
If there are those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have attained the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, [the Buddha] preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve liberation.
(Xie Li says: From the stage prior to the third fruit, all positions of the noble ones belong to the category of those in training. This includes the sixteen moments of mind of the Path of Seeing.)
By severing the afflictions pertaining to the Four Truths and realizing the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), one is said to "attain the emptiness of the Four Truths.

Subsequently, upon advancing from the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one severs the eighty-one grades of innate afflictions across the three realms and realizes a portion of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*). Therefore, it is said that "one enters cessation through the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*)."
Xie Li said: "To sever the coarse delusions beneath the Four Noble Truths is called attaining the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths.

To rely on the cultivation of the Truth of the Path and realize the fruit of the Truth of Cessation is called entering cessation through the path of cultivation. This is not yet the subtle substance that independently realizes the nature of emptiness;

therefore, it is said that 'the supreme nature manifests its perfection. The reason the four types of noble ones do not include the Bodhisattva is that they are already subsumed within the stage of Buddhahood."
If there are sentient beings who desire to attain clear awakening... [he] preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve it.
(Gushan says: The Brahma King is the Lord of the Form Realm, named Śikhin, which means "Crest.
What is here called "Brahma" should refer to the summit of the First Dhyāna, for by means of the dharmas of vitarka, vicāra, and speech, he attained sovereignty over a thousand worlds.)
Regarding the one who preaches the Dharma: as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the Great Brahmā King expounds the Discourse on Transcending Desire (*niḥsaraṇa-śāstra*).

Śakra, the second lord of the heavens in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), preaches the Dharma, namely the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala*). Īśvara is the highest heaven within the desire realm.
In full, he is called Vaśavartin; this means "Mastery over Others' Emanations. Because he utilizes the creations of others to fulfill his own pleasures, he is the Māra King.
Mahāśvara is the Maheśvara Deva at the summit of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu). As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"He who has three eyes and eight arms, rides a white ox, and holds a white fly-whisk—this is he."
Letan said: "Because Brahmā transcends the realm of desire, his mind is able to attain clear awakening;
he does not violate the dust of desire, and his physical faculties are pure, whereby he is born there. Śakra is the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, governing the thirty-three heavens;
liberation allows him to leave behind the dust of desire. He wanders with sovereign ease, hence he is named the Sovereign Heaven (Īśvara), which is the pinnacle of the realm of desire."
He also transforms others. Flying through the void, he is named Maheśvara; this is Mahesvara at the summit of the realm of form (rūpāvacara).

From the initial mention of the Brahma King up to this point, [the text] proceeds from the heavens of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the heavens of the form realm, skipping directly to the summit of the realm of form;
its intention includes the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) as well, to clarify that there is no land where he does not appear.
If there are sentient beings who love presiding over ghosts and spirits (up to: he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve fulfillment).
(Wenling says: The previous passage cited the primary sovereign; this passage cites the ministerial assistants.)
Gushan said: "The Heavenly General serves as the supreme commander for Śakra Devendra, presiding over ghosts and spirits. The Four Heavenly Kings are his ministers;
they serve Śakra and preside over the world. The princes of the Four Heavenly Kings are those such as Nāṭa, who are capable of driving away ghosts and spirits."
If there are devas who desire to leave their celestial status... [and so forth]... he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
(Gushan says: *Yakṣa* here means "light and swift. *Gandharva* means "fragrance-body"; in the new translation it is rendered as "seeker of fragrance.
This is the music deity of Śakra. *Asura* means "not upright," because while the women are beautiful, the men are ugly.)
The name is derived from the male [aspect]. The new translation is *asura* (non-god), because they lack the conduct of gods due to their flattery and deceit.

According to the section on the "Universal Gate" (*Samantamukha-parivarta*), this category lacks the *garuḍa*, which is the golden-winged bird (*suparṇin*). The *kiṃnara* has a form resembling a human, yet clearly possesses horns; for this reason, they are called the "doubtful deities.
They are the musical deities of the celestial lord (*indra*) who play stringed and wind instruments; they are slightly inferior to the *gandharva*. The new translation says...
Gāndharvas; mahoragas (Master Shi [Xuanzang] says "earth dragons"; Master Zhao [Sengzhao] says "great pythons that travel on their bellies").
Changshui says: "Those with form include those such as the *xiujiao* and *jingming*; those without form include those such as the *kong*, *san*, *xiao*, and *shen*;
those with thought include spirits and ghosts; those without thought include spirits transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone—all of these are not [the true self]."
(They are human beings).

Wēnlíng says: These are the classes such as the devas, nāgas, and the eight divisions of spirits who delight in being human and aspire to be human. Although these classes resemble humans, they are not truly so;
therefore, they take pleasure in being born into the human realm. "Various non-humans" refers to those with form and those without form, those with thought and those without thought.
These are spirits of refined intelligence who preside over fortune and misfortune, belonging to the category of those who are empty, scattered, and submerged.

As for why the six classes of ordinary beings do not include hell-dwellers, ghosts, and animals—it is because these types are currently sunk in profound obscurity and have not yet been able to hear the Dharma; therefore, [the Bodhisattva] uses the power of bestowing fearlessness to rescue them.
This is called the wondrous purity of the thirty-two manifestations (up to) the accomplishment of effortless, wondrous power and sovereignty.

(Wu-xing says: Although the thirty-two manifestations differ slightly from those in the "Universal Gate" chapter in their specific appearances and omissions, they are essentially the same in their fundamental nature.)

In brief, there is nothing that transcends the ten realms. Within these ten realms, the fact that both sutras lack mention of the bodies of bodhisattvas and hell-beings is merely a condensation of the holy word.
Wenling says: "To manifest traces among those of the same class while the mind is free from attachment and views is called 'wondrous purity.

To give rise to great spiritual efficacy based on non-active wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) is called 'wondrous power. To respond universally according to conditions, being both unconditioned and uncreated, is called 'the accomplishment of mastery.'"
“World-Honored One, by further cultivating this practice of hearing through hearing, I have obtained fourteen kinds of fearless merit.
(As Wēnlíng says: ‘Because I do not observe my own sounds, others obtain liberation from suffering; because I know and see how [the faculties] revolve back, ...’”)”
Yet he is able not to be burned; therefore it is said that "within my body and mind, he has attained the virtue of fearlessness.
First, because I do not observe myself [as a separate entity], I bestow the power of fearlessness upon sentient beings, fully equipping them with merit.

(Wu Xing said: "The Sage has no self-interest; he benefits only all things. Therefore, by applying the wisdom of Avalokiteśvara to the capacity of those who observe sounds, they are liberated from suffering before their feet have even turned.
These three—'at hearing,' 'in speech,' and 'in observation'—are like 'sound,' 'speech,' and 'observation' respectively.
(Xie Li said: "Entering into the mundane world without destroying the world is skillful means (*upāya*). Skillful means belongs to...")

*Quán* (Skillful Means). Skillful means is able to manage affairs; therefore, it gives rise to the male. The establishment of the Great Perfect Mirror-like *Tathāgatagarbha* belongs to Real Wisdom (*shizhi*).
Real Wisdom accords with principle; principle is able to contain and nurture; therefore, it gives rise to the female. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of Bodhisattvas; Upāya is taken as the father. This is precisely that meaning. (Gushan says: "The fundamental root of perfect penetration...")
The wondrous [name] contains both self and other without duality; thus, it causes the merit of holding my name to be equal to that [of the Buddha].
This should accord with the equality of the one and the many within the Dharma-realm. Generally speaking, this applies to a single body and multiple bodies, as well as to other realms and this realm.

When one cultivates a single merit and a single wisdom, one attains true perfection without limit. As for names and things, each is perfectly pervasive yet distinct. (Supplementary Note: This is the interpretation of Wénlǐng.)

The interpretation of Wuxing holds that "observing sound" refers to the response [of the Buddha]. The interpretation of [Zhi]wen holds that "observing sound" refers to the capacity [of the practitioner]. These two explanations must not be discarded unilaterally;

therefore, they are preserved together. Wenling says: "Not observing by means of the ear" means not following the cognitions and views that arise from the sense-object of sound. By means of observation...
"Observation" means turning back the mechanism of hearing and reflecting inward upon one's own nature. When no cognitions or views arise, there is nothing delusory;
when one reflects inward upon one's own nature, all things are truly quiescent, and no further suffering or affliction can be found.
This is true observation, pure observation, and the observation of great wisdom; it can shatter the darkness of ignorance and subdue calamities. First, internally and externally...

The four great elements are constantly interacting and influencing one another. Vision and cognition belong to fire; hearing and listening belong to water. Thus, when the activity of vision interacts, one sees fierce flames;
when the activity of hearing interacts, one sees surging waves. Now, you know that when vision turns back upon itself, there is no longer any activity of vision.

When seeing and hearing revolve back to their source, the karma of hearing ceases; this is the second. When deluded thoughts are extinguished, the mind is free from killing and harming; this is the third.
When one perfumes the deluded hearing until it becomes the true nature of hearing, once a single faculty is perfected, the six faculties are all dissolved and restored.
They become identical to the hearing of sound, no longer obstructed by physical forms; this is the fifth. The brilliance of the hearing-perfuming scatters that profound darkness.
Sixth: When the nature of sound is completely dissolved, there is nothing within to which one is bound. When hearing and seeing turn back inward, there is nothing without to which one is entangled.
Seventh: When sound and hearing stand as two, then object and self become adversaries. Now, when sound is extinguished and hearing is perfected, there is no dependence on either internal or external.
Eighth: Sentient beings join with sensory objects through the habit-energy of desire, and are thus ravaged by form. One who can [use] gold...
Thus, through samādhi, the cultivation of hearing perfects one's nature, enabling one to depart from sensory objects. When the nature is perfected, the craving for desire dries up;

when one departs from objects, the faculties and their spheres no longer encounter one another. This is the ninth [stage]. Anger arises from the violation of one's sentiments and is produced in response to external objects.

Since the nature of sound is pure, there are no longer deluded objects; thus, it is perfectly integrated and free of contradiction, with neither subject nor object to oppose. This is the tenth [stage]. As for ignorance...
Obscured by delusive objects and shrouded by ignorance, when the dust is dissipated there is no obscuration, and when the light is turned inward there is no shroud.
Thus, the external dharma-realm and the internal body and mind become crystalline, pure, and brilliantly penetrating—this is the eleventh [stage].
When form is dissolved, obstruction ceases; when returning to hearing, the nature is true. Therefore, one enters the world without movement or decay, and is able to pervade it all.

Throughout the ten directions, they make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, receiving and upholding their teachings as each becomes a Dharma-son. By making offerings to the Buddhas, they possess sufficient merit;

by receiving the Dharma, they possess sufficient wisdom, thereby able to succeed the Dharma King and embody the Way of a man. This is the twelfth [stage]. Regarding the phrase "the six faculties are perfectly penetrating" (*liugen yuantong*):

because they are perfect (*yuan*), there is no duality; because they are penetrating (*tong*), they encompass the realms. Their luminous illumination is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
This is her substance. To contain the realms is the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness.

Possessing this, she is able to accord with the Dharma-gate and receive it without error. "Accordance" is the gentle virtue of the earth (*kūn-yí*); "receiving" is the domestic duty of the inner chambers.
Such is the way of a woman—this is the thirteenth [point]. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also contains such a comparison; and now, upon observation...
Only then did he fully understand the meaning of that passage. It is because the faculty of hearing is sharp among the sentient beings of this land that those who receive the Way are numerous;
therefore, Avalokiteśvara’s transformation is superior. Because the other faculties are dull, those who receive the Way are few; therefore, the transformations of the other sages are inferior.
This shows that although the stages of practice are equal, there are differences according to the capacities of the practitioners.

Even if one were to match all those beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges against Āvalokiteśvara alone, it would cause these two merits to be specifically declared as equal. Based on this teaching, the Ear-faculty Perfect Penetration has already been subtly singled out;
for those who do not yet understand, we await Mañjuśrī’s detailed selection. As for the "ten billion suns and moons," [it refers to the ten billion worlds].
"A hundred billion lands. This is the concluding summary below.
(14) "World-Honored One, I have further attained this perfect penetration... up to the four inconceivable, effortless, and wondrous virtues."
Wenling says: "Manifesting manifold forms and reciting each individual mantra, he gathers and transforms sentient beings, perfectly responding to their needs.
This principle arises from the unconditioned (*asamskrta*); its spiritual resonance occurs in the unfathomable. Thus it is named 'Inconceivable and Uncreated Wondrous Virtue'."
First, from the time I first attained the mind of wondrous and sublime hearing (*śruta-citta*) until I achieved great mastery in rescuing and protecting sentient beings.
(Xie Li said: "However, whereas the former [section] manifested forms in response to seekers alone, this is called 'inconceivable' (*acintya*). The former was a brief manifestation;
this further clarifies it deeply. For instance, manifesting eighty thousand heads and arms within a single body is truly beyond the reach of thought.")
(Complementary Note: From the truly wondrous and perfect, one again gives rise to the truly wondrous; this is called the "wondrously wondrous hearing-mind.
When the hearing is turned back to detach from sound, one returns alone to the true source; this is called the "essence of mind leaving behind hearing.

Because one attains this wondrous state of leaving behind hearing, the myriad sensory objects do not obstruct the single, perfectly integrated awakening, and thus manifestations respond without impediment). (Some say that the eighty-four thousand [dharmas] merely represent the Dharma. One...
What can the body possibly bestow? This is merely using a mind of conceptual thought to gauge the Bodhisattva’s realm of perfect penetration.
Now, the body contains the ten voids, and within a single hair-tip, entire lands appear. Those voids and lands are not merely like heads and arms;
those eighty-four thousand heads and arms are no more than the eighty-four thousand pores of a human being. Not yet...
How extraordinary are the words of the Sage! They accord with both phenomena and principle. Since they are called "inconceivable virtues," there is nothing by which to limit their intent.
To contemplate and deliberate upon them: *śakara* means adamantine, firm, and indestructible; *mudrā* means seal—each possesses its own wondrous seal.
The pure jewel-eyes are free from dust and united with awakening. Through compassion, they gather and transform beings; through majesty...
Subdue them with concentration (*samādhi*), restore them to stillness through meditative absorption, and awaken them through wisdom (*prajñā*).
This collectively indicates the many wondrous manifestations [of the Bodhisattvas]. Wēnlíng says: "The mention of 'initially attaining' refers to the original cause.
'Head' represents the compassion that gathers and receives; 'eyes' represent the wisdom that illuminates and understands. Each is expanded according to its original number, up to eight."
The "fourteen thousand" represents relying upon the six fundamental functions and fundamental wisdom and compassion to respond universally to worldly afflictions and attain great mastery;
this is the wondrous practice of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) within the eleven stages. This occurs prior to the ten stages of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Relying still upon fundamental wisdom, one nurtures great compassion until the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*), where the cultivation reaches its consummation.

At this point, it becomes purely great compassion, constituting the essence of the *dharmadhātu*. Because it manifests perfectly together with wisdom, the hands and eyes of Avalokiteśvara pervade his entire body;
thus, he is celebrated as "Great Compassion."
Second, by means of my hearing and contemplation, I have emerged from the six sense-objects... (up to) "giving up their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassionate pity.

(Changshui says: The secret mantras of the Guhyatantra were mostly created by Avalokiteśvara; they can bring peace and happiness to sentient beings and are called 'Bestowing Fearlessness'. (Xielü says:

By means of the wisdoms of hearing and contemplation, one emerges from the dust of the senses without obstruction; therefore, he manifests forms and recites mantras, displaying wondrous spiritual transformations.)
Power. Each is unimpeded; this is called "wondrous capability. Wēnlíng says:
When the fundamental root is pure, there is no attachment to anything; therefore, one can cause sentient beings to abandon all stinginess and attachment.
As for those who seek my compassion, I receive them with compassion and perform buddha-work for them.
Fourth, I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate [state], seeking great nirvāṇa and attaining great nirvāṇa.

(Wuxing says: These four inconceivables—the first two pertain to the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and the latter two correspond to the capacity of sentient beings. Within the response, both benefits of form and voice are fully manifested.
Although the initial passage mentions the recitation of mantras, it primarily demonstrates the benefit of form; this is the functional power of the response-body.)
Furthermore, although the subsequent passage manifests his physical form, it primarily demonstrates the benefit of his voice—that is, his renown is heard everywhere).
Wēnlíng says: "Attaining the realization of the Buddha-mind fulfills wisdom; offering precious jewels fulfills merit.
Because both merit and wisdom are fulfilled, he extends his influence to all sentient beings, causing their aspirations to be realized according to their wishes."
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, and I [responded] from the gateway of the ear... (up to) "therefore, the name Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

(Wuxing says: According to the *Avalokiteśvara Samādhi Sūtra* and the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra*, it is stated that this Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood long ago in the past, with the title *Saddharmaprabhāsa*.
Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that in the past, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha conferred [the prophecy upon him].)
