When afflictions are purified and clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.
The great assembly and Ānanda, turn back that inverted hearing-faculty... (up to)... it is not only Avalokiteśvara [who does so].
(Zhenji said: "The Gate of Nirvāṇa" refers to the essential path for transcending birth and death and realizing true permanence.
No realized beings of the three periods of time have failed to pass through this; therefore, future practitioners should rely upon this Dharma.)
Wenling said: "To be able to overturn delusion and turn back to hear one's own nature must rely upon this nature to achieve the Unsurpassed Way;
this is the actual efficacy of this Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration."
"Truly, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, questioned me regarding various skillful means (up to) 'teaching the Dharma equally regardless of depth,' (Gushan says:
'As' [ji] is like the blind man regaining his sight through the Vinaya; Pi-ling losing his body upon touching thorns;
Wu-chu ascending to enlightenment through revulsion for desire; and Chi-ti awaiting the Buddha to dissolve his dust—all these are simply matters of one's own self). (Wuxing)
It is said: This is because those in this land who attain enlightenment through various skillful means do so by the power of the Buddha.
(If it were otherwise—that in other lands the faculty of the ear were sharp while other faculties were dull—the implication would be evident by contrast.)
Wenling said: "To achieve the wondrous mind of nirvana—which is neither born nor extinguished—the faculty of the ear-root is supreme.
Other methods rely on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power to bestow grace, causing one to abandon worldly toil through one's own immediate practice;
they are not teachings for long-term cultivation that apply equally to both shallow and deep capacities. To enable such long-term cultivation for all alike, none is like that of Avalokiteśvara."
...the Dharma-gate.
I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, the untainted and inconceivable (until) the true mind, thus [ends the verse].
(Changshui said: The Tathāgatagarbha is the Three Jewels in essence, for it is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature.)
"True mind" (refers to Mañjuśrī’s pointing to the mind he had already selected as the perfect penetration).
Lètán said: "This concludes the praise of the three periods of hearing-perfuming. It is the gate of the untainted Dharma of the Tathāgata-garbha.
It is an exhortation for those in the future to rely upon this for cultivation and realization; it can transcend other samādhis. Such is the true heart-essence."
Thereupon Ānanda and the great assembly (until) clearly understood the path leading back to their home.
[Changshui said: "Ānanda and the others had just realized that the perfect penetration lies in entering through the faculty of hearing, yet they had not yet attained realization;
therefore it is said that they 'clearly understood the path leading back to their home'."]
Wuxing said: "In the third fascicle, the verse by Ānanda states: 'I have eliminated my inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas;

without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, I have attained the Dharma-body. Yet, in the fourth fascicle, he requests entry into the 'flowered house,' whereas previously it was said that he had heard the Buddha’s instructions."
Doubts were eliminated, and his mind awakened to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). At the end of the fifth fascicle, following the verses of the Tathāgata, it says:
"The eye and mind opened and became clear; he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Furthermore, regarding the request for the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), it says:

"Today our bodies and minds are radiant and bright; we have swiftly attained unimpededness. Combining the previous instances with this one, Master Yuan clearly and manifestly realized the truth on five occasions.
To judge this, it is necessarily logical that this serves to increase Ānanda’s realization of the Path.

One should understand that the author of the sutra points to the wondrous enlightenment of Bodhi and Nirvana as the "home," and the true cultivation of the perfect penetration of the ear-organ as the "path.
Were it otherwise, the nature of the Joyful One (Ānanda) would have been nearly obscured by ignorance.
Ānanda adjusted his robes amidst the great assembly... [until] he attained a state of non-retrogression regarding the Bodhi-mind. (Wenling’s Commentary states:

Ānanda intended to use this Dharma to deliver sentient beings; fearing that during the many calamities of the final kalpa, demons and malevolent spirits would easily cause the mind of awakening to regress and make it difficult to enter right concentration, he requested that the mind be gathered to keep distant from demons, so as to establish a pure site for the Way.)
[The rules of conduct].
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly... [omitted] "...you should now listen attentively; I shall speak for you. (Gushan says:
The studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom are practiced equally by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. This demonstrates the principle of resolute progress in cultivation.)
Ānanda and the great assembly responded, "So be it," and received the instruction... (up to)... this is what is called the Threefold Training in the Absence of Outflows (*trīṇy-āśravakṣayāṇi*).

[Xie Li says: From here below, the four grave offenses are specifically shown; namely, among the ten precepts, the first four—sexual misconduct, theft, lying, and the four *pārājika* offenses—are the fundamental grave sins.
What is meant by "his mind does not engage in sexual misconduct" and "his mind does not steal," and so forth, are all...]
This ensures that there is no transgression through thoughtlessness; in maintaining the rules of conduct (*vinaya*), nothing is more esteemed than this. Wēnlíng says:
"Among the Three Piṭakas, the *Vinaya* is the Piṭaka of Discipline (*vinaya-piṭaka*). This is the general designation for the precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
In the Hīnayāna, receiving the Dharma constitutes the precept, which roughly governs the external manifestations. In the Mahāyāna, the restraint of the mind constitutes the precept, which is subtle."
To sever its root: regarding the precept of the Dharma, it is simply to refrain from transgression; regarding the precept of the mind, it is to have no thought of transgression.
Now, if one is able to restrain the mind, concentration arises thereby, and wisdom is developed thereby. When these three are perfectly clear and bright, all outflows are forever exhausted;
therefore, they are called the Threefold Training in the Outflow-free.
Ānanda, how does one restrain the mind? That which I call "precept" (śīla) [extends] until each individual claims to have realized the Unsurpassed Way.

(Gushan says: To maintain [the precepts] is to emerge from the entanglements; to violate them is to fall into the ways of demons and māras. (Gushan says: To commit the four grave prohibitions is a sin that leads to the hells;
yet now, by the power of practicing dhyāna, one merely falls into the paths of ghosts, devils, and the like. If we consider this from the perspective of the unconditioned...)

They come to transmigrate through the cycles of existence; it is clear that they must pass through the three miserable realms. (Xing Jianzi said: "These correspond to the following two sections, which demonstrate to sentient beings how to sever lust and cultivate dhyāna.")
Wenling said: "All sentient beings bind themselves to birth and death because they take their true nature and destiny (xing-ming) through lustful desire.

If the craving for desire were to wither away, then this residual physical form would no longer continue. Even Māra possesses great wisdom and practices dhyāna, yet he does so because he has not severed lust."
Therefore, one does not accomplish the Noble Path. To practice dhyāna while harboring lust inevitably leads to this class [of beings].
This is my first definitive, pure, and clear instruction for the period of the Final Dharma after my parinirvāṇa.

(Zizhong said: "Observe Ānanda’s initiation of the teaching: he was shown to have encountered defilement by the wicked, yet from the very beginning of his resolve for enlightenment, he first loathed the turbidity of desire.
Throughout the three gradual stages, he rectified each one at its head. Only then did his body and mind become wondrously perfect and attain great peace and stability.

At the initial stage of the ten faiths, because the craving of desire had been dried up, his nature of wisdom became perfectly luminous, and he subsequently ascended through the stages of the Equal and Wondrous [Enlightenments]. Worldly...)

When the human mind does not flow toward dissipation, clarity and brilliance arise. This gradually extends through the six heavens; therefore, true cultivation that encompasses within must first involve the departure from desire.
Wēnlíng says: "In all sutras, the prohibition against killing is placed at the head, for the establishment of transformation takes compassion as its foundation. This sutra..."

The precept against sexual misconduct stands at the forefront. This is because true cultivation takes the departure from desire as its foundation. For the energy of desire is coarse and turbid, defiling the wondrous clarity;

the habitual tendencies of desire lead to madness and delusion, easily causing one to lose right concentration (*samāpatti*). Nothing is more extreme than this in terms of perpetuating birth and death and losing the eternal truth.
Therefore, it must be the foremost precept, serving as the primary and most luminous instruction for purity.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever lust... (up to) if it is not spoken thus, it is the speech of Pāpīyān.
(Changshui said: "If gold is used to make vessels, the vessels are all gold; if earth is used to make vessels, the vessels are all earth"—referring to such things as sand and stone.
(Wenling said: "The 'trigger' (*jī*) is that which is spontaneously aroused by the lustful mind; while the nature of severance is not non-existent, it is triggered when it encounters the stimulus.")
"Indeed. Pāpīyan (the name of Māra). Xie Li said:
'The fundamental substance is not beautiful; to seek and hope for it is but vain labor.
Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds... [down to] ...those who eat the flesh of sentient beings are called sons of the Śākya."
(Xing commented: "This combines with the following section to show sentient beings how to cultivate dhyāna by severing the taking of life.

Wuxing said: "Regarding the five kinds of pure meat, the Vinaya clarifies three kinds of purity: not seeing that it was killed for one's sake, not hearing that it was killed for one's sake, and not suspecting that it was killed for one's sake.
The present mention of five kinds adds two more: meat from animals that died naturally and meat left over by birds. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* lists nine kinds of pure meat.
That is, regarding the three types of pure meat, each is opened up to include the actual transgression as well as the preliminary and subsequent preparatory acts. (Wenling says:

Not seeing, not hearing, and so forth constitute five [conditions]. That which is transformed by supernatural power is called "pure" because it originally lacks the life-faculty. This, however, is a provisional teaching of the Hīnayāna.)
If true compassion and true liberation were both subject to cessation, [it would contradict the following]: "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) is a general term for those who practice pure conduct.

Because the Brahmins are considered the highest among the four castes in the West, the land of the five heavens is designated as the "Country of the Brahmins," and the *saṃgha* is also referred to as "Brahmins."

Wenling says: "You owe me my life; I return your debt. This is why [the cycle of] continuity persists. The passage beginning with "If the murderous intent is not eliminated" refers to practicing dhyāna while harboring a murderous mind;
such a person will inevitably fall into the class of spirits. Gushan says: Question: All the Vinayas clarify that fish and meat may be consumed as "timely food" (*kālika-bhojana*).
Yet, only the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the present sutra all proclaim the total abstention from meat. Why is this so? Answer:

In preaching the Dharma to suit the capacities of beings, there are both sudden and gradual approaches. This is true for meditative concentration and wisdom; it is likewise so for the precepts and regulations.

Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* establishes a sudden prohibition against eating meat, intended for those with the capacities of the Separate and Perfect Teachings. However, since the Deer Park, the *Vinaya* has established prohibitions gradually.

For those of the *zàng* (Āgama) and *tōng* (Vaipulya) capacities, he thus opened the three [stages of] purity. As his path of transformation was nearing its end, he withdrew the gradual and returned to the sudden;

thereupon, all three sutras proclaimed the cessation of meat-eating. While the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* restricted this to Bodhisattvas of the *zàng* and *tōng* vehicles, this sutra restricts it universally for all three vehicles.
Thus, it says below: "Pure bhikṣus and all bodhisattvas do not tread upon living grass," and so forth. Furthermore...
Until the attainment of Nirvana, he further strictly regulated the śrāvakas, earnestly instructing and informing them.
(Xie Li said: "Regarding pure meat, one must further exclude ten types—humans, snakes, elephants, horses, donkeys, dogs, lions, boars, monkeys, and apes.
This is because these ten types, even if one has neither seen nor heard of their slaughter, are nonetheless forbidden to eat.")
"You all should know that these people who eat meat—[omitted]—if they do not speak in this way, it is the speech of Pāpīyān. (Wenling says:

To cultivate meditation in order to avoid transgression, yet instead commit acts of killing; to plug one's ears to avoid others, yet instead raise one's voice loudly—this is to conceal what one desires and yet reveal it all the more.
Not intentionally treading upon things, not intentionally pulling them up—their benevolence and compassion extend even to plants and trees, let alone [human beings].)
"Or do they eat the flesh of sentient beings?
Ānanda, furthermore, from the beings of the six realms in the world... each and every one of them claims to have realized the Unsurpassed Way.
(Wenling says: To take what is not given constitutes theft; if one exceeds the amount owed and is still pursued for the surplus, how much more so...)
This was then stolen; could it not be that this is a retribution for the past? (This refers to the previous continuity of birth and death.
Xie Li said: "The heterodox path is treacherous and deceitful; therefore, a thief will surely fall into the class of ghosts."
"After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma (up to the point where) immeasurable sentient beings fall into the Avīci Hell.
(Master Zhaolun said: "There are briefly four intentions for begging for food: first, to bring benefit and merit to sentient beings; second, to subdue arrogance;
third, to realize that the body is subject to suffering; and fourth, to eliminate attachment. The present sutra intends to cause them to abandon greed.")
Not cooking food for oneself means gradually removing attachments. Accomplishing the path of Bodhi means protecting the power of the Way to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Knowing that the body is but a temporary lodging and the world is but a transient sojourn, one does not amass stores nor harbor any lingering attachments;
these are what is meant by "following the proper direction. To be unable to follow this direction, yet greedily and gluttonously create karma, is to ruin the Dharma.
"Because they destroy [the Dharma], they are called 'thieves'.

Wēnlíng says: "Method" means the way. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Begging for food is called 'participating in the protection' (*fenwei*), meaning that one distributes alms to the community of monks and thereby protects the power of the Way."
"You teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*... (up to) if it is not stated thus, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
(Xing Jianzi said: "This combines with the preceding two sections to show sentient beings how to sever theft while practicing dhyāna.")
Master Xingjian said: "Below this, there is still the precept against great falsehood, which is not recorded here. Wénlǐng remarked:
"The three trainings were initially set forth, yet the conclusion stops at four precepts because the aspects of concentration and wisdom have already been fully provided in the preceding text."
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Attainment through the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Chapter Seven:
"Ānanda, regarding your question on the gathering of the mind, I shall first explain [up to] how all demonic activities arise."

(Xie Li said: "The four dharmas of the mouth are the root; the remaining precepts are the branches. (Zhenji said: "The 'four of the mouth' refers to the four beginning with false speech and frivolous talk.
Thus, the 'false speech' mentioned previously refers to the major [offense], while this 'false speech' here refers to the minor. Alternatively, it may simply be citing the total number.")
Wenling said: "Internal restraint is the essential; therefore, the wondrous gate is explained first. First, one maintains the four precepts.

When the four precepts are pure and clean, the branches and leaves do not sprout, conditions and dust do not encounter one another, and demonic affairs are subtly eliminated, so that one may enter right concentration.
The 'three of mind' refers to the three of the mental faculty; this fully enumerates the ten grave precepts."
Moreover, what difficulty could there have been for you in your past lives—from your time with Mātanga to being carried aloft by a favorable wind?

(Wenling says: Even one of such lustful nature as Mātanga was still able to realize realization so swiftly; how much more easily can those with the capacity of a Śrāvaka receive the aid of the profound mystery.)
"How much more so when they are combined? (Xie Li said: "Dust represents long-standing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); wind is like a divine spell (*mantra*).
To scatter dust by fanning it with the wind is easy; to eliminate habitual tendencies by reciting spells is no less difficult.")
Wuxing said: "The eternal liberation from the heart of attachment" refers to his initial hearing of the mantra and attaining the stage of Anāgāmin.
"Attaining Arhatship" refers to the period following Mañjuśrī’s selection of the perfect means of penetration (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) mentioned in the preceding text.

If this is so, since he only attained the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) by virtue of hearing the Dharma, how can it be said that his spiritual power provided secret assistance? This is because he secretly received the power of the mantra while manifestly relying on the sound of the Dharma; internally...

It is only through external cultivation that one can realize [the goal] swiftly. If it were due to the mantra alone and not due to the Dharma, why was it previously stated that the Bhikṣuṇī Śīlavatī attained Arhatship after hearing the recitation of the verses?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [up to] "...mixing the soil to form mud with which to smear the site. (Wenling says:

This is a request for the detailed rules regarding the establishment of the altar. As for the statement "knowing one's own cultivation and realization," it means knowing that the power of the mantra provides secret assistance, and that the holy fruit can be expected.
(Changshui says: The milk of the snow-mountain cow is entirely *ghṛta* [the finest essence].)
All meat-eating is abandoned; it is most fragrant and pure. (Wuxing says: "The altar is the foundation for construction;
faith is the root of entering the Way. The white ox of the Snowy Mountains is taken for its absolute purity. (Gushan says:
"Now, one who wishes to take up the site of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa must base themselves on vast faith and rely upon pure wisdom and wondrous goodness to bring them to maturity. )
The great root of pure unity is so abundant and overflowing that it is more than sufficient to accord with the Dharma. Its fragrance surpasses the ten stages;
thus, it can adorn and perfect the site of nirvana. Since the great root of supreme faith is unattainable, one seeks the next best.
Therefore, by adopting this "middling-of-the-middling" faith, although one may not yet surpass the ten perfections and myriad practices,
one who is able to possess it can likewise achieve solemn completion.
Wenling says: "The Dharma King’s words on the Dharma encompass both phenomena and principle. Phenomena do not arise in isolation, nor are phenomena established in vain.
Even a single character of the *Avataṃsaka*’s Dharma-gate would exhaust the ink of the ocean without being fully recorded.

The characteristics of the five stages of practice are manifested through conventional truth; how much more so for the ritual implements and arrangements, which must necessarily embody symbolic imagery. Thus, these altar arrangements and requisites..."
This is not a description of external phenomena. The mountain represents lofty ground; the Snowy Mountains represent pure, supreme faith. The great, powerful white ox represents the pure, great root.
The fragrant herbs and clear water represent wondrous, excellent, and pure wisdom. The abundance of withered grass represents the remains [of practice].
Superior sandalwood is the foremost among the ten perfumes, the synthesis of the ten perfections, and the crown of the myriad practices.

The original state is level ground, which signifies faith. That the surface of the earth has not yet been purified signifies that, within the number five and within the color yellow, one takes the purity of the "middle-of-the-middle" faith.
The ten fragrances are the Dharma-fragrance of the ten *pāramitās*. Grinding them into fine powder and spreading it signifies the subtle and wondrous myriad practices.
A square and circle of sixteen *zhang* form an eight-cornered altar... (up to)... place whatever lotus petals are available within the water.

(Letam said: "The dimensions of the eight corners at sixteen *zhang* symbolize that one perceives the Path through the sixteen moments of mind, proceeding from the four fruits and four stages of the seeker.
Changshui said: "An 'altar' (*tan*) is made by clearing the ground; it is what we call a sacrificial mound (*shan*) today. Wuxing said: "Not so.")
The previous statement regarding the site was that it could be like a *śmaśāna* (sacrificial ground). Now, since it is designated as a *maṇḍala*, it must be constructed by raising earth.

Thus, one first clears the ground to form the site, and subsequently takes yellow earth, mixes it with incense to make clay, and applies this clay over the site to create the appearance of a *maṇḍala*.
Wenling says: The altar is the essence of quiescent extinction and level reality. Because its essence possesses both the partial and the correct, it is octagonal;
because it subdues the eight heterodoxies, it measures sixteen feet square. The lotus flower at the center of the altar represents the wondrous practice of the Middle Way.

As for the lotus, its flower and fruit share the same substance, and its defilement and purity originate from the same source; this symbolizes the grand principle of wondrous practice. Gold and silver are used [for its adornment].
That which is fashioned from copper and wood represents the practice of wondrous conduct. Gold and silver, though refined a hundred times, become ever more pure without changing;
this is the image of righteousness, for copper is firm yet capable of being tempered. Wood can grow upward to cover what lies beneath; this is the image of benevolence.
The alms bowl is the vessel of response, representing the capacity to respond to things according to their measure. Dew provides moisture in the shade, occurring in autumn.
It was in the eighth month, the middle of autumn. That the flowers and leaves grow within the water represents the conduct of benevolent coverage;
that they follow where the moisture is applied further illustrates responding to things according to their measure. This is a manifestation of silent transformation through hidden benefit.
Take eight circular mirrors and place each in its respective direction... (until)... burn pure aloeswood incense so that no fire is seen. [Zizhong says:

"Outside the mirrors" refers to outside of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*). Through the establishment of skillful means (*upāya*), the heterodox and the orthodox are made to encompass one another, and virtuous conduct is made to mutually permeate them.
It is hoped that through this, over time they will transform one another until both heterodoxy and orthodoxy are forgotten. Regarding "burning pure aloeswood": do not let [the fire] be seen...).
"Fire" refers to reversing the function of the treasury of merit and extinguishing both vitarka and vicāra; only then can one accord with the ground of quiescent extinction.
Wénlǐng says: "The perfect mirror" is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). As for each being settled within the eight directions surrounding the flower-bowl:
Wisdom and practice are mutually dependent, responding appropriately to the square and the round.
As for the sixteen lotus flowers and incense burners placed outside the mirrors, those set at intervals represent wondrous practice, while the incense represents wondrous virtue.
Every time at mealtime or during the middle watch of the night, one should burn [the incense] until the smoke is exhausted to offer to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
(Zizhong says: When King Bhaiṣajyarāja burned his body, he first consumed dūrvā grass incense; this was intended to [purify] the mind, which is why he took moistened charcoal.
(Xielü says: For those who dwell in the field of quiescent extinction and partake of the nourishment of dhyāna-joy, they should apply their whole hearts to this.)
Wenling says: The Buddha receives his meal at midday; therefore, offerings are always presented at midday. "Midnight" is used as an analogy for "midday. Honey is produced from flowers;
this represents the harmonious manifestation of the practice of the Dharma. Ghee is produced from milk; this represents the harmonious manifestation of the flavor of the Dharma.
"Half" is a number representing the center, while "three" is a number representing completion. The small incense burner is the square-inch awakened mind.
It is also by using fragrant water to wash the charcoal that the method of awakening is initiated. Yet, one must cause it to blaze fiercely;
by casting ghee and honey into the flaming furnace and burning them until the smoke is exhausted, the practice of the method is completed. One must not allow this to remain stagnant at the end;

rather, within the awakened mind, one should forge and refine with vigor so that habitual tendencies are melted away entirely and the shadows of conditions vanish together, suddenly becoming like what is called a red-hot furnace.
Once the "dotting with snow" is completed, it is then enjoyed by the Buddha.
Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them inverted in the void (until) their forms and shadows interpenetrate one another in successive layers.

(Zhenji said: "The bodies and lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings interpenetrate one another. Without tiring the steps, and without waiting for the mind to conceive them, every dharma is all-pervasive and every phenomenon is unimpeded.
When one lifts the eyes, a thousand sages appear simultaneously; wherever one touches, the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest.

A single flower or a single incense offering universally makes offerings to all lands within the dust motes; a single action or a single characteristic expands infinitely. This does not rely upon supernatural powers... )
To engage with the realm of phenomena is the very nature of the Dharma at the site of enlightenment; the cultivation and realization of the secret cause reach their ultimate subtlety here.
Wénlǐng says: "The mirror within the altar is mixed with things and has a basis; it is the wisdom of the practitioner.
The mirror in space is detached from things and has no basis; it is the wisdom of the Buddhas. Only that which is mixed with things and has a basis can [function as such]."

When illuminating objects, before one has fully illuminated them, one must necessarily attain the wisdom that is detached from objects and has no dependence. These functions interact with one another;
only then do object and self illuminate each other, and mind and phenomena both merge into oneness.
"Ānanda, if this bhikṣu was originally ordained by his preceptor... [you] ask about the establishment of the *dōjō* (place of practice), it is as follows.
(Wenling says: "To 'attain the stage of Srotāpanna' means to have entered the stream of the sages; it does not refer merely to the minor fruit. (Wuxing says:
"The ritual procedures for the altar-dharma are difficult to practice in the final age in this land. However, regarding the dhāraṇī recited, the following text also..."
It was permitted that they did not enter the *maṇḍala*, so that those with the karmic affinity might receive benefit according to their capacity.
Guishan said: "The stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), when examined by its position, corresponds to the first level of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

If one follows the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it refers to the initial entry into the stages of 'ground' (*bhūmi*) and 'abiding' (*vihāra*) in the Distinct and Perfect Teachings. If this were not the case, how could one know for oneself that the attainment of Buddhahood would not be erroneous?"—Wen.

Ling said: "From the point where [the Buddha] was invited into the Flower Pavilion in the fourth fascicle up to this point, it is collectively termed the 'Section on the Cultivation of the Path' (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

The subsequent text begins separately and is named the 'Section on Realizing the Fruit' (*phala-prāpti*). At the beginning of the Section on Realizing the Fruit, Ānanda specifically inquires about the stages of cultivation and realization.
In the World-Honored One’s response, he first enumerates the twelve classes of sentient beings, and subsequently elucidates the fifty-seven [stages]."
As for "position," it means to cause all sentient beings to rely upon this Dharma-gate, proceeding from the state of ordinary beings into sainthood,
investigating and perfecting it layer by layer until reaching the ultimate state of wondrous enlightenment, and only then ceasing once the unsurpassed Way has been accomplished.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "What is meant by a Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment?
(The *Zhēnji* states: "The forty-four minds" refers to the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, four stages of application, and ten grounds.
However, in the text where the Buddha answers below, there are fifty-four minds; this is because within the first abode, they are opened out horizontally.)
The ten faiths, when combined, are simply the first stage (*ādikṣānti*). This differs from the "ten faiths" as a semblance-stage (*pratirūpaka-bhūmi*) found in other sutras;
thus, the "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) here already subsumes the ten faiths of other sutras, establishing it as their collective designation.
Gushan said: "There are two intentions behind Ānanda’s request. First, since he has already received the practice-methods (xingmen), there must necessarily be a sequence of stages (weici).
It is like having entered a house through its gate; one must know the depth and arrangement of the halls and rooms. For this reason, he makes his request.

Second, at the beginning of the sutra, the Buddha spoke to Ānanda, saying that because his mind and words were direct, [he was able to hear] from the beginning down to the final stages of the path (dìwèi)."
"Between them, there has forever been no trace of crookedness. Since the previous stage of practice and understanding was perfectly integrated, the mind and speech were straightforward.
As for the stages and positions being free from curvature, I do not yet know their characteristics; therefore, I request an explanation of them."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "...this is the Tathāgata’s true *samādhi*. (Wenling says:
"Arising and ceasing, truth and falsehood, *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*—these are all what are called various names and marks.

Within the wondrous nature, they are originally perfect and integrated. It is due to the causal conditions of deluded appearances that there is cultivation and realization. Thus, it is transformed... )
Awakening, one relies upon Bodhi; by overturning birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one relies upon Nirvāṇa—this is called the name of the two-fold reliance (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). (Xielü says:
"If one wishes to cultivate correct reception, one must first recognize the cause of delusion; therefore, he speaks of the two kinds of inversion to clarify the root of transmigration.")
(Xie Li says: "The previous section explained the threefold continuity; this section clarifies the two causes of inversion. These are discussed by opening and closing [the categories].

What follows, stating 'perfuming forms karma,' subsumes both karma and its fruit. However, while the former clarified the characteristics of arising, this clarifies the essentials of cultivation and abandonment;
thus, while the meaning is the same, the intent differs)."
Wuxing said: "The previous discussion on the continuity of worlds referred solely to the *pariṇāma-nimitta* (the dependent retribution), such as the arising of the four great elements and so forth.
The present discussion on the inversion of the world refers instead to the *upabhoga-nimitta* (the primary retribution), namely the twelve classes of living beings.
The reason for this is that the previous response to Pūrṇa’s question concerned how the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise; the present response is to Ānanda."

This is because one enters the stages [of cultivation] through the practice of samādhi. Why is this? The stages are attained through awakening; yet entry into awakening must necessarily proceed from delusion.

Delusion constitutes the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), while awakening constitutes the state of a sage (*ārya*). These are matters pertaining to the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*) of sentient beings, not characteristics of the external vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*).
Therefore, it differs from what was previously explained. By practicing samādhi, one is able to recognize the cause of inversion; only then can one sever and remedy it. As for inverted delusions—*
Upon birth, they return to their original nature; therefore, it is said that this is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi.
Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of sentient beings (up to) the establishment of worlds and all sentient beings?
(Wu Xing says: "This 'fundamentally non-abiding'—abiding is precisely reliance. Tracing from the root to the branches, one finds there is absolutely nothing upon which to rely.
This passage generally indicates two inverted phrases; below, the distinct directions will clarify the two aspects.
Here, a single term is used for both the introduction and the conclusion because the world is being described in relation to sentient beings)."
Wenling says: "The luminosity of nature" refers to the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "The luminosity and perfection of nature" means not abiding in its own nature.
Because it does not abide in its own nature, through deluded luminosity it gives rise to deluded nature; because of deluded nature, deluded views arise.
Thus, from the signless reality, there is formed the delusion of signs. Therefore, it is said: "From ultimate non-existence..."
Thus, ultimate existence is established. Yet, this capacity to exist and that which exists, the capacity to abide and that in which one abides, are all not caused by causes;
they are all without a fundamental root. This is seen throughout the text. Based on this non-abiding, the worlds and sentient beings are established;
thus, one knows that these two are without cause and without substance, being entirely nothing but inverted delusion.
"Delusion fundamentally obscures perfect luminosity, giving rise to deluded awakening... (up to)... for this reason there are sentient beings who are inverted.
(Wuxing says: "Regarding 'about to restore the true,' etc., this cites the practice of accord to illustrate the practice of opposition, thereby clarifying the characteristics of inversion.
This means that if one contemplates the true nature through a circular [conceptual] observation and seeks to restore it, this is already not the true *tathatā* nature.)
Why is this? Because apart from True Suchness (tathatā), all practices and entries into the path belong to the provisional (upāya). Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng) says:
"If one attempts to discern Complete Enlightenment while not yet having escaped saṃsāra, that nature of Complete Enlightenment will itself be subject to the cycle of transmigration.

If this is so even when practicing in accordance with the truth, how much more so when practicing in opposition to it? (Chángshuì says: "Birth and death arise because of lustful desire; they perish because of killing and stealing.")

Wenling says: Because one is deluded regarding the fundamental nature, one desires to restore its reality. However, the arising of such aspirational desire already constitutes a departure from that reality;
hence it is said, "To desire reality is already not the true Suchness-nature. To seek to restore reality by means of what is not real results in a circuitous progression into delusion;
hence it is said, "It thus becomes a non-characteristic. Consequently, the mental states of arising and abiding [become] a hundredfold...

They do not arise simultaneously; rather, they are produced through successive and cumulative conditions, and thus the various characteristics arise in competition with one another. That which was non-existent and suddenly exists is called "arising" (*jāti*).

That which has arisen and remains for a time is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). The continuous succession of objective conditions and mental preoccupations is called "mind" (*citta*). The differentiation between defilement and purity is called "dharmas" (*dharma*). It is from these that the delusions of sentient beings arise.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion of the world" (*loka-viparyāsa*)? [This continues] until: "transforming sentient beings into twelve categories. (Wenling says:

Following the previous section, this explains that which exists and possesses existence, yet is not caused by causes. Because there is that which exists and possesses existence, there is segmentation;
because there is segmentation, there are directions and positions. Since the "realm" (*dhātu*) constitutes these directions and positions, it is established based on this realm.)
Where there is no cause, there is no abiding. Where there is no [intrinsic] nature, there is constant flux. The world is characterized by flux;

therefore, it is through this world that [the cycle] is established. By means of the world one traverses the directions, and by means of the directions one traverses the world; together they constitute the twelve [links].

Thus, the primary retribution of sentient beings—the harmony of cause and effect—likewise constitutes the twelve. Therefore, all those who traverse the interval between them follow these transformations.
This is the reason for the inversion of this world). Guishan said:
"From ultimate non-existence, one establishes ultimate existence; therefore, there arise the divisions of east, west, south, and north.
Pointing to these divisions, they are called 'realms' (*dhātu*). However, as for what exists therein, it originally has no cause; hence it is so stated."
It is not the cause of causes; this is merely an illusory dwelling. Therefore, it is said that there is no dwelling and nothing to dwell upon.

Since it is not the eternally abiding true nature, there are the past, present, and future, flowing on without staying still; thus the three periods of time are established. Through these periods, the spatial dimensions are traversed.
When the "Phases" (fang) and the "Worlds" (shi) intersect, both together form twelve. Thus, the primary retribution of sentient beings, through the conjunction of cause and effect, also forms twelve.
Wuxing said: "In the fourth fascicle, when the Phases and Worlds intersect, the addition of the three cycles of flux and transformation results in twelve."

This refers to the objective environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) in contrast to the subjective retribution (*upapatti-vipāka*), manifesting that the merits of the six sense faculties (*ṣad-indriya*) each consist of one thousand two hundred [units].
Within this context, they interpenetrate; by taking the environment as derived from the subjective, it clarifies the world’s inversions and establishes the twelve classes of beings.
That which was previously termed "merit" is here termed "inversion. As for the ancient masters using this to explain the first three layers [of the *Avataṃsaka*], can it not be harmonized?
Therefore, the world arises from movement and possesses sound (up to: exhausting the twelve transformations as one revolving cycle).
[Wuxing says: This takes the object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*) as the cause in its own essence. From this causal sound, there is form (*rūpa*), up to taste (*rasa*) and cognition (*vijñāna*).]
The dharmas thus successively cause one another, thereby manifesting the characteristics of the six types of confusion. Finally, regarding "knowing dharmas":

"knowing" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*), and "dharmas" refers to the objects of mind (*dharmāyatana*). By analogy with what follows, there are likewise the meanings of hearing sounds, seeing forms, and so forth;
moreover, since it speaks of the "six confused delusive thoughts," we know that hearing, perceiving, knowing, and seeing all ultimately revert to delusive thought.
Gushan said: "All things arise from movement to form their shapes. Movement gives rise to sound, and shape is precisely color (form).
Therefore it is said that sound exists because of movement, and color exists because of sound. Fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects (dharmas) are all fully present through mutual causation.
From these six objects, the six sense-faculties are aroused; these are called the six deluded妄 thoughts. They constitute the very essence of delusion and karma."
This is the essence; therefore, it is called the nature of karma. The twelve classes of beings revolve because of this.
The worldly sounds, smells, tastes, and touches refer back to the aforementioned six categories of deluded wandering thoughts.

This is because their distinctions are each twelvefold, and their transformations are likewise each twelvefold; thus, the forms of the six deluded wanderings evolve from ignorance-conditioned formations (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskāra*) down to...
Old age and death; ending and beginning again. Therefore it is said that the twelve transformations reach their limit and constitute one cycle of revolution.
Because one rides upon this wheel of inverted characteristics (until) reaching the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
(Letang said: "The karma, afflictions, and fruits—these three—are clarified; among these, birth from eggs, birth from wombs, and so forth are the categories of fruit.
The supplementary note says: This is a general heading. Because the twelve divisions exhaustively undergo transformation and return to their source, they revolve in delusion;
each possesses its own twelve [factors], and through these transformations, sentient beings are formed into twelve classes.
Ānanda, due to the causes and conditions of the world’s false transmigration... (up to) humans, animals, dragons, and immortals, their various kinds fill [the world].
(Wu-xing says: "That which arises from an egg is called egg-born; that which emerges from containing and storing is called womb-born; that which arises by relying on moisture is called moisture-born;
that which suddenly exists where there was none is called transformation-born. These four types of birth arise from the internal mind's thoughts and karma.")
The internal [factors] serve as the cause, while the external egg, womb, moisture, and warmth serve as the conditions. Depending on the number of these conditions, the sequence is established:
those born from eggs possess all four; therefore, birth from a womb is mentioned first. Those born from moisture possess three; those born by transformation possess two;
and those born spontaneously possess only one, namely, the karma of volition (this is according to the interpretation in the *Yogācārabhūmi*).
Wenling says: "The egg-born are produced solely through thought; this delusion is precisely 'thought. The essence of thought is light and buoyant, which is termed 'the inversion of movement.

The egg is formed through the intermingling of vital energies, termed 'formation through harmonious energy. The predominance of thought leads to ascending and sinking, termed 'confused thoughts of flying and sinking.'"
Thus, it is through these that beings such as fish and birds—those who float or sink—are moved.

As for the statement that each of the twelve classes [of beings] has eighty-four thousand [forms], this is because each is produced through the transformation of eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). *Kalala* is translated as "congealed mucus";

it is the initial stage of entering the womb, the state when the embryo and the amnion have not yet differentiated. The womb exists because of emotion (*ch'ing*); defilement is precisely emotion. Emotion gives rise to...
Regarding craving, it is called the perversion of desire. The union of semen and blood is called the formation through harmonious blending.

When the mind has partiality or correctness, it is called the confused thoughts of horizontal or vertical [rebirth]. Thus, one receives birth as the horizontal or vertical classes of humans and animals.

*Ārbuda* (遏蒲曇) means a "blister," which refers to the stage where the embryo or egg gradually begins to divide. Through false delusions, defilements, attachments, and obstructions, all sentient beings...
It is complete; it is merely that beings are categorized according to what they predominantly experience.
(Xie Li says: "Arising from an egg is called birth from an egg. Xie Li says: "Emerging from what is contained within is called birth from a womb.")
"Due to the world's attachment to saṃsāra... (down to) crawling insects and wriggling creatures, their kinds fill [the world].
(Lectan said: "That which arises through moisture is called moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*). *Bishi* refers to soft flesh; this is the initial sign of moisture-born beings.")
Since they do not enter the womb, the first two stages do not exist for them. All ten modes of birth are rooted in sexual desire and arise from emotional attachments;

because deluded emotions increasingly give rise to false imaginings, the principles of transformation become ever more distorted, leading to the dissipation of the spirit into emptiness or the hardening of the mind into wood and stone.
Although the branches of these delusions differ, the root of delusion is one and the same.

Wenling says: "Moisture arises through union and response; 'attachment' is precisely this union. Union proceeds from the stagnation of craving; as one moves toward and clings to objects, it is called 'inverted movement.

Moisture arises from yang; thus it is called 'the formation of warmth through harmonious union. That which is moved toward has no fixed destination, hence it is called 'reversing and chaotic thoughts.
Therefore, it gives rise to the class of wriggling and crawling creatures that turn over and over."
"Due to the causes of the world’s transformation and saṃsāra... (up to) they shed their skins and fly, their species filling the air.
[Létán said: "That which suddenly exists where there was none is called birth. *Kalala* means hard flesh; 'shedding' refers to the formation of the body, which is its soft aspect.
Those below are all termed *kalala*; this is the general designation for all such classes. As for the fifth, the *peśī*..."
(Qie says: "Forming a body" means that each follows its own physical appearance; it is not a general term). (Gushan says:

"The transformation from non-existence to sudden existence is like the molting of a grubs; thus the skin joyfully takes on new substance, and because the intention is to fly upward, it is called 'transforming and flying'").
Wenling says: Transformation responds through separation; change and alteration are themselves separation. To leave this and entrust oneself to that is called "false inversion.

To touch upon categories and undergo transformation is called "the formation of contact through harmony. Because the old turns and the new approaches, it is called "the chaotic thoughts of the new and the old."

Therefore, the retribution of karmic response is likewise so. Because one sheds the old, one proceeds toward the new; it is like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly, whereby walking is transformed into flying.
Or like a sparrow becoming a clam, whereby flight is shed for submergence. In all cases where different forms are transmitted to one another, it is a process of transformation and shedding.
From the obstruction of the world leading to saṃsāra... (up to) "the spirits of auspicious and inauspicious omens fill the realm.
(Wenling says: All these brilliant spiritual beings are manifestations of emotion. Because their thoughts have already coagulated, they form a brilliant essence;
thus they possess only form. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The eighty spirits all arise from the fundamental source of obstructive thoughts.")
"Essential radiance. Although this is most refined and most spiritual, it has not yet departed from the characteristics of that wheel-turning inversion.

(Xie Li said: "This which possesses form is essential radiance with lingering obstruction; it is the form of karmic fruit. Therefore, there are distinctions between rest and calamity, fortune and misfortune.")
Zizhong said: "To serve the sun, moon, water, and fire, harmonizing and uniting their light while clinging to them with stubborn persistence so that they cannot pass through, is called 'obstruction.
Because the essence and brilliance become manifest and distinct due to this, it is named 'form and appearance' (rūpa-nimitta).

When stars, planets, the sun, and the moon are auspicious, they are termed 'rest' (xiū); when they are inauspicious, they are termed 'calamity' (jiù). As for torches and the pearls of oysters, all are likewise of this nature."
The category [of *kalala*]. From the dissolution of the world of causes and the cycle of rebirth... (up to)... its types fill and pervade as they disperse into emptiness and sink away.
(Ziqing says: This refers to those with perception who lack form; because they do not yet constitute a physical body (*karmabhava*), they are also called *kalala*. Furthermore, there is...)

Delusion and karma are heavy and dark; form and color are worn away; the body merges with empty obscurity, and consciousness clings hidden within the aggregates. This is also like the category of those who are empty, scattered, dissolved, and submerged).

Wénlǐng says: "Those who are weary [of the world] cling to emptiness; they extinguish the body and return to non-existence. This is called the cycle of dissolution. They are deluded and leaking, without..."
"Listening" refers to deluded inversion. To loathe existence and seek refuge in non-existence is to rely upon the obscure and dark emptiness;
thus, it combines with darkness to form what is called the "shrouding, hidden, and chaotic ideation. This is precisely the class of non-Buddhists belonging to the Formless Realm.
"Due to the causes of the world’s illusory transmigration... (up to) spirits, ghosts, and numinous essences, their kinds fill [the world].
(Wenling says: "Being false and losing the truth, they are erroneously attached to images. Having no basis for their forms, they arise from recollection and imagination.
Within this illusory state (*wangxiang*), they secretly form appearances; their spirit is not luminous and thus becomes a ghost in obscurity, while their essence is incomplete and disperses.")
[They are regarded as] spirits, yet they possess no substantial form; there is only the appearance of mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*).
Zizhong said: "Those who follow footprints or cling to shadows are all born from recollective conceptions (*smṛti-saṃjñā*).

When discussing their causes, they may be like non-Buddhists or ordinary worldlings who pray to divine beings and entrust themselves to physical images, serving them throughout their lives with the ambition of yearning for spiritual efficacy."
Penetration. Because cause and effect repay one another, beings are born into their respective categories.
From the world of causes—where the ignorant and dull transmigrate in cycles (up to) being transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone—their various types fill and obstruct all space.
(Wenling says: "If one does not understand the principle of the Truth, then one will be stubborn and ignorant, and the spirit will be transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone.
(Xielü says: "To know that the spirit has been transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone, such that there is no longer any emotion or thought, is itself to be withered and parched.
This is like the stone of Jīvaka, the trees at the tomb of King Yan Zhaowang, and the person named Huan of Zheng—these are all instances of the spirit [having become thus].")
This is the transformation of the spirit.

Zizhong said: "Non-Buddhists reckon that insentient things possess life; that metal and stone are solid and firm; or that through the practice of meditative concentration, ash congeals, and through single-minded thought, one withers away.
Their minds change according to their environments, taking form upon encountering objects—just as a *huabiao* pillar gave birth to the spirit Huangtou."
Fossils and the like are such examples.
From "due to the world's mutual dependence and cyclic existence" (up to) "using shrimp as eyes," their various kinds fill the space.
(Wenling says: Creatures such as the *jellyfish* take water foam as their body and use shrimp as their eyes; they originally have no color.)

Waiting for external things to complete its own color, it cannot employ itself; waiting for external things to have utility, it loses its innate truth. Clinging persistently to the floating and false, self and other become distinct substances.
Because defiled conditions combine, it is said that they serve as causes and supports.

Zizhong said: "Through the clever fabrication of combinations, they alter the old to create the new; sometimes they falsely rely on causes and conditions, successively forming alliances for mutual support.

Thus they sustain their bodies and nourish their lives, with karmic fruits revolving in succession. Because they do not receive a body from within their own kind, they are called those without the characteristics of form and so forth.
Within the bodies of sentient beings, there are eighty thousand families of worms, all of which belong to this class."
"Due to the mutual attraction of worldly phenomena, beings revolve in saṃsāra... (up to)... born through curses and incantations, such that their kind fills [the world].

(Wenling says: "Evil karmas attract one another, causing nature and temperament to become inverted; thus, riding upon incantations and entrusting consciousness to them, they do not follow the principles of natural life but falsely respond to the calling of names.
This refers to the evil arts of the mundane world—curses and incantations, as well as the birth resulting from spirits, demons, and objects of sorcery.")

Zizhong said: "There is a class of beings who, because they are called by name through sound, develop their nature through that stimulus. This is like frogs and the like, which attach their eggs to sound.
Regarding the cause, it may be a fondness for lewd sounds; through habitual practice, attachment arises from one's own nature."
These categories do not depend on anything else for their formation; they are called "formless" (arūpa) because their substance is manifested through sound. Thus, they are termed "formless.
Due to the world's causes, beings revolve in delusion, leading to the mutual formation of diverse substances until these categories fill all space.

(Wenling says: When these two delusions combine, the nature and emotion become utterly obscured. Distinct substances mutually constitute one another, and the principles of life become entangled, just as the *puluo* worm originally a silkworm lacks the thought of being a bee, yet comes to possess the thought of being a bee.)
Zizhong said: "To deceive and misappropriate another's property, taking it as one's own, is called the perversion of deception.

To turn one's back on one's parents and instead follow a sense of 'righteousness,' to entrust one's funeral rites and the care of an orphaned heir to others, and to forget one's own ancestral sacrifices while claiming the lineage of another—these are its causes. Wuxing said:

Because they are of a different substance, they do not possess the characteristics of perception; yet because they are formed by those characteristics, they constitute the *kalala* stage of perception.
Due to the world’s cycle of mutual enmity and harm, [beings] all become their prey, and their kind fills the realm.
(Gushan says: "The earth-owl and the 'broken mirror'—Meng Kang says that *xiao* is the name of a bird; it eats its mother, and the 'broken mirror' eats its father.
The Yellow Emperor wished to exterminate their kind and thus ordered that they be used in sacrifices to all creatures. The 'broken mirror' resembles a wild boar (*chú*) but has tiger-like eyes.

The fact that it is now called a 'bird' (*niǎo*) likely stems from an error by the translator; perhaps the character for 'bird' should have been 'equal' (*děng*), which was later arbitrarily altered)."
Wenling said: "When resentment and harm are requited, injury and killing follow in turn. Such a way of life is strange and perverse, utterly abandoning human ethics and righteousness;

thus it evokes the kind of creature known as the earth-owl, which takes form from earthen clods and poisonous fruit. It is not that it lacks the notion of a bird, yet fundamentally it lacks any [innate] notion.
Zizhong said: "When parents have affection, this is called the characteristic of 'not lacking thought. When there is resentment, there is no affection."

Therefore, it is called "non-conceptual" (*asaṃjñin*). Question: Since these are enemies and lack the conditions for rebirth through sympathetic resonance, how can they be born by means of attachment?
Is there not love even within enmity? Answer: It is like raising pigs or sheep; one keeps them because of a craving for their slaughter. Is this not love existing even within enmity?
These are called the twelve types of sentient beings.
Wénlǐng says: "All of these fail to understand the wondrously enlightened luminous mind; deluded and trapped by emotional desires, they give rise to a proliferation of falsehoods."

To follow along with the turning of the wheel is not true practice; one cannot escape or be liberated thereby. Therefore, the subsequent text demonstrates the method for eliminating delusion and attaining realization through cultivation.

Ānanda, within each and every class of these sentient beings, they are fully possessed of such false and deluded discursive thoughts.
(Gushan said: "The fundamental is truly possessed. This possession has no characteristic of possessing; all things are empty. Only by understanding this can one begin to discuss the Way.

Wenzheng said: "Because each and every category of deluded seeds is fundamentally possessed—those that manifest are called 'factually created' (*shizao*), while those that remain latent are called 'principially possessed' (*lizhi*). Since delusion has no inherent substance, it is fundamentally the true mind.")
Wenling says: The twelve inversions range from the inversion of movement to the inversion of desire, up to the inversion of killing.
Because these delusions disturb the true mind, they give rise to eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts. These are both individually present and mutually inclusive.
"You now cultivate and realize the Buddha-samādhi" (up to) "thirdly, advancing against its manifest karma.
(Wuxing says: Removing the metaphor of poison and honey means removing the auxiliary causes and excising the primary nature.
Hot water is like correct practice; calamitous incense is like auxiliary practice; nectar represents the principle realized. (Changshui says: The previous question...)
To what gradual sequence does one attain the eye of cultivation? It is because these two constitute the correct practice that they are called "true cultivation."孤山 (Gushan) says:
"As for 'gradual sequence,' it refers to the gradualness of phenomena and the perfection of principle; it is not the same as the gradualism of the partial teachings. Question:

To which stage among the "six levels of realization" (*liujì*) in the Tiantai system do these three gradual stages belong? Answer: They correspond to the stage of "names" (*míngzì*), wherein one cultivates so as to accomplish contemplative practice (*guānxíng*) and give rise to the semblance of true realization (*zhēnsì*).
"What is the auxiliary cause? Ānanda, such a world [is characterized by] the first stage of progressive cultivation and gradual advancement.

(Wuxing says: By mentioning "eating sweets" and so forth, he illustrates the harm and benefit of solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); this is intended to eliminate the auxiliary causes of the five pungent roots.)
Because the five pungent vegetables can arouse lust and anger, they are like food that causes death by poison. (Gushan says:

Regarding the "five pungent vegetables," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states they are asafoetida, garlic, leeks, scallions, and *hingukha*. Master Ying says that *hingukha* is a corruption of the Sanskrit pronunciation.)
The correct term is *xingyi* (興宜). Master Cimin (慈愍) of the Tripiṭaka said: "Its root is like a radish; when it emerges from the soil, it is pungent and foul-smelling.
Since Master Cimin went to that land during the winter solstice and did not see its sprouts, it does not exist here [in this region]; therefore, it was not translated.
Wenling says: Regarding the four kinds of nutriment: the nutriment of humans is "edible food," meaning that what is consumed must necessarily be in distinct portions.

The nutriment of ghosts and spirits is "contact-food," whereby they are satiated merely by inhaling contact. The nutriment of the dhyāna-heavens is "volition-food," wherein when food arrives, they may be satiated simply by thinking of it.

The devas perceive through consciousness and perceive food; since they possess neither form nor color, they rely solely on the ideation of consciousness. This passage directly clarifies that all sentient beings subsist on clothing, food, and shelter.
Regarding the precept of abstaining from the five pungent roots (pañca-gandha) due to food, there is no need for further external citation: within these five pungent roots, sexual desire is aroused.
Therefore, it is called an auxiliary cause. Hatred externally attracts malevolent spirits.
How is it that the right nature, Ānanda, for such sentient beings [up to] the second stage of progressive cultivation?

(Letang said: "Pure precepts" refers to the four parājikas. (Wuxing said: "Because there is no lust, the mark of birth does not arise," and so on, up to "because there is no falsehood, one does not repay past debts.
Since he [the Buddha] made a great false claim out of greed for offerings, this is spoken of in terms of stages;
it should be placed outside [the formal list]. This applies generally within all contemplative practices. (Zizhong said: "This is like the manifestation of the body in the Lotus Sutra...")
The attainment of the six sense organs' purity is precisely the stage of semblance (*sādṛśyāvasthā*).
Wēnlíng says: "To excise the fundamental nature of lust and killing, one must uphold the precepts. Not drinking alcohol is the ultimate means of preventing disorder;
not eating raw meat is the ultimate means of preventing the taking of life. Within the Vinaya, the five types of fruit must all be 'purified by fire,' which serves as a demonstration..."
One must not consume the vital breath. To regard lust as a venomous serpent or a vengeful enemy is because it can harm the Dharma-body and slay the life of wisdom.
One must restrain the body so that there is no transgression, and restrain the mind so that there is no thought of transgression. Lust and killing follow one another in succession.
Theft and robbery arise from mutual indebtedness due to a lack of restraint; when the precepts are perfected, these two types of karma will forever cease.
When the nature of karma is completely eradicated, the wondrous nature becomes perfectly luminous.
"What is present karma? Ānanda, such purity [extends] through the third stage of progressive cultivation.
(Lētán says: These three stages of gradual progression take the precepts as their essence. (Chángshuǐ says:
When the world is pure and as clear as lapis lazuli, then the manifestation of true emptiness is realized. This is what is called 'pure śamatha,' like a mirror manifesting all things.)"
[The text says: "Like [an image] as well. (Wuxing says: Here, it specifically refers to the stages from the First Abode upward as the "sage stage" (*ārya-bhūmi*).

However, if the subsequent passage states, "Because of the threefold advancement, one can accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi," then this includes the ten levels of faith [*daśa-śraddhā*] as well.
(Supplementary Note: "Secret principle," "perfect wisdom," and "pure, wondrous practice" refer to the Dharma-body and the other two [the Sambhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya]).
[De] (Xielǐ said: "I shall now distinguish the fifty-two stages of the *yíngluò* (necklace of jewels) in relation to the present [system].

There is the aspect of 'one unification and three openings. The 'one unification' is the unification of the ten faiths (*śraddhā*) as the stage of dry wisdom (*kandhī-bhūmi*). The 'three openings' are: opening the first abiding (*prathama-vihāra*) into the ten faiths;

opening the ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) into the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*); and opening equal enlightenment (*samya-saṃbodhi*) into the diamond-like dry wisdom (*vajra-kandhī*). )
...as it is said: "Only when one restrains the four [senses] does the Way [manifest]. Wēnlíng says:
"To flow and escape toward the dust of the world gives rise to manifest karma; by means of the prohibitions of the precepts, one attains non-flowing and non-escaping."
This is able to distance [the senses] from [objects], so that they do not flow out or stray; this is due to severing the adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).

Turning back to the source and returning to oneself is gradually entering the principle of the Tathāgata-garbha. Since "dust" is no longer conditioned, this further advances to shatter fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
The previous section pertained to the stages of cultivation, merely stating that one does not flow out excessively; now, by attaining true realization, it concerns the faculties themselves.
When the dust of delusion has vanished, one flows against the current of ignorance; there is nothing but the pure, singular true nature.
Subtle arising and ceasing no longer function within the six sense-faculties; thus, the land, body, and mind are wondrously perfect and pure.

Being in union with the Tathāgata, the secret and perfect mind and the pure, wondrous nature of all Tathāgatas are all manifested therein. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in its "Ten Patiences," states in the third:
The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) means not seeing the arising of even the slightest dharma, nor seeing the cessation of even the slightest dharma.

Being free from all emotional defilements, without fabrication or aspiration, one dwells securely in this path; this is called "patience. As for the term "patience regarding dharmas," it refers to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) within the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*).
When karma is purified and the nature is luminous, one may then initiate practice and ascend to the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*).
There are fifty-seven stages, each established according to its specific mode of practice so that one may contemplate their names and meanings to understand what is being cultivated and advanced.
Wuxing said: "The three preceding gradual stages are merely distinguished by way of coarse and subtle, or prior and subsequent.

If one practices in the Perfect [Teaching], is it not the case that contravening one's present karmic activities constitutes the very foundation for initiating the mind and developing contemplation? Therefore, the first..."
The gradual sequence is described as follows: "One who cultivates bodhi must forever sever the five pungent roots. One should know that bodhi itself has no gradual sequence;
yet, by means of the gradual sequence one attains bodhi. This is like the vast ocean or the great void, which possess no limit or measure.

It is only due to the difference between rowing a boat or flapping wings that distances are reckoned. What follows here—the stage of dry wisdom and so forth—constitutes the latter two gradual sequences.
This is the stage that follows next.
Ānanda, because the craving for existence has withered away in this good man—up to the point where his wisdom is dried up—it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*).
(Wuxing says: "This good man" refers to a person at the level of the external ordinary person (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) of the Perfect Teaching. (Wuxing says: [Regarding] "person and dharmas...")

The two attachments are realized to be devoid of substantial nature; therefore, it is said that the mind of attachment is empty and luminous. Thus, delusion becomes wisdom, and its essence possesses both quiescence and illumination;
hence it is said that [the light] pervades the ten directions and all realms. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the first of the ten stages is named "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vijñāna*).

Tiantai established the five grades of practice prior to the ten stages of faith in the Perfect Teaching, stating that by inference according to the meaning, they correspond to the stage of Dry Wisdom in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Alas! Zhiyi...

It accords with the times. Although this sutra had not yet arrived, the names and positions established [by the sages] coincided with the Buddha’s mind from afar. Who but a sage could have accomplished such a thing?
Wēnlíng says: "The moisture of desire and the delusions of the faculties and their objects create karma; thus the cycle of birth and death continues—this is nothing other than this."

Therefore, when the objects of desire wither and the external world recedes, the remaining physical form no longer continues; being free from all turbid intermixture, one maintains patient endurance that is empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom.
However, at the initial stage of entry, one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma, and thus possesses only dry wisdom.
The noble stages begin with the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), taking faith as the primary cause; furthermore, regarding this faith:

Prior to the [first] stage, one establishes Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana*); prior to the stages, one establishes the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*); and prior to the Sublime [stage], one establishes the Vajra-like [samādhi].

These three constitute the essential points for the transition of stages and the skillful means for ascending. Initially, starting from the state of an ordinary person, the nature of wisdom is not yet perfected;

thus, one cannot enter the stage of faith to become a worthy one (*ārya*). Once the conduct of a worthy one is accomplished, if one does not apply further effort, one cannot ascend to the [bodhisattva] stages to become a sage (*ārya*).
The stages of the sages having been completed, it cannot be that one attains the wondrous perfection of Buddhahood without severing [delusions] through Vajra-wisdom.
When the habitual tendencies of desire have first dried up but one has not yet attained the pure truth of the Middle Way of the Tathāgata, this is called the Abode of Faith.

(Wu Xing said: "By means of the mind of contemplative practice, one takes the principles within [the teachings] as an object; continuing without interruption, one flows into the first stage of faith. (Zhen Ji said:
"The phrase 'the perfect and wondrous blossoms' refers to the delusions of views falling away first, such that the Three Truths appear to manifest.

The passage beginning with 'From the true, wondrous, and perfect' explains the preceding sentence; it means that from the true, wondrous, and perfect mind of the Stage of Dry Wisdom, this present stage is again brought forth.")
The wondrous mind of faith: because the mind merges with principle, it is said that "wondrous faith abides eternally.
Changshui said: "Having abandoned desire and love and transcended the stage of dry wisdom, one still remains on the level of an ordinary person and has not yet entered the stream of the Dharma;
therefore, one must flow into and out of the ocean of the Tathāgata’s *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) without partiality or stagnation, whereby the perfect wondrousness [is realized]."

The nature thus blossoms; yet, because there still remain residual delusive habits that are not truly wondrous and perfect, one must further give rise to true wondrousness from within that true wondrous perfection, maintaining constant and wondrous faith so that all delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder.

The path of the "middle among middles" is pure and true, without delusion; therefore, it is called the abiding of the mind of faith (*śraddhā*). All other dwellings are further developed from this, and there is no other separate method.
When true faith clearly understands all things as perfectly penetrating, one reaches the point where nothing is forgotten; this is called the abiding of the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
(Zhenji said: "When the mind is true and luminous, all things are perfectly penetrating and the *skandhas*, *āyatanas*, and *dhātus* do not obstruct it;

thus one can clearly illuminate past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and remember their remedies without omission. (Letang said: "That which is capable of habitual conditioning is called the 'mind of recollection' (*smṛti-citta*).
The *skandhas*, *āyatanas*, and *dhātus* are precisely the habitual tendencies regarding the places of birth within the mundane world.")
Wuxing said: "Discarding one body and receiving another refers precisely to the death and rebirth of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).

All habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) refer to the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) of the delusions of thought (*vicikitsā-āsrava*). Therefore, the text below, when explaining the five *anāgāmin* heavens, states that the desires abandoned there are also called 'habitual tendencies.

Furthermore, it should be understood that both types of death are collectively termed 'discarding the body,' while the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) are collectively termed 'habitual tendencies.'"
"Wondrous, perfect, pure, and true; from this true essence, transformation arises" (up to) "advancing toward true purity is called the mind of diligence.

(Gushan says: Although there was recollection previously, the habitual tendencies had not yet been dissolved. Here, however, the spirit is refined and bright, and thus transformation is attained. (Wuxing says: "Transformation" means change.
It refers to changing all deluded habits so that pure, true illumination is perfected. This speaks of its refinement. Only [the following]...)
This indicates his progress. Wēnlíng says:
"When the nature of wondrous, perfect penetration is both pure and true, then deluded habits are all transformed, leaving only a single, brilliant clarity that advances toward true purity.
Because one's practice is free from admixture, it is called 'penetration through mastery.'"
When the essence of mind manifests before one and consists purely of wisdom, it is called "the dwelling of the mind in wisdom" (hui-xin-zhu).
[Xie Li said: Through diligence, wisdom then becomes purely luminous.]
Wenling says: Since delusive habits have been exhausted, the essence of the mind manifests before one; thus, all progress, movement, and action consist purely of wisdom, free from habituation.
This state—where one maintains the luminosity of wisdom, which is all-pervasive, tranquil, profound, and eternally concentrated—is called the "abiding of the settled mind."
(Gushan said: "If there is wisdom without concentration, the ultimate virtue will not coalesce; therefore, one uses concentration to consolidate wisdom. Wenzheng said:
"Since wisdom is already pure and luminous, it must be sustained by concentration. Wuxing said: "It is all-pervasive, tranquil, and profound."
That which is called the function of concentration is its quiescent, wondrous, and eternally凝 (constant) state; that which is called the essence of concentration is the radiance of concentration.
When this radiance is emitted and the luminous nature penetrates deeply, advancing solely without retreating, it is named the "Non-retrogressive Mind."
(Zhangshui said: "When concentration is prolonged, light arises; when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, movement occurs; thus one is able to advance. Wénlǐng said:
"To maintain wisdom through concentration until it reaches profound stillness is the nature [of the mind]. Through this illumination, one penetrates deeply into the Way."

When the mind advances with serenity and maintains this state without loss, such that the vital energy (*qi*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is received and interfused, it is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.
(Wuxing says: "If one advances for long, one encounters movement and loses serenity; therefore, one must maintain it. (Changshui says:

"Being able both to penetrate deeply and to maintain [this state], so that one's Way is the same as that of the ten directions and one's energy merges with that of the Tathāgatas—this is what is meant by 'protecting the Dharma'").
