(Wenling says: The tongue devours living beings, causing them to endure suffering; thus, it undergoes bitter experiences itself as it causes others to endure them.
Because it relies on views to crave flavors, it can become molten gold and stone. Because it relies on hearing to give rise to evil, it can become sharp weapons and blades.
Because it relies on smelling to indulge greed and captures all manner of aromas, it can become a great iron cage. Because the flavor of touch harms things, it brings about [retribution].)
[They] wound themselves with bows and arrows. Because they contemplated objects for the sake of their flavor, they are thus moved by flying iron to provide that flavor).
Guishan said: "Following the pattern of the eyes, ears, and nose, one should say 'seeing, hearing, and smelling' here; it ought to be called the retribution of tasting (*cang-bao*).
The term 'retribution of flavor' is named after that which is tasted. If one is greedy for flavor, one sets nets and traps and burns the wilds to capture birds and beasts."
One sees the appearance of iron nets and fierce flames; "to bear" (*chêng*) means to accept through speech, and "to endure" (*nên*) means to willingly receive the sound [of suffering].
Fifth, as for the retribution of touch that invites evil fruits: [the body] then becomes a mass, becomes flying, and becomes roasted and grilled.
(Wenling says: "The great mountains coming together, as well as the iron city, the fire-dogs, and so forth, are all manifestations of the sensation of adverse contact (*duḥkha-spraṣṭavya*).
Contact is that upon which karma depends; it does not go beyond the states of separation and union. 'Slaughter and tearing' refers to the aspect of separation. 'The path' is the road leading to hell.

'Gazing at the gates of the hell-king' refers to the two watchtowers. The 'hall' and the 'pressing chamber' are both places for punishing offenses; they are all bases for bodily contact. This summarizes [the point].")
A sack is for containing breath. Because the karma of thought is turbulent and drifting, it brings about the occurrence of flying and falling. "Stabbing" (剚) refers to driving a blade into the flesh;
"stabbing and shooting" (剚射), along with "torture and binding," are then mutually related and arise in succession.
Gushan said: "The swords and blades [of the mountain] are all brought about by the attachment to the bodies of men and women.
Sixth, the retribution of one's thoughts draws forth evil fruits, such that throughout ten thousand lives and ten thousand deaths, one is cast face down or face up."

(Xie Li said: "Thought must have a locus; therefore, when thought is bound, it becomes the recipient [of karma]. When one's views are able to witness and verify [the truth], then when views are bound, they become the witness.
In the affairs of a person who has committed an offense, when hearing is bound, it can become the great assembly, such as the stones and so forth. This is the mutual resonance of water and earth.
Vehicles, boats, and enclosures are the transformations of disordered thought arising from the cessation of vital breath. 'Taste' refers to the faculty of the tongue. Sound..."
This is what is initiated from within. From "great" down to "small," all refer to the body; it is produced by the transformations of karma that contacts and chaotic thought (*cetanā*).
Wēnlíng says: Thought belongs to the element of earth, yet it is volatile and turbulent; therefore, one first perceives evil winds blowing away the country and its soil.
Matter is the basis for the karma of volition; it does not transcend delusion and awakening. Wandering wildly is deluded volition; knowing suffering is awakened volition.
Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six fruits of hell (up to: there are ten kinds of *ṛṣis* in places inaccessible to humans).
(Wu Xing says: This summarizes the ten causes and six fruits mentioned above. (Gu Shan says: The *Baopuzi* states:

"One who seeks immortality must take loyalty, filial piety, harmony, obedience, benevolence, and trustworthiness as the foundation. If one does not cultivate virtue but devotes oneself solely to esoteric arts, one will ultimately fail to attain longevity.")

Wenling says: "Xian" (仙) means "transcendence. It refers to the human form and spirit being able to transcend and not die. Therefore it is said that by maintaining mental visualization one can solidify the physical form;
yet, in the end, it still returns to decay and ruin. Compared to heaven, this is inferior; compared to ordinary humans, it is superior. For this reason, it is established as a separate category.
Ānanda, those sentient beings who firmly take these medicinal elixirs... [until] they awaken and achieve perfection, being named *atyantagāmin* (Transcendent Practitioners).
(Xing Jianzi said: "These all transcend the world and leave secular life; they stretch like bears and extend themselves like birds. (Xie Li said:

"The vital fluids moisten within, making them graceful and pure; this is called 'Heavenly Practice' (*devagati*). By absorbing the refined essence, they draw forth radiance and color; this is called [the practice of the Transcendents].")
"Common Practice. (Xie Li said: "To refine one's thoughts with clarity and for the mind of contemplation to shine alone is called 'Illuminating Practice. Xie Li said:
'The interaction of Kan and Li, water and fire, is the work of the practitioner of cultivation.'")
Wenling says: Those who prolong their lifespan for a single period by means of medicinal herbs, yet are unable to ascend lightly, are earth-walking immortals (*dixingxian*).

Those whose conduct and practice (*xinggong*) involve consuming yellow essence (*huangjing*), pine, cypress, and the like, until their bodies become light over time, are flying immortals (*feixiangxian*).
Those who refine metallic elixirs (*jindan*) and the like, transforming their bones and changing their forms, can grasp soil and transform it [into gold].
Those who roam among humans for sport are the *yóuxíng xiān* (wandering immortals).

Those who ride upon the movement of yin and yang to regulate their qi, consolidate their essence, cast off their physical forms, and traverse the void are the *kōngxíng xiān* (void-traveling immortals).

Those who stir the celestial pond, swallow their own fluids, remain as pure and graceful as ice and snow, do not consort with worldly desires, and are no different from the heavens are the *tiānxíng xiān* (heaven-traveling immortals). They inhale and absorb the refined essences and colors.

Those who wear rainbows as robes and drink mists, whose refined essence passes through in secret, are *xingxian* (walking immortals). Those who are able to employ ritual arts and methods to expound the spontaneity of the Dao are *daoxingxian* (Dao-walking immortals).
Those who clarify and concentrate their refined contemplation until they can long respond with illumination are *zhaoxingxian* (illumination-walking immortals).
Whether one visualizes the crown of the head to emit the spirit, or fixes the mind upon the cycle of rebirth to refine the elixir—all these are matters of recollection and mental cultivation.
This is the Perfected Accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna*). Internally, it involves the union of the male of the *kan* trigram and the female of the *li* trigram, matching them as husband and wife;

externally, it consists of gathering the Yin to assist the Yang and conserving the vital essence (*jing*). Such a person is a "Transcendent of Essential Practice" (*jing xing xian*). As for those who employ visualization and transformation as their principle, whose minds follow perverted awakenings, and who can effect great transformations such that their conduct transcends the world—these are "Transcendents of Transcendent Conduct" (*jue xing xian*).
"Ānanda, all these [beings] refine their minds among human beings... until their retribution is exhausted, they return once more and disperse into the various realms of existence.
(Changshui says: "Regarding 'among human beings,' this is because there is no separate general retribution for the realm of immortals;
rather, it is upon the general retribution of the human mind that one adds the ten preceding types of cultivation, refining and transforming them into immortality.)"

Wuxing said: "The *Shanhai jing* states that on Mount Kunlun, in the wilds of Guangdu, at the Mound of Xuanyuan, lies the Land of the Immortals, where there is neither cold nor heat, and people all live for several thousand years. This, too, is a collective shared portion rather than a place without a fixed location.
Yet, if one merely seeks to preserve the physical form without refining the mind while hoping to reach a thousand-year lifespan, it is like seeing..."
To seek for the night-watch while still in the egg—is this not too hasty a calculation?
Ānanda, those people of the world who do not seek the permanent—[up to] such a class as these are called the gods of the Four Great Kings.

(Xie Li said: "The six heavens are attained by cultivating the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions. Now, regarding those who wish to slightly increase their excellence, desire is the root of saṃsāra.
The previous section clarified the beginning of falling into decline; this section clarifies the beginning of transcending and ascending.
Even if a beginner is unable to achieve meditative concentration and wisdom, they can nonetheless swiftly sever the root of saṃsāra.")

(Warmling says: "If one has not yet been able to leave desire behind, but can nevertheless block it so that the waters of craving do not flow, then the nature of stillness will be clear and translucent;
thus, one is able to take birth in the first heaven.")
Those whose lustful desire for their own wives is slight—such a class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Gushan says:
*Trāyastriṃśa* means "the Thirty-three," namely the realm of Śakra).
Wenling says: Because this craving is weaker than that which preceded it, its retribution is situated above it; the subsequent stages follow in the same manner.

"Pure Abodes" (Śuddhāvāsa) refers to the time when one dwells in purity for oneself, yet they have not yet fully realized the flavor of complete purity because a subtle degree of craving still remains.
The sun and moon dwell on the waist of Mount Sumeru, while the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven dwells upon its summit. Because their clarity and brilliance increase, they are able to surpass it.
When encountering desire, they engage briefly, yet upon departing, they are free from thought or recollection; such a class of beings is called the Tuṣita Heaven.

Because sensual desire does not arise, movement is slight and stillness is predominant. Among the six heavens of the Desire Realm, the lower two are called the Earth-Residing Heavens (*bhūmi-vāsin*), and the upper four are called the Space-Residing Heavens (*antarīkṣa-vāsin*).
They do not require the sun or moon; they are perpetually luminous, and day and night are distinguished by the opening and closing of lotus flowers.

Therefore, they are named "Divisions of Time" (*kāla-bhājana*). [Zhenji said: "They also cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); coarse abiding and subtle abiding are what is meant by the 'heavenly karma' of Tuṣita."]
Wenling says: Regarding the phrase "at all times remaining still," although one may be still in body, if the mind is increasingly active, one cannot avoid being touched by sensory objects.
This is the ability to have few desires, but it is not yet the state of being without mind. Among the Tuṣita Heaven there are inner and outer courtyards;

while the three calamities reach up to the third dhyāna heaven, this statement does not refer to that [outer realm], but speaks specifically of the inner courtyard where subtle essence is not contacted. All...
This concerns the affairs of the inner court.
"I have no mind of desire, yet I respond to your activities" (up to) "this kind of class is called the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations.
[Zhenji said: "All heavens possess realms of retribution, yet this heaven delights in its own transformations; because its enjoyment transcends [ordinary experience]..."
Regarding the phrase "in the lower heavens" (hence the name *yuèhuà*, "transcending transformation"), Wēnlíng says:

"This refers to the state where the environment spontaneously arrives while the mind is without intention; it is called 'laid out horizontally. The expression 'chewing wax' means that [the flavor] is not yet very thin."
They lack worldly thoughts yet engage in worldly activities (up to: this class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
(Wenling says: "To transcend clearly" means that there is no flavor [of effort] at all. "Emanation" refers to the fifth heaven; "no emanation" refers to the lower heavens.
Regarding the various objects of sensual pleasure, they do not trouble themselves to emanate them; rather, they enjoy them with mastery as they are emanated by others.)
[This is] named Paranirmita-vaśavartin (the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations).
Wu-xing said: According to the teachings of Tiantai, the karma of the six heavens of the desire realm all takes the ten wholesome deeds as their basis.

If one additionally possesses a mind that protects the Dharma, this is the karma for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. If one additionally possesses a compassionate transformation of others, this is the karma for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. If...
Furthermore, not afflicting sentient beings and being skillfully proficient constitute the karma for the Yāma Heaven.

If one additionally cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the coarse abiding (*audārikasthiti*) and subtle abiding (*sūkṣmasthiti*) constitute the karma for the Tuṣita Heaven. The concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) constitutes the karma for the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.

The threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) constitutes the karma for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. In this sutra, the six heavens are distinguished solely based on the gravity of desires within the desire realm.
There should be two meanings: first, because Ānanda is the condition that initiates [this discourse]; second, because it is the basis for taking birth within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Thus, from the point where Ānanda’s form among the six heavens begins to move, down to this point, it is called the Desire Realm.
Xie Li said: "Although one has emerged from the disturbances of the mundane world, one has not yet severed desire; therefore, it is collectively termed the 'Desire Realm' (*kāmadhātu*). Wu Xing said:
"Though the physical form has emerged from movement, this refers to the two destinies of humans and immortals.

It receives the name 'emerging from movement' because the traces of the mind are still manifest—meaning that the traces of the desiring mind still possess the characteristics of sexual union. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:"
The six [heavens] experience desire through embracing, holding, laughing, and gazing; this refers to those dwelling on earth. The two heavens above engage in physical union:
in Yāma they embrace, in Tuṣita they hold hands, in Nirmāṇarati they gaze at one another while laughing, and in Paranirmita-vaśavartin they merely look at each other.
One must understand that those texts describe the experience of desire according to each of the six heavens. The present sutra, however, speaks only in terms of human beings.
Distinguishing the gravity of desires serves to reveal how the retributions experienced by the six heavens differ.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Fascicle Nine.
Ānanda, all those in the world who cultivate their minds in this manner—this class is called the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (Brahmakāyika).

[Wenling says: The preceding section clarified the six heavens; although they have emerged from the disturbances of the mundane world, they have not yet severed desire, and thus they are collectively termed the Realm of Desire (Kāmadhātu).
From here downward, eighteen heavens are clarified; although they are free from the defilement of desire, they still possess material form, and thus they are collectively termed...]

The Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) is further collectively termed the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*), as its inhabitants have already abandoned the defilement of desire. It is collectively designated as the Four Dhyānas, as its inhabitants have already abandoned distraction and agitation.
While the gods of the Desire Realm are born through the influence of the ten wholesome actions alone, these gods are born through the combined influence of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Nevertheless, their practice consists merely of the six types of activities associated with tainted (*sāsrava*) dhyāna-contemplation.

Wenling says: Regarding the "six practices," one feels aversion toward the desire realm as being suffering, coarse, and obstructive, while taking delight in the form realm as being pure, subtle, and free from attachment.
This constitutes the path of mundane transcendence by which ordinary beings suppress their delusions.

As for the phrase "without relying on *dhyāna*," etc., it means that although this is not the correct cultivation of true *samādhi* and lacks right wisdom, one nevertheless cultivates these six [practices].
By practicing the subduing of desire so that defiled attachment does not arise, one will not remain in the realm of desire.

Since coarse afflictions do not stain them, pure retribution manifests before them, and thus they are immediately born into the Brahma world. First, they are called the *Brahmapāriṣadya* (Retinue of Brahmā), which refers merely to the common assembly.

Next, they are called the *Brahmapurohita* (Ministers of Brahmā), who are the great ministers of Mahābrahmā, culminating in the status of Mahābrahmā itself. Their advancement follows a sequential order.
Once the habitual tendencies of desire have been eliminated and the mind free from desire manifests, those of this class are called the Brahmā-purohita devas (The Retainers of Brahmā).
[Xielü said: That which is associated with precepts and meditative concentration is called the "precept concomitant with concentration" (samādhi-sahagata-śīla).]

Wenling says: At the beginning, the gods of the heavens were merely able to control their bodies and subdue their desires; these gods, moreover, have attained the precepts concurrent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*), and by conforming to the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) and practicing the virtue of Brahma (*brahmacarya*), they therefore transcend them.
With body and mind wondrously perfect and their deportment unimpaired... such a class as this is called the Mahābrahmā Heaven.

(Gushan says: "The reason the three heavens above do not explicitly mention the cultivation of dhyāna but only speak of upholding the precepts is that this sutra supports the Vinaya to encourage future generations.")
Wenling says: "From the preceding purity of mind, majestic deportment, and preceptual practice, one advances to the stage of wondrous, perfect, and pure clarity;
further augmented by brilliant awakening and transcendent penetration, this constitutes the height of sublime virtue, and thus one becomes a Brahma King. Zizhong says:
The Great Brahmā Heaven departs at the end of the kalpa and arrives before the kalpa is formed; because the non-Buddhists do not comprehend this, they cling to it as being eternal.
Ānanda, these three superior streams—wherein all suffering and affliction (up to) the various outflows do not move—is called the First Dhyāna.

(Gushan said: There are four types of dhyāna. First, contaminated dhyāna (*sāsrava-dhyāna*), which refers to the present four dhyānas. Second, uncontaminated dhyāna (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), referring to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
Third, both contaminated and uncontaminated dhyāna, referring to the six subtle gates (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*), the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the clear illumination (*vibhūti-prakāśa*).
Fourth, neither contaminated nor uncontaminated dhyāna, which refers to the samādhi of principle within the Śūraṅgama King Samādhi at the beginning of this sutra.)

The True Limit (bhūtakoṭi) says: "Are there not indeed 'flows' (āsrava)? There are the flow of ignorance, the flow of birth-and-death, the flow of desire, the flow of excellence, the flow of the four fruits, and the flow of nirvāṇa;
each proceeds according to its respective category of flow. As for the flow of desire, it leads toward birth-and-death;

even reaching the sixth heaven is not sufficient to be considered 'excellent,' for this heaven has already emerged from the flow of desire, yet all [those below] remain within the course of birth-and-death."

Because it is supremely pure, all four dhyānas are called "supreme flows" (viśeṣa-bhāgīya). Having already abandoned the eight sufferings of the desire realm, it is said that "suffering and affliction do not oppress.

Having already abandoned the scattered and agitated mind of desire, it is said that "the outflows (āsrava) are unmoving. This is called the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion (vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi);
it means that by being separated from the defiled evils of the desire realm, one gives rise to the bliss of pliancy (praśrabdhi).
Ānanda, next there is the Brahmā Heaven, which governs the Brahmās... (up to) this class is called the Heaven of Limited Light. [Zizhong said:
"From the second dhyāna upward, there is no verbal speech; rather, light is emitted from the concentrated mind.

According to whether the light is superior or inferior, their status as high or low is distinguished. [Lectan said: "Previously, when first attaining concentration, one was unable to produce light; here, however, it is profoundly still and clear."]
Therefore it is named "Limited Light" (Parīttābha). (Changshui says: Since both body and environment are absent, the ten directions transform into lapis lazuli.

(Zhenji says: Regarding the phrase "reflecting the realms of the ten directions," this refers to the light of meditative concentration according to what is experienced; it is spoken of in terms of east, west, and so forth, but does not mean it pervades the entire world-system of the ten directions.)
Wenling says: This refers to ascending through the practice of Mahābrahmā. Because one is endowed with precepts, concentration, and wisdom, it is called "perfect.
Because of this perfection, one can clarify the mind of doubt so that it does not move according to external objects, and from this profound stillness, light arises.

However, at this initial stage, although one is able to detach from clinging and restore the state of profound stillness, the light is still inferior; therefore, it is named "Little Light" (Parīttābha).
Light illuminates light, shining forth without end... (up to) this class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābhā*).

Wēnlíng says: "The power of meditative concentration becomes increasingly bright; wondrous lights flash forth in succession. The environment, following the light, becomes pure, universally forming a world of lapis lazuli."
Inhaling and retaining the circular light, one accomplishes the essence of the teaching (up to):
"This class of beings is called the Heaven of Light-Sound" (Gushan says: since the teaching takes speech and sound as its essence, it is called 'Light-Sound').
Wenling says: In various worlds, the substance of the teaching differs. Thus, in Sahā, it consists of written words;

in Gandhavyūha, there are no written words, but the teaching is proclaimed solely by means of various fragrances. In this heaven, sounds are produced from the circular radiance to proclaim and disseminate the Dharma;
therefore, it is named "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara).
Ānanda, when these three superior streams have all subdued the coarse outflows (*āsrava*) of anxiety and apprehension, it is called the Second Dhyāna.
(Wuxing says: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* names the Second Dhyāna "Dhyāna Accompanied by Joy" (*prīti-sahagata-dhyāna*). When this concentration arises, it is produced together with joy;
therefore, it is now said that one cannot be assailed by any anxiety or apprehension. [The character] "懸" may also be written as "愁".)
[This is an] error).
Wēn-líng says: In the second dhyāna, one is free from sorrow and attains supreme joy and bliss; hence it is said that "sorrow and anxiety do not oppress.

In the first dhyāna, one merely attains a mind free from outflows (*āsrava*), yet has not yet subdued them. This deva, however, has already subdued the coarse outflows, and thus his karma gradually [diminishes].
"Inferior. This refers to the gradual superiority of practice. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "This is called the stage of joy and bliss born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
It means that the water of concentration moistens one's karma, such that the distress of anxiety does not oppress one."
Ānanda, in this way, among the devas and humans, those who have perfected their radiant halos and their voices—up to this point—one such class is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha).

[Master Xingfu said: "They have developed and perfected refined practice and entered the bliss of quiescent extinction; they no longer concern themselves with speech and sound, hence it is called 'Limited Purity'."]
Wenling says: Based on the aforementioned teaching of the perfect light as the essence of the Dharma, the wondrous principle is revealed;

this gives rise to refined practice, which departs from the prior agitation of joy and produces pure bliss. This bliss is not an external object, but arises from the pure nature, characterized by tranquility and stillness.
It is called the bliss of tranquility (*śānti-sukha*). However, because its purity is still inferior, one has merely attained access (*sāmantaka*) and has not yet achieved full realization.
Because it is still inferior, its purity is slight.
When pure space manifests before one and induces boundless [purity], such a class of beings is called the gods of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇa-śubhā devāḥ*).

(Wuxing says: "Looking upward, it has not yet reached the limit; looking downward toward the sages, they are numerous. Therefore, it is called 'Immeasurable' [Amitābha]. (Zizhong says: "The pure realm is immeasurable;
when both mental and physical activities attain pliancy, it is therefore called 'Immeasurable' [Amitābha].")
Wenling says: "Purity and emptiness" refers to a state of meditative concentration that is free from all agitation and does not take external objects as its objective support.

By expanding this state, one causes the mark of purity to become boundless and to accord with the wondrous nature; thus, body and mind become light and at ease, and the joy of the nature is perfected.
Because it is boundless, it is called "immeasurable purity."
"The world, body, and mind are all perfectly pure" (up to) "this class is called the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
(Letam says: Body and environment are both perfect; because this superior reliance is manifest before one, it is named 'Perfect Purity'. Wuxing says:
Above, the lightness and ease of body and mind were discussed in terms of the internal; now, 'the world' and so forth, comprehensively include the external.)
Wenling says: Because pure emptiness is boundless, the worlds, bodies, and minds are all perfectly pure.
When the virtue of purity is accomplished, the nature of bliss takes refuge therein. Because everything is perfectly pure, it is called "Universal Purity" (Parīśuddha).
Ānanda, these three superior streams possess great conformity (*anuloma*)... [up to] ...and being fully endowed with joy (*prīti*), they are called the Third Dhyāna.
(Wuxing says: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* designates the Third Dhyāna as the "Dhyāna Conjoined with Bliss.

Because the merit of this concentration arises together with bliss pervading the entire body, although the first two dhyānas possess the factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*), it was obstructed by the factor of joy; now, that joy is extinguished.)
It is pure bliss; thus it receives its name). Wēnlíng says:
"Possessing the nature of refined conduct and bliss, it is named 'Great Accordance' (mahā-anuloma); therefore, it is immeasurably peaceful and secure. Regarding "joy being fully perfected":
this is called the stage of "Sublime Bliss Apart from Joy" (prīti-viveka-sukha-bhūmi). This means that although the mind is apart from joy, there is nevertheless joy and bliss.
This is self-evident.
Ānanda, furthermore, there are gods and humans whose bodies and minds are not oppressed [by suffering], up to: "this class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Born" (*Puṇyaprasava*).
(Wenling says: Because they have abandoned pleasure and pain, the coarse and heavy characteristics are extinguished; because their equanimity and mindfulness are pure, their nature of merit is pure.)

This concludes the section on birth. From here downward, the four dhyānas are elucidated; in total there are nine heavens. However, within the retribution realms of the four dhyānas, there are only three heavens.
The fourth, the Unconscious (asaṃjñin), is actually the third, the Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala). These are all separately opened as retribution realms for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Above these four are the five heavens of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*); these are attained through the distinct cultivation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) by noble sages and differ from those of ordinary beings.
Wuxing says: "Furthermore" and below concludes the virtues of the third dhyāna. "Pleasure is not inferior" reveals the faults of the third dhyāna.
"Suffering and pleasure are inferior" correctly demonstrates rebirth. Although it is called "pleasure," the third dhyāna lacks the causes of suffering found in the lower realms.
Pleasure must inevitably perish, and its perishing likewise constitutes suffering. Now that pleasure has been relinquished, suffering does not arise;

this is specifically termed the dhyāna associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-sahagata-dhyāna*). Its meaning is the same [as previously stated]. Zhenjì said: "The preceding meditative practices were limited to self-benefit."

They were unable to benefit others. Upon reaching the fourth dhyāna, they diligently cultivated the altruistic minds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
With their mind of equanimity becoming perfectly integrated and their resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) purified—to such an extent as this, this class is called the Puṇyaprasavā devas.
(Wu Xing said: "Attaining marvelous compliance" refers to complying with the following text, which constitutes the second path.

Because this essence of pure merit is free from obstruction and characterized by love and joy, one cultivates the supreme and wondrous Dharma; this is thus the second path of the provisions of merit. It does not merely pertain to the present life;
therefore, it is said to "reach the limits of the future.")

Wenling says: Because both suffering and pleasure are forgotten, the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is perfectly integrated. Because the mind is free from all entanglements, its resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) is pure.
Consequently, merit is without obstruction, and one attains wondrous accordance. From tainted meditative concentration (*sāsrava-dhyāna*), one gives rise to untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*).
Reaching the ultimate limit of the objective realm, it is said: "exhausting the bounds of the future. Such is the nature of concentration and merit. This constitutes [the section on]...
Because they are lovely and delightful, they are called the Puṇyaprasava (Merit-Born) devas.
Ānanda, from this realm there are two diverging paths... [up to] ...this class is called the Bṛhatphala (Vast-Fruit) devas.

(Zizhong said: "This Heaven of Vast Results [Bṛhatphala] is so named because it is induced by vast merit—the merit of meditative absorption infused with the four immeasurable minds—which has detached from the defilements of the lower stages.")
Wenling says: From the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*), there diverge two paths. One is the direct path leading to the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*);

the other is the circuitous and deviant path leading to the Heaven of Non-Perception (*Āsaṃjñika*). If, in one's prior mind, one does not harbor heterodox attachments and directly cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), causing the merit cultivated from the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābhā*) up to the Heaven of Merit-Love to abide in perfect clarity and brilliance—this is the meditative merit of that heaven.
Because it is exceedingly vast, it is named "Vast Fruit" (Bṛhatphala).

If, from the preceding state of mind, one simultaneously feels weary of both suffering and pleasure—[continuing] up to this point—one such class is called the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva-deva).
[Ziqing said: This person does not understand that the nature of delusion is empty in essence; instead, they grasp at arising and ceasing as a weariness, and thus feel aversion...]
This involves the cessation of arising and ceasing while seeking non-arising and non-ceasing; it is not true non-arising.

It is merely that the sixth consciousness does not function, like water held between one's fingers where even the subtlest arising and ceasing goes unnoticed, leading one to falsely claim it is *nirvāṇa*.
Wenling said: Although the preliminary mind can subdue delusions and cultivate dhyāna, it still involves falsehood and retains heterogeneity;

it takes the presence of mind as birth-and-death and takes the absence of thought as nirvāṇa. Consequently, one comes to simultaneously loathe both suffering and pleasure, focusing exclusively on cultivating the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
By inclining toward non-conception, one discards all objects, the body, and even mental conceptions until everything is relinquished; this is called the path of perfect and ultimate relinquishment.

When the mind and its deliberations become ashen and motionless, this is the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). By means of this, one receives retribution and is born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
Their lifespan is five hundred kalpas. The *Abhidharmakośa* states that when first born into this heaven, they are not yet entirely without perception;
it is only after half a kalpa that they become so. When their retribution is about to end, they again possess perception for another half a kalpa before their life-span expires.
Ānanda, these four superior streams, which reach the pinnacle of all worldly realms through the full maturation of their functional application, are called the Four Dhyānas.

"The conditioned realm of space is that which all sentient beings collectively experience; how can one person alone be able to dissolve and extinguish it? Moreover—" )
Throughout antiquity and the present, many have manifested the Truth; yet the realm of emptiness remains as it was. How can it be said that [the world] is thereby dissolved? Xuán said:

"What is induced by common karma does not depart from obscurity and darkness. When one manifests the Truth and returns to luminosity, that [karmic state] may indeed be dissolved. However, sentient beings cannot be exhausted, and worlds cannot be exhausted.
Even if a single person manifests the Truth, the multitude will again be moved to continue the lineage. Therefore, it remains so as to cause those with common karma [to persist]."

If these people are all equally able to give rise to the truth, then the mountains, rivers, and the physical world of the vessel-realm will, by their mere thought, transform into supreme awakening and become a pure and wondrous Buddha-land.
(Supplementary Note: When deluded, one turns the essence of awakening into empty space; when enlightened, one realizes that all of empty space is the essence of awakening.
Therefore, when one person gives rise to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space perceived by that one person is entirely [the essence of awakening].)
It perishes and becomes the essence of awakening; this is what is meant by the "mind-essence penetrating through to the source. It is limpid and still right where it is.
That one has not yet seen its perishing is because they have not yet been able to give rise to the truth and return to the source.
Wenling says: The essence of the awakened mind is what is called the true source (*zhenyuan*).

Due to delusion regarding principle and turning one's back on the truth, delusion is transformed into the establishment of the false, forming the realm of outflows that serves as the basis for demons. "Transforming delusion" means shifting and changing in accordance with delusion.
An empty space arises within great awakening, like a single bubble surfacing from the ocean; it is further likened to a fragment of cloud to clarify that the world is illusory and subtle.
The sharp edge [of delusion] is easily worn away and destroyed. Only the substance of the True Origin is fundamentally vast and empty;

the lands of space are all established through the deluded and stubborn false thoughts of sentient beings. If even one among you were to give rise to the truth and no longer be deluded, then there would be nothing established.
Therefore, they naturally collapse and shatter. This, along with the following text, describes the manifestations of Māra. For...
The conditioned realm of space is the dwelling place of Māra. If it were now to collapse and shatter, Māra would find no peace.
When you practitioners of dhyāna adorn yourselves with samādhi and enter into samāpatti, he will come en masse to harass you.
(Wenling says: Māras rely upon obscurity and darkness. Now, as one cultivates dhyāna and adorns samādhi, the wondrous mind becomes brilliant and refined;

thus, one is able to tear asunder the realm of Māras, which consequently leads to their provocation and harm. [The "ordinary beings" are the heavenly Māras. [Question: The great earth is insentient, and the various species of water and land differ from one another;
why are they all equally considered Māras? Why do they all tremble with fear? [Answer: Guishan replies: It is due to the majestic spiritual power of samādhi.)*
It is inconceivable. For instance, when the Great Tree Kinnara King moves his lute and song, the sound shakes the great trichiliocosm, causing Mount Sumeru to surge and subside;
how much more so the power of the Bodhisattva’s Śūraṅgama-samādhi—how could one raise objections based on the distinction between the sentient and the insentient?
Wenling says: "Adorning" means solemn adornment (*vyūha*). This refers to using the merit of cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to adorn the originally existent true *samādhi*.
Because of this cultivation and adornment, the nature of mind realized by those Bodhisattvas and Arhats becomes universally identical and harmoniously unified.
This is the cause for the arousal of Māra. As they are about to emerge from the realm of *samādhi*, the palaces of Māra and his followers [are shaken].
It naturally collapses and cracks; this too is a precursor to returning to the source.

As for the statement that "ordinary beings are dark and dull-witted and do not perceive the gradual transformation," this is an explanation intended to dispel lingering doubts. It anticipates the doubt of one who might say: "If Māras and the various devas have already seen these signs..."
Ordinary beings do not perceive or understand this at all. Therefore, the commentary explains:
"Yet those various Māras, despite their great rage... [until] they roll about in ruin and fall, beyond all hope of rescue."

(Changshui said: "These words refer to the true essence of wondrous enlightenment, which is neither moving nor decaying; when the power of the correct is applied, the deviant energy naturally dissipates. (Letang said:

"Right concentration overcomes the deviant, yet the deviant may also overcome the right. That these lead to either accomplishment or disruption depends entirely upon the 'host' within the five aggregates of the mind.
(Gushan said: "To compare a courtesan to a celestial Māra is to diminish the latter; it is because [the former] is so meager and inferior.")

The precepts are comparable to one’s entire body; the matter [of violating them] is trivial and inferior. By citing the inferior to illustrate the superior, it shows that the power of the "path-accompanied precepts" (mārga-sahagata-śīla) of the first fruit (srotāpanna) naturally prevents transgression;
hence the phrase "the mind is pure," and so forth. Regarding "confiscation of property" (jimen): the *Hanshu* states, "to remove one from the registers" (*chujishu*), which refers to this.
The confiscation of a minister's property serves as a metaphor for falling into evil while having attained the stage of enlightenment.
Wenling says: "The 'five aggregates' refer to the master, which is the true mind. 'The shadows dissipate and enter into clarity' refers to one who has awakened to the truth.

Dāngakā was shallow and inferior, yet she could only destroy the precept-body; various demons are fierce and evil, and they can ruin the precious awakening. Therefore, one must certainly guard against them deeply."

Ānanda, you should know that from your sitting at the site of enlightenment [until] the point where "solid delusions serve as its foundation," this refers to the state where the subtle clarity of the mind has not yet emitted light—the sign that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has not yet been shattered. (Guishan says:
This means that while one is still in the stage of names and words, it seems as though the teaching is being held too low. (Wenling says: One attains the primordial luminous awareness...)

To claim it possesses the nature of neither arising nor ceasing would be like ascending too high; one should instead follow the interpretation of Wuxing, which assigns it to the stage of contemplative practice (guanxing).
This is precisely where power is gained through dhyāna and when the afflictions of worldly toil are temporarily stilled.
Lectan said: "To cause all thoughts to subside means to use profound stillness to reverse the illusory arising and ceasing.

To be brilliant and clear when free from thought means to attain the fundamental luminous awareness that is devoid of arising and ceasing. Because it is profoundly tranquil, movement and stillness do not displace it."

Because they are free from discursive thought, memory and forgetfulness are as one. Although such is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has not yet been shattered.

Thus, it is like being in a dark place despite having clear vision; although the essential nature is wondrously pure, the mind has not yet emitted light. This is the characteristic of the aggregate of form.
The *skandhas* (陰) take "concealing and covering" as their meaning. Because they confine and limit the true nature (*dharmatā*), they are called "the realm" (*yǔ*).

(Supplementary Note: As previously explained regarding the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) depends upon the *rūpa-skandha*; therefore, when form is exhausted, one can transcend it.
The remaining four turbidities follow this same principle.)

Wenling says: The characteristic of the exhaustion of the five aggregates does not mean that the body is extinguished and returns to nothingness; rather, it means that through the power of contemplation, one penetrates and illuminates them so as no longer to be obstructed by delusion.
Therefore, it is likened to the eyes becoming clear and bright, such that the ten directions open up completely.

As for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it initially arises from the false entanglements of the three—father, mother, and self—therefore it is said that "solidified false conceptualization" is its root. These five kinds of falsity...
The Sūtra has not yet explained this itself:
"Ānanda, you should investigate the wondrous clarity within this [state]... if you take it as a realization of sainthood (*ārya*), you will immediately succumb to various demons.
(Gushan says: Whenever various objects arise, even if they are auspicious signs, grasping at them results in perversion; even if they are evil signs, if...)
One does not grasp or cling. Even the heterodox becomes correct, because the objective realm follows the movement of the mind. (Lectan said: "The ten māras all arise based on objects.

That the body can transcend obstructions is due to the power of contemplative observation; it causes the brilliant and lucid mind and the physical body composed of the four elements to be mutually non-interfering, and thus one is able to transcend obstructions.
[The phrase] 'the preceding realm' refers to the causal basis. 'Physical form' is precisely the brilliant and lucid mind.")
Because it penetrates inwardly through the body, the *yū* and *hī* worms [can exist within it].

Wēnlíng says: "This 'within' refers to the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The wondrous essence is fundamentally harmonious; it is only due to the deluded substance that obstruction is formed."
When one exhaustively masters its subtle functions, the four great elements do not entwine, and the body is able to pass through obstructions.

However, this occurs specifically when compelled by extraordinary power, causing the subtle and wondrous to overflow; it is temporary rather than constant, and therefore is not a realization of the Sage.
Ānanda again took this mind and investigated its subtle brilliance (until: "If you take this as a holy realization, you will immediately be possessed by various demons"). Wēnlíng says:
When the true essence of subtle brilliance overflows into the external realm, there is nothing outside that can obstruct it;

when it overflows into the physical form, there is nothing inside that can block it. Therefore, it is able to emerge from within the body like a *rāji* or a *krimi* worm. This, too, is merely temporary.

Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate thoroughly both internally and externally—up until the point where one forms a holy understanding—one immediately succumbs to various demonic influences.

(Wenling says: The previous thorough investigation first enabled external emptiness and subsequently internal penetration. This further thorough investigation of both internal and external results in a state where both are empty and penetrating;
consequently, the *hun* and *po* souls lose their regularity and interfere with one another. Thus, the habitual perfuming from former lives...)

"One can manifest [these insights] spontaneously, yet they may suddenly be heard [as inspiration]. Now, when one focuses the will and concentrates the spirit to the utmost in discussion, marvelous texts and elegant compositions often shine forth brilliantly, obtained even in dreams.
It should be understood that through diligent study and intense exertion, the spiritual essence occasionally manifests in a similar manner.
(Zizhong said: "If one cultivates the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), this realm will appear before one, just as it does for those who cultivate the *sūtras*...")

The union of "Ra" (羅) and "He" (合) is called the true mark (*samyak-lakṣaṇa*). If one practices other forms of contemplation and even sees the form of a Buddha, it is still not correct, because the mind and its object are not in accord.
How much more so when contemplating True Suchness (*tathatā*)—if one does not grasp at any marks yet still has attachment, is this not surely the work of Māra?

Wuxing said: "Excluding the appropriated body, all others involve mutual interpenetration. This means that apart from the physical body, the six internal constituents—the *hun* and *po* spirits and so forth—interpenetrate one another.
Regarding their acting as host and guest to one another: when the other five enter the *hun*, the *hun* is the host and the five are the guests;
this continues until they enter the *shen*, at which point the *shen* is the host and the others are the guests. They thus alternate with one another.

As for "separation and union": this refers to when the *jing* (vital essence) leaves its original position and unites with the *po* (corporeal soul), or when the *po* leaves its original position and unites with the *jing*, and so forth.
Furthermore, when this mind becomes clear, manifest, bright, and penetrating—if one takes this as a realization of sagehood, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

(Wu Xing says: "To suppress, subdue, and restrain; to transcend and respond. This refers to the four categories of afflictions, or as in the following text, to the elimination of the nature of the four great elements. These names are abbreviated and then concluded.")

Wenling says: The realms of purity and defilement constantly correspond to the mind’s resonance. Thus, when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, the spirit and soul are imbued with spiritual awakening, and the Buddha-realm manifests within the radiance of the mind.
Furthermore, with this mind, one minutely investigates the wondrous clarity (until: "if one takes this as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
[Gushan says: Because the observation transcends limits and the spiritual clarity penetrates everywhere, the empty space of the ten directions manifests forms in successive layers).
Wenling says: By thoroughly investigating the wondrous luminosity and suppressing miscellaneous thoughts, one establishes a superior mental resolve;
through this power, its function transcends all bounds, so that the wondrous application reaches its ultimate limit and manifests in brilliant clarity.
Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate until it becomes clear and transparent—yet if one takes this to be the realization of sainthood, one will immediately fall prey to various devils.
(Lectan said: "When the settled mind is clear and transparent, its refined radiance is undisturbed; thus, one can see in the dark. That objects are not eliminated means they are all real phenomena.")
Wenling says: There are indeed those whose innate clarity spontaneously manifests so that darkness cannot obscure them;

yet it is only by stabilizing the subtle mind and making it lucid and undisturbed that one can perceive dark objects. These are not removed, for they are all real objects that do not change according to the state of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, by means of this mind, one enters perfectly into emptiness and fusion (up to: "if you take this to be the realization of sainthood, you will immediately be possessed by various demons").
[Zhenji said: "By the power of casting away [attachments], the four limbs become empty and fused; therefore, blades and fire cause no harm.
This is what is meant by 'entering fire is not difficult' and 'entering water is not drowning']."

Wenling said: "When the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is empty and harmonious, the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are simultaneously extinguished and the four elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) are cast aside.
Pure awareness leaves the body behind, so there is no injury from contact. Sustained by the power of meditative concentration, fire cannot burn it.

If those in the world who sit upright to relinquish the self can cause their bodies to become like withered wood and their minds like extinguished embers, how much more so the power of true concentration!"
Furthermore, when this mind achieves purity—up to the point where one forms a holy interpretation—one immediately falls prey to various heterodox influences.
(Wenling says: To loathe the coarse, turbid, and obstructive substance, while delighting in the wondrous, pure, and ethereal fusion, is called "achieving purity.")

As focused contemplation deepens day by day, one undergoes spontaneous transformation after a long time; thus, one is able to penetrate and observe all things, attaining non-obstruction. (Zhenji said:
As the aversion to conceptualization deepens day by day and the merit of the pure mind reaches its peak, one perceives that the ten directions are all Buddha-lands.)

Furthermore, if one uses this mind to investigate the profound and far-reaching [realms]—up to the point of forming a holy understanding—one will immediately fall under the influence of various heterodoxies.
(Zhenji said: "Because the power of contemplation and its application are so profound and far-reaching, they force the mind to fly out; therefore, many instances of obstructed vision occur.")
Wenling said: "By refining the mind to exhaust its depths and exerting the spirit to the limit, one transcends the body and reaches a realm of profound darkness;

thus, one is able to see and hear events from distant places. All of the above cases have not yet escaped the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha); they merely rely on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to transcend obstructions and extend their vision and hearing to the far reaches.
If the aggregate of form were exhausted, then the ten directions would open up clearly, and there would no longer be any obscurity."
Darkness. When the six supernormal powers are exercised with ease in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one will surely pass straight through mountain walls without doubt.
Furthermore, if one investigates this mind to the ultimate degree of refinement and yet forms a conception of it as being "saintly," one will immediately fall prey to various delusions.
(Zizhong said: "This person previously possessed the seeds of a deviant mind, which conjoined with external demonic realms to arrive in succession.
This is not a wholesome state; it is purely demonic harassment. It differs from the preceding nine cases, all of which were called wholesome states.
Only when one gives rise to a mind to seek realization does it become a demonic obstacle)."

Wenling says: "The knowledge one perceives is a manifestation of Māra. While the preceding nine [sections] clarify only the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this alone clarifies the affairs of Māra.
When the power of concentration has not yet been perfected, one cannot move Māra; however, when one’s investigation reaches its ultimate refinement, the affairs of Māra gradually emerge.
Therefore, in the following text, the affairs of Māra become increasingly severe."
Ānanda, these ten kinds of meditative states (*dhyāna*) that manifest (up to) maintaining and protecting [the practitioner] so as to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
[Lectan said: "The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) each serve as the basis for ten seeds of demons, totaling fifty layers.

These all arise during the initial stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), which is why there is retrogression and falling away. If one enters the stage of semblance [realization], one falls into a state where progress is not achieved for a long time; therefore, the Buddha next..."
Next, I shall minutely distinguish their characteristics so that those with beginner's minds may recognize the manifestations of these energetic impulses.

For example, while the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has not yet been dismantled, there may appear the manifestation of a celestial Māra; this is precisely what is manifested by the energetic impulses of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).
Wuxing said: "The phrase 'the minds interacting' means that the mind of *dhyāna* and the solid delusions of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) interact;
therefore, these phenomena appear. This should be understood by analogy for the aggregates up to consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Why?

Because each of the five delusions, within the domain of its respective aggregate, becomes the object of observation for *dhyāna*; as they are about to be destroyed but have not yet been destroyed, they are like a lamp."
When he sought to extinguish it, the light blazed up even more fiercely. Thus, he engaged in a battle of merit with the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Whether he succeeded or failed therein distinguished, at that moment, the paths of Mara and the Buddha.
"Ānanda, that son of good family who cultivates *samādhi* [from here until] 'takes empty clarity and deluded thought as its basis.

(Gushan says: There are two kinds of reception, the correct and the deviant. Correct reception belongs to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while deviant reception belongs to Māra. Therefore, if one loses correct reception, one will inevitably fall into ruin. (Zhenji says:
When deluded views and perceptions arise, they turbidly disturb the tranquil nature; this is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). This is precisely reception...)"
This is the essence of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Therefore, once the aggregate of sensation is exhausted, one transcends it.

Wēnlíng says: "Sensation takes the meaning of receiving and taking in external objects. Having already destroyed the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the internal and external have become empty and harmonious."
Therefore, one perceives the minds of all Buddhas as images appearing in a mirror. The minds of all Buddhas are precisely my own wondrously enlightened and luminous mind.
As for these images appearing in a mirror, it means they are pure, empty, and still, being understood to be devoid of form or obstruction.

Although it possesses this wondrous essence, it has not yet been able to exercise its function, because it is shrouded by sensations—like a person overcome by sleep, whose limbs are fully present [yet inactive]. Six...
The faculties are clear and discerning, yet one cannot move them; this is the characteristic of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Wēnlíng says:
"One whose form has been completely eliminated has already parted from physical obstruction; however, because they are haunted by sensation, they are unable to employ it.
Therefore, when the aggregate of sensation subsides, one can immediately detach from the body and observe inwardly, moving or staying without hindrance. This is due to opposition.
Following these illusory objects, one gives rise to false perceptions of gain and loss; thus, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has no substantial body, yet there is a void clarity.
Therefore, it is called the delusion of "void clarity."
"Ānanda, that good man, while within this state (up to the point where he) loses his right concentration (*samādhi*), shall fall into ruin.
(Changshui said: "Within this" refers to the meditative absorption of the aggregate of sensation. (Xingfu said: "Great radiance" refers to the mind of correctness and the realm of clarity.
(Wuxing said: "His mind illuminates" refers to the perception of the aggregate of form mentioned in the following text.)
"Eliminated. This refers to the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). (It is incorrect for some to explain this by means of "wild wisdom. Wénlǐng says:
Having already shattered the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), there is no longer any darkness; thus, one attains great radiance.

Knowing that the aggregate of sensation is the source of fault, one internally suppresses and subdues it to destroy it. However, if one suppresses and subdues it to excess, one loses one's compassionate gentleness. Therefore—
Because they have excessive compassion, the demon of pity (maitrī-māra) takes possession of them.
Ānanda, furthermore, those good sons within that state of concentration [from "until" (yāvat)] will lose their correct attainment (samyaksamādhi) and fall into ruin.
(Zhenji said: "Because the preceding [five] aggregates of form all arise in dependence upon objects, whereas this one arises solely in dependence upon the mind;

thus, it gives rise to compassion and embraces all. (Letang said: "Vigor and diligent application give rise to effort and impetuosity. (Wuxing said: "'Impetuous' refers to a courageous mind that is lofty and unrestrained.")
Wenling said: "When form is exhausted and sensation manifests, it constitutes the superior sign of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Because success is achieved through joy, one is moved with such fervor and vigor as to believe that the fruit of Buddhahood can be attained and that meritorious practice can be easily realized. This was the error of Wenling; thus, mad demons attached themselves to him.
Nowadays, those who consider a little to be sufficient, who are arrogant and transgress their proper bounds, and who regard themselves as having no equal—all of these are like Wenling."
This is due to the fault of over-exertion.
Furthermore, those good sons within that state of concentration (up to) shall lose their right reception and fall into decline.
(Wenling says: In practicing contemplative cultivation, one must maintain the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom; only then can one avoid error. Now, this concentration is excessive...)

His wisdom is subtle, yet the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is not yet exhausted; thus, he makes no new realization in his progress. Because the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already dissolved, he loses his former dwelling.
Between this progress and retreat, he is utterly without support; this is called the "ground of mid-collapse.

Because he lacks support and vision, he becomes parched with thirst and sinks into recollection, and the demon of recollection (*smṛti-māra*) attaches itself to him. Because the mind of recollection is falsely bound, it is as if he were being suspended by a hook.
Furthermore, those good sons within that concentration (up to) will lose their right reception and fall into decline.
(Wenling says: Previously, concentration was strong while wisdom was slight; here, again, the power of wisdom exceeds concentration. In both cases, there is mutual deficiency.)
Therefore, it is called "desire for meditative concentration" (*samādhi*). (Changshui says: Because the power of concentration (*samādhi*) is weak, constant and thorough examination is lost;
because the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) is excessive, one sinks into mere intellectual views.)
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (up to the point where they) lose their right absorption and shall fall into ruin.
(Wenling says: Because they lose their hold on both advancing and retreating, their minds perceive danger; thus they give rise to perverse anxiety, which leads them to bring harm upon themselves.)
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their right reception (*samyaksamādhi*) shall fall into ruin.

(Wu-xing says: Among the seven factors of enlightenment, lightness-and-ease (*praśrabdhi*) has the nature of concentration. If concentration is accompanied by wisdom, the Path of Rightness can be traversed.
Now, since that which has been aroused lacks the self-sustaining power of wisdom, concentration instead becomes distraction; thus Māra gains the opportunity to cause joy.)
They take pleasure in associating with them).
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their right reception (*samyaksamādhi*) shall fall into decline.

(Wenling says: There are seven names for pride (*māna*). To rely on oneself and look down upon others is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"). To be arrogant toward those of equal virtue is merely called...)

It is said: "Pride (*māna*). To vie for superiority among equals is called *abhimāna* (overweening pride). To vie for superiority over those who are superior is also called *abhimāna*. To claim one has attained what one has not attained is called *adhimāna* (conceit).
To boast of oneself while being inferior is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride). Not paying homage to stupas and temples and so forth is precisely *mithyāmāna* (false pride).
The deluded people of today who neither pay homage nor recite [the scriptures] are all under the influence of the demon of pride (*mānamāra*). (Xielü says: "Layered flowers and precious scarves...")
...a category).
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose right reception shall fall away from it.
(Wuxing says: "Light ease" (*praśrabdhi*)—though the name is the same as before, its meaning is different; for it is said that through wisdom one attains all...)
Because it is light and pure: this means that through the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), one is free from the delusions of heaviness and turbidity regarding all sensory objects;
thus, one is said to have become a sage and attained great mastery.

Wenling said: "To take the dissolution of form as 'vital clarity' (jingming), and to take that vital clarity as 'perfect enlightenment' (yuanwu), and then to believe one has attained great compliance and light, pure autonomy—these are all cases of taking a little as sufficient; they belong to the ranks of those who have heard nothing."
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that samādhi (up to) will lose their correct absorption and fall into ruin.
(Wenling says: Because they attain a state of empty clarity, they mistakenly cling to nihilistic emptiness and commit various errors;
all who act thus are victims of the demon of emptiness. (Zizhong says: This arises from the seeds of false views, drawing this demon of emptiness into the heart and viscera.)
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Māra can enter the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to take refuge in Māra with a bond as firm as glue or lacquer;
even if their hands and arms were severed, they would not consider it difficult."
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until they) lose their right absorption and shall fall away from it.
(Wenling says: Because the mind of attachment mostly arises due to compliance, when the state of concentration complies with the mind, perverse attachment becomes a fault.
(Wuxing says: This is like the *Tiantai Zhiguan*; it is the sign of the afflictions and the realm of desire about to arise. Zhiyi [the Wise One] departs from birth...)

Desire and form may be suppressed and brought to rest; however, that which has now arisen is a delusion of such intense fervor that, upon encountering external objects, the mind becomes deranged and the vision darkened—like a sleeping lion that roars when touched. If one does not recognize it, it can lead a person to commit grave transgressions.
Since the present text states that "Māra has entered their minds," this implies that both the afflictions (*kleśa*) and Māra have simultaneously manifested as objective conditions.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of meditative states (*dhyāna*) manifest as objects (up to: maintaining and protecting them so as to achieve the Unsurpassed Way).
[Lectan said: "There are three types of attachment-phenomena. Among the various objects, that which arises as sorrow, decline, anxiety, and longing is the object of suffering and aversion.
That which arises as valor, great joy, arrogance, and desire is the object of pleasure and conformity. That which arises..."*]
It serves as pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Regarding "the mind of emptiness dispels doubt": this refers to the neutral object (*avyākṛta-viṣaya*).
Wēnlíng says: In all the textual passages concerning the aggregates (*skandha*), the terms "maintaining," "protecting," and so forth appear;
these signify the profound intent of guarding against error and assisting the path.
Ānanda, when that good man cultivates *samādhi* [up to this point], it is called the realm of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
(Changshui says: Because he has not yet broken through the aggregate of perception, it is like the muttering in one's sleep;

because there is a portion where he attains the stages of sagehood, it is like the orderly sequence of phonemes. It causes those who are not asleep to all awaken to its meaning, just as when one realizes the state of a sage, one knows.)

They possess the potential for the stage of the noble ones; therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā says: "The Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that these persons shall all achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Xie Li said: "Thoughts are the floating manifestations of mental deliberation; they are the delusive habits of the discerning consciousness.

"Although not yet descended" means that although one has not yet been able to see those sentient beings individually, the causal basis for their pursuit of the fruit and the initial threads of their practice have already been established.)

One can see, in general terms, that these classes of beings all arise from formative activities (*saṃskāra*); thus they are called this "aggregate of formations" (*saṃskāraskandha*), serving as the common basis for their arising.

"Wild horses, mirages, and floating dust" refers to the shimmering, radiant, and flickering appearance [of the world]. "Agitated clarity" refers to what will be explained below as "profoundly clear yet agitated movement.
(Gushan says: The two demons of formations and perceptions take views and afflictions as their substance; among the formations, there are various views.)
There are sixty-two [views], which refers to the sixty-two transformations). Wénlíng says:
"This generally describes the cessation of thought and the manifestation of activity. Floating and shifting are deluded habits;

when the day is bright, there is thinking, and when the evening is dim, there is dreaming. These turbid disturbances of the true nature cannot be unified; these agitations of awakened clarity cannot be stilled."

Therefore, for one whose aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, dream-thoughts are extinguished; waking and sleeping are always one. The clarity of awareness is empty and still, like a cloudless sky.
The five aggregates are coarse at the beginning and subtle at the end; thus, when perception is exhausted, there are no longer coarse or heavy shadow-events.

Although one contemplates the myriad phenomena, there is no conceptual thought. Therefore, it is like a mirror’s bright reflection: without attachment and without trace, it receives illumination in emptiness.

It should be understood that there is no longer any lingering habituation; there is only the singular, refined truth. Because its clarity is thus extreme, the hidden *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is thereby revealed.

Since formation (*saṃskāra*) is the root source of the arising and ceasing of the myriad transformations, when its characteristics are revealed, the origins of the twelve classes of beings are fully seen.
Each life’s continuity is its own thread; this is consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is the common basis for birth, and it is formation (*saṃskāra*).
It stirs and agitates the profound and hidden; thus it is likened to wild horses suddenly appearing and suddenly vanishing, hence it is called "flashing" (yìyì).

Since there are no longer coarse shadows, it is called "pure agitation. The movement and cessation of the faculties and their objects both originate here; therefore, it is called the "ultimate pivot and aperture."
If this turbid flickering is the primordial nature (up to: ... takes obscure and hidden delusive thoughts as its basis).
[Zhenji said: "When thought ceases, this mind becomes clear. When the practice of emptiness manifests, the drifting dust becomes turbid and flickering.

(Wenling says: The habit-energies of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) have become one's nature; therefore, they are called "fundamental nature" and "fundamental habits.

Therefore, when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, one transcends it. Because this aggregate of formations shifts secretly without any conscious awareness, it is called "subtle and hidden delusive thought."
