To see that what has ceased in one practice arises again is called "subsequent existence" (*paunarbhavika*). To delusively calculate the fruit of *nirvāṇa* within the five destinies is to "rely upon saṃsāra.

To "transform the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) means to transform reliance on saṃsāra and rely instead upon *nirvāṇa*. Alternatively, it refers to awakening to the principle of perfect luminosity within the desire realm.

Thus, the desire realm itself is the locus of transformation; alternatively, the first dhyāna is the locus of transformation because it is free from grief, the second dhyāna because it is free from suffering, the third dhyāna because it is the height of joy, and the fourth dhyāna because it is the height of equanimity. These are called the five nirvāṇas.

As for those who are deluded regarding existence and so forth, they do not know that these heavens all belong to the outflows (sāsrava), are not the fruit of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and are not the ultimate state.
Based on this speculative reckoning, there arise the five types of present nirvāṇa, up to the five types of present nirvāṇa which are inverted views of the mind (Xiali says:
"This reckoning should have flowed from the sixth non-Buddhist school; its horizontal and vertical categorization is similar to that of the seven and nine [schools]").
Wuxing said: "The preceding section sets forth the subsequent stages, while the present conclusion regarding the five types of present [realization] reflects their mutual relationship in the text.
From 'Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings of dhyāna' (up to) 'acting as the Great Awakened King’s pure pointing-out instruction.'"
(Wenling says: Previously it was said that "dhyāna-manifested objects" provide an opportunity for celestial māras;
here it is said that "dhyāna-deluded understanding" is when mental māras themselves give rise to deep sprouts.)
Lectan said: "Whenever one’s realization of the Way is not authentic, manifold false calculations arise; these are all merely deluded understandings and are termed 'demonic minds.

One must guard against them most deeply. You who propagate [this teaching] below should take the words of the Tathāgata and spread them everywhere for the sake of all sentient beings, maintaining and protecting them so that demons do not invade and calamities do not arise, ensuring they do not fall onto deviant paths nor grasp at [false views]."
To attain the stage of enlightenment directly through minor realizations is called "pointing the finger toward the King of Great Enlightenment. Wuxing says:

This refers to the "demon of the mind" (*citta-māra*); later, in the section on the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it is called the "demon of views" (*dṛṣṭi-māra*). These two delusions—views and craving—are none other than the "demon of afflictions" (*kleśa-māra*).
Ānanda, when that good man cultivates *samādhi* [up to this point], this is called the realm of the *vijñāna-skandha*.

(Gushan says: These ten demons of the *vijñāna-skandha* are the source of the life-force. When the activity [of the *saṃskāra-skandha*] is exhausted, consciousness manifests; therefore, one deeply penetrates the source of life.
While the activity of the *saṃskāra-skandha* flows on, it does not transcend the phenomena of sense organs and objects. Because the resonance and response are suspended, the internal and external...)

Profoundly clear, it does not summon any categories of beings; therefore, it enters that which has nothing to enter. (Wuxing says: "The primary source of receiving the life-force is the synthesis of consciousness, breath, and warmth to form life.
At the moment of taking birth, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) comes first.)"
Wenling says: This passage provides a general exposition on how karma brings about the cessation of consciousness and the manifestation of phenomena.

Karma is the essential nature of the world’s constant flux and the pivotal mechanism that stirs the forces of birth. It is the profound conduit through which *pudgala* reaps their karma; it is capable of obscuring the celestial realm of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
The six sense-faculties gallop wildly, turbulently agitating what is inwardly serene; they serve as the ultimate pivot and aperture for the floating sense-objects and dust.

Therefore, when the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is exhausted, the governing cords and knots of the life-force suddenly break apart. The deep-seated channels of the *pudgala* are severed, and the resonance between cause and effect is suspended.
Yet, the celestial nature (*prakṛti*) is on the verge of great awakening, and the six sense-faculties no longer gallop wildly. Because they do not gallop wildly, the internal and external...

Profoundly clear, because there is no driving away of the burrow, one enters that which has nothing to enter; movement is reversed and becomes still, becoming deeper and yet deeper—hence it is called "inner and outer.
The *nirvāṇa*-nature, the celestial realm, is shrouded by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), as dark as a long night.

When the first three aggregates are exhausted, it is like the first crowing of a cock; although the dawn is approaching, one still remains submerged in the remaining two aggregates, and the refined colors have not yet been distinguished.

This marks the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It is like the crowing of a rooster at dawn; with only one remaining aggregate, one is on the verge of awakening to the Great Illumination.

The primary source from which life receives its mandate is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Because the aggregate of formations has ceased and consciousness now manifests, one penetrates deeply.

Since it lacks a pivotal opening, it can be observed; since it lacks shifting flow, it can be grasped; since it lacks the impulse for birth, it cannot be summoned. Thus, one finally realizes the ten directions of both the environment and the beings therein.

All are transformations of consciousness. Thus, having already attained the same nature as the devas of the Heaven of Reflected Images, although their refined forms are not yet clearly manifest, the subtle and secret perceptions have already begun to appear; this is the characteristic of the aggregate of consciousness.

(Zizhong said: "Consciousness is the ground to which one returns; therefore, the various vehicles falsely establish it as their causal basis and seek realization as their fruit, collectively forming the ten demons.")
If, among the six faculties, one has already attained sameness within them... [up to] ...taking inverted false imaginings as their root.
(Wuxing says: "The six functions are not separated; they all interpenetrate one another. This is precisely what is clarified in the *Lotus Sūtra* as the purity of the six sense organs.
(Gushan says: "'Wangxiang' (imageless) also imitates 'xiang' (image); both describe a state of unreality.)
Wenling said: "The 'simultaneous summons from the multitude' refers to the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-skandha*), which is the life-essence of the twelve categories of beings.

If, within this state, one employs the power of concentration and wisdom to dissolve the six gates, so that the sense organs merge without division and their respective domains open without obstruction, then seeing and hearing will become perfectly interfused and the six faculties will function interchangeably. From this, as for the external world and the internal..."

Body and mind are no longer subject to obstruction; this is the sign of the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The nature is fundamentally one true reality, yet it is separated by sensory objects.

Between the nature and its functions, the standards for identity and difference are lost, which is termed the turbidity of life-force (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). Therefore, when consciousness is exhausted, one transcends it.
Consciousness is but a reflected luminosity of deluded awareness; it originally has no self-substance. Arising from inversion, it is called "the formless phantom" (*wangxiang*).
"Empty, non-existent, inverted, and deluded thoughts.
Ānanda, you should know that such good sons (up to) turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa and give birth to the seeds of external paths.

(Xie Li says: This refers to the attachment to what is not a cause as being a cause. (Wu Xing says: Those whose awareness and cognition are universally pervasive and able to enter the perfect and fundamental [nature]...)

This indicates the signs that arise during contemplation. These are merely temporary attainments through effort; such states, which lack superior conviction (*adhimukti*), are called "wholesome realms.
Because one gives rise to false attachments, one falls into the category of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Wenling says: Consciousness flows from volitional formations; therefore, when formations are emptied, one returns to the source. Since the aggregate of formations has been emptied, the cycle of birth and death has already ceased.
Yet, because one still relies upon the source of consciousness, quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.

Nevertheless, one can gradually shatter the aggregate of consciousness and dissolve the six gates; thus, the six faculties of cognition merge harmoniously without separation, and the various modes of awakened nature become universally integrated.

Second: Thus one is able to enter the perfect source (*yuan-yuan*). The perfect source is precisely the fusion of the faculties; it is the source-consciousness that penetrates through the various categories of beings.
If one takes this to be the true ground of return and establishes it as the true cause, one falls into the attachment to the cause and the object of the cause.
In essence, a true cause is not an object; whatever exists as an object is delusory.
The *Sāṃkhya* heretics take that which is prior to the manifestation of the *ālayavijñāna*—the dark, primordial state—as their "true cause" toward which they turn; this is precisely the same [error].

Because the mind has something to grasp and there is a result to which one returns, both cause and effect fall into the delusion of objects. Therefore, this contradicts perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
It turns its back on *nirvāṇa*.
(Gushan says: The *ālayavijñāna* is the object of the samādhi of "dwelling in happiness in the present life" for all noble ones (*āryas*).
It serves as the cause for the various destinies of humans and devas, as well as for all Buddha-lands, and constantly acts as the seed-nature (*gotra*) for all vehicles.)

This is the meaning. Ānanda, furthermore, if a son of good family exhausts all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to the point of emptiness—[continuing] until—he gives rise to the seeds of the Great Brahmā Heaven, conceiving a self that is omnipresent and pervasive.

(Xie Li says: "This is the grasping at the non-existent as existent; by calculating that the self produces that [state], one forms the seeds of omnipresence and pervasiveness. Changshui says: "Great...")

The "haughty deva" refers to Maheśvara. Because he claims what he cannot do to be what he can do, he is called one of "great pride. As for "pervasive and complete," it means he reckons his own essence to be spherical and to pervade the entire realm of space.

Wenling says: Clinging to the source of consciousness as one's own self-nature, one claims that all sentient beings flow forth from this, and thus clings to the notion "I can produce them," even though in reality it cannot.
Therefore, it is called "clinging to the capable as incapable. Maheśvara is the Māra-king at the summit of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
He falsely calculates that "I can manifest and give rise to boundless sentient beings," and he also [claims]...

It is not that which can be categorized as such. That which is capable of performing the functions of the mind and producing its fruits—calculating "I" to be the basis for those [functions] and capable of accomplishing those tasks—is so called.

Furthermore, O son of good family, one who exhaustively investigates the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (down to) turning their back on the city of Nirvāṇa, gives rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.
(Wu Xing said: "That which flows forth from that" refers here to the *vijñāna-skandha* as the destination; it does not refer to another person. (Xie Li said:
"This is the attachment to the permanent as impermanent; by reckoning that [the other] gives rise to the self, one completes the inverted seed.")
Wenling says: Because one takes the source of consciousness (*vijñāna-mūla*) as that upon which one relies, one suspects it to be that which can produce both oneself and all phenomena.

Consequently, one reckons the place from which they arise and flow forth to be the true, eternal, and birthless essence. This is to falsely reckon something as permanently abiding amidst birth and cessation;
thus, one is both deluded regarding the true nature of non-arising and confused about the presently manifesting phenomena of birth and cessation.

Because one takes what is impermanent to be permanent, this is called the "clinging to permanence and impermanence. Since one reckons that [the ālayavijñāna] can produce the self, it is identical to reckoning that Īśvara can produce all things.
This arises from relying on the source of consciousness and falsely reckoning it to be eternally abiding.
Therefore it is said: establishing the cause depends on the mind to produce a falsely conceptualized fruit. The former [view] held that the self produced the world;
this [view] holds that the world produced the self. Hence it is called "inverted completeness."
Furthermore, good sons, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness (*yāvat*), they turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa and give rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.
(Ziqing says: "The eternally abiding true mind is a single essence without duality. Through the employment of various false thoughts, the primary and secondary [worlds] are distinguished.

Therefore, sentient beings, grasses, and trees are all like flowers in the sky. One should know that grasses, trees, mountains, and rivers are all sentient beings. From: *The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment* (Yuanjue jing), translated by Śikṣānanda; commentary by Ziqing.
Because they are transformations of the mind, they are called sentient beings. When there is Buddha-nature, it is said that grasses and trees possess nature;
when sentient beings attain Buddhahood, it is said that grasses and trees attain Buddhahood. Since there are no objects external to the mind, there is no space external to the flower;

thus, waves do not depart from water. Therefore, those who cling to [the literal] fail to understand and claim that each individual blade of grass and tree possesses consciousness, and thus speak of "wood."
"When a person dies, the person becomes wood. (This does not clarify that they are of one substance; it is a deluded calculation regarding pervasive omnipresence). Wénlǐng says:

"That which is known" refers to the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) which is being observed. This means that consciousness possesses cognition, and all phenomena arise through transformation based on this cognition.
Consequently, by calculating that the essence of cognition is omnipresent throughout all phenomena, a divergent interpretation is established, claiming that insentient things [are sentient].
It possesses universal cognition without any discrimination; therefore, it is called "undiscriminating universal cognition.

Because it takes non-cognition to be cognition, it is termed the "clinging to the cognition of non-cognition. Bhāṣika and Sañjīni are two non-Buddhist teachers who cling to the notion that all things are consciousness.
This refers to the attachment to the notion that all things possess cognition. This erroneous calculation takes perfect knowledge as the cause of the mind;
thus, the result will ultimately be empty and false. To take non-cognition as cognition is inverted cognition.

Furthermore, the good man, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) into emptiness—[extending] up to turning his back on the city of *nirvāṇa* and giving rise to the seeds of delusive transformations (*viparyāsa*).
(Wuxing says: "Delusive transformations" refers to what is perceived within meditative observation; it is the realm of consciousness-only, wherein there is pervasive integration and transformation.)

The arising of a single function is precisely the characteristic of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). When one contemplates the accomplishment of these particles (*rajas*), they are specifically named the earth element;

yet by extension, these various particles refer to all four great elements. Having seen that at this stage they all arise through transformation, one then calculates that, ultimately, they will be fully realized as the fruit of fruition.
Because one does not perceive the brightness of fire emerging from it, nor the purity of water, and so forth, it is said that these are the fundamental causes for the arising [of such perceptions].
This establishes the understanding of permanence. Kāśyapa is also a distinct clan of the Brahmins; those mentioned below collectively encompass his kind.
Wenling said: "To exhaust the consciousness aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) means to dissolve the six sense-gates so that the various faculties function interchangeably.

Since this has not yet been fully exhausted here, one merely attains compliance with it. Because of this compliance with the perfect interfunctioning, one then calculates that all phenomena are capable of perfect transformation, giving rise to superior fruits;
for instance, claiming that fire can manifest radiance, or even that dust can achieve [such results]."

Regarding the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), they consequently engage in perverse seeking and perverse contemplation, diligently honoring and serving it while clinging to it as that which can produce superior fruits;
yet in reality, it cannot. Therefore, this is called "clinging to the non-arising as arising. These are the likes of the three Kāśyapa non-Buddhist sects.
Having become deluded regarding the true mind and seeking hope from external objects, both cause and effect are false, and the principle of transformation is inverted.
This is called the lineage of inverted transformation.

Furthermore, good sons who exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—[extending] up to those who turn their backs on the city of *nirvāṇa*—give rise to the lineage of nihilistic annihilation.

(Wuxing says: "It is not that they extinguish the manifold transformations; it is not that they are particularly destructive. 'Manifold transformations' refers to the four great elements and so forth. (Xielǐ says: [as above]).
To take that which has no refuge as a refuge and to calculate it as the basis for eternal extinction is to form the seed of annihilationism.

Wēnlíng says: "Because one does not clearly contemplate the principle, one erroneously falls into nihilism; thus, within the perfectly luminous nature, one calculates everything to be void and non-existent.
Thereupon, one cuts off all transformations and returns to eternal extinction, yet remains unaware that this is wrong—this is called 'returning'."

There is no grasping at a refuge. *Śūnyatā* means "emptiness. To speak of "emptiness of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-śūnyatā*) is precisely to grasp at the emptiness of annihilationism, which belongs to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Because they grasp at the emptiness of annihilationism, they take the perfect void as their causal mind and thereby produce the fruit of nihilistic emptiness;
this eternal extinction of the basis is the nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, the good man, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena to the point of realizing their emptiness (up to the point of turning his back on the city of Nirvāṇa), gives rise to the seeds of false prolongation.
(Wenling says: "Asita" means "Incomparable"; he is the Long-lived Immortal. Although he lived for a long time, he ultimately returned to destruction.
Now, if one seeks to solidify this delusory body in order to attain permanence, it will only result in empty and protracted toil. This is "false prolongation.")
[The character for] "ear" (耳). [Changshui says: "Cháng-láo-guǒ" (Long Fruit) is likely an error for the sound "láo" (to bind/secure). Wuxing says:
Relying on the observation of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) as perfect and eternal, one clings to the source of consciousness as the perfect essence (*vimala-viśuddha*).

Consequently, one desires to firmly preserve the body so that it may coexist with it; through false craving for solidity and duration, one does not realize its falsity. This is called "craving what is not to be craved. Consciousness—
The essence of the *skandhas* is pure and lucid; that which remains unmoving and serene is called "constant.
Now, seeing this constancy, you grasp at the physical body as being identical to this pure, perfect essence. The body is fundamentally impermanent and truly not to be craved as something enduring.
Because you now stubbornly cling to it, it is said that "craving is not craving, but grasping."
Furthermore, good sons who exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (up to) turning their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa and being born into the lineage of celestial Māras.
(Gushan says: "Grasping at the unreal as real" refers to retaining desire and clinging to life, thereby becoming of the lineage of celestial Māras. (Xielǐ says:
"Cakravartin [or Ṭakkirāja] can transform sensual objects to amuse himself.")

Wenling says: Taking the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the source of life, it interpenetrates the three periods of time. If the consciousness-aggregate were to be exhausted, my life would also be exhausted;
who then could testify to its permanence? Therefore, within meditative concentration, he transforms various objects of desire in order to maintain his involvement with worldly defilements.
It does not allow them to be exhausted. Relying on such perverse thoughts, they desire to realize the true and eternal, yet do not know it is not so;
this is called the "attachment to the non-existent as existent. *Ṭakkirāja* is a class of gods belonging to the category of the Lord of the Summit (*Śakro devānām indraḥ*).

Because of their perverse thoughts, they induce birth as celestial Māras; indulging solely in worldly desires, this is called the "fruit of blazing dust," and the *Yuanmei* (Beautiful Woman) is its manifestation.

Furthermore, good sons exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—[extending] up to turning their backs on the city of *nirvāṇa* and giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.

(Gushan says: "Turning their backs on the path of pure liberation" refers to those who, having already developed the limited understanding of the Lesser Vehicle, turn away from the path of perfect, harmonious, eternal, blissful, self, and pure [the four virtues]. Here, among these four virtues, only one is briefly cited. (Xielü says: "Śrāvakas of fixed nature"...)
It is said that "clarifying the sūtras" refers to "fear. If one loathes the body and sets one's will upon nirvāṇa, one falls into the stage of an arhat.
Wénlǐng says: "Clarifying destiny" means that by exhausting the *vijñānaskandha*, one deeply clarifies the fundamental cause of sentient beings receiving their life-destiny.
Since arising and ceasing are like consciousness and refinement or coarseness depend on karma, one distinguishes and determines them according to the Four Noble Truths.

Taking suffering and its origin as coarse and false, and cessation and the path as refined and true, one then focuses exclusively on cultivating the causes of the path to seek the realization of the fruit of cessation.
Being satisfied with little, one rests immediately upon abiding in cessation; this is the specific nature of the overweening pride of the *śrāvaka*.
This refers to the "perfectly refined responsive" (*yuanjing ying*). It constitutes the causal mind that achieves the minor fruit of quiescence.

As for the "perfectly refined responsive," it involves decisively selecting against coarse karma; it seeks only to realize the partial truth through the perfectly refined responsive, remaining entangled in emptiness and tending toward quiescence alone.

Furthermore, the good man exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)... [up to] ...giving rise to a perfected and luminous awakening, which is not transformed into a perfected seed. (Chen Xieli says:

"The perfectly wondrous true body, in which both thought and habituation are exhausted, is called pure awakening. Being luminous within quiescent subtlety, it reaches the ultimate state of fundamental truth.
By investigating and refining this profound subtlety, one takes this as the fruit; this is called a *pratyekabuddha* of fixed nature. (Changshui says:...)

The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) presides over all; entering into consciousness and becoming one with consciousness is the fundamental root [of all]. Therefore, this provides a general exposition of the various methods of cultivation and realization for the śrāvakas.

Wenling says: "The fusion of purity, awakening, and clarity is precisely the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Although it is free from the habits of delusion and is perfectly integrated and pure, it has not yet transcended consciousness;
therefore, it is called 'awakening-clarity. If one takes this to be profound and subtle, establishing it as a realized fruit of enlightenment," [it would be a mistake].
This refers merely to those of fixed nature who are pratyekabuddhas. This is the case where one takes the *ālayavijñāna* as the causal mind and achieves the stagnant fruit of profound clarity.
Regarding "the *ālayavijñāna* is like the mind": it means that although one has mastered the *ālayavijñāna* through awakening and awareness, one remains stuck within the *ālayavijñāna*.
To be "stuck" means that one merely attains penetration with the true awakening but does not proceed further. "Profound clarity" (*zhanming*) is precisely the perfectly interfused awakening-clarity.

The object of awakening ceases within the perfectly luminous essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-śukra*), yet its settled nature does not revert; therefore, it is called "perfectly awakened" (*jueyuan*).
This clarity does not transform into the perfect seed.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* (up to... have been accomplished from the beginning without encountering bypaths.
(Wu Xing said: "Those who speak great falsehoods" specifically refers to the preceding eight types. While the preceding eight share a general name, they may also be distinguished individually:
seven are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and one is a demonic adversary (*māra*). Since neither has severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said that they fall into hell.)
The two vehicles differ from this; therefore, it is said that they do not advance. Regarding the statement "seeing Māra": "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) is defined by its opposition to principle.

Among these [ten], the first eight oppose the Truth (*tattva*); the middle two give rise to false views within the realm (*dhātu*) based on principle; and the final two oppose the Middle Way (*madhyamārtha*), giving rise to false views outside the realm.
This is because the wisdom of the two vehicles is itself ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, among the first eight, seven are purely views, while the eighth possesses both [views and afflictions].
"Attachment. Because it retains the dust of worldly toil and gives rise to a false resolve.
Wénlǐng says: "When one exhausts the Way but loses its true direction, one becomes deranged midway. Turning toward byways and branches, one says that what one relies upon is delusion;
yet that which one loves due to prior habituation is precisely a heterodox transmission and erroneous understanding. To keep this secret as a 'true attainment' is to finally come to rest [in error]."
The mind is intended to be the ultimate ground of refuge; yet, by being merely self-deceived, demons and malevolent spirits take advantage of it, leading one ultimately to fall into the evil realms.
If the followers of the Two Vehicles rely upon it, they will fail to progress. One must guard against this most deeply.

Erroneous views and misconceptions act as demons and calamities, causing the body and mind to stumble and fall; these are called the "demons of views. The mind becomes internally fettered, and such views ought to be...

The external fetters. Thus, while the former [section] guarded against the demon of the mind, this guards against the demon of views; in this way, the essentials for aiding the Path are fully exhausted.
Such a Dharma-gate begins from the past world until the fulfillment of Bodhi through non-attainment.
(Zhendi said: "The sages of antiquity rode upon this mind to open it and attain the Way; it is only fitting that later students should strive to investigate it thoroughly.

When consciousness is exhausted, the six gates are dissolved, and thus the various faculties function interchangeably. From within this mutual functioning, one enters adamantine wisdom and gives rise to the perfectly luminous mind—this is the matter of the mind opening.
To transcend directly through faith and the other stages, entering the ocean of the Tathāgatas and returning to non-attainment—this is...)"

This is the attainment of the Way. The Vajra-dry-wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*) constitutes the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). The various stages of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute the gradual sequence of progressive cultivation.

Those who are able to directly transcend these without passing through them do so because the cultivation and advancement through those various stages were intended to counteract the habitual tendencies of delusion;

now that consciousness is exhausted and there are no more habits, they are able to transcend them. Regarding the phrase "Equal Enlightenment is perfectly luminous and returns to non-attainment": from the initial stage of dry-wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment...
Awakening is not yet perfectly luminous; there is still something attained because consciousness has not been fully exhausted.

Only upon attaining the Vajra-mind and utterly shattering the subtle consciousness can one achieve perfect luminosity, enter the ocean of wondrous awakening, and return to the state of non-attainment. This is the ultimate path of true cultivation.
Wuxing said: "Such a dharma-gate refers, for the time being, to the manifestation of signs during *dhyāna* within the *vijñāna-skandha*.
There have been no Buddhas of the past who did not awaken to this and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore it is said that 'by means of this, the mind opens.

To be able to enter the adamantine *prajñā* is to transcend from the stage of semblance and enter the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This is what Tiantai elucidates as the Perfect Teaching."
Those of sharp faculties who, in a single lifetime, transcend and ascend to the ten stages correspond to this.

From "Perfectly Bright" (*yuanming*) down to "Jewel Moon" (*baoyue*), the realization attained at the final mind is demonstrated through both dharma and metaphor, essence and function. The adamantine dry wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*) is the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*) of wondrous enlightenment;
upon entering the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is precisely wondrous enlightenment. Therefore, it is said: "He enters into Suchness."
...and so forth. The Ocean of Sublime Adornments is the ultimate of merit; the perfection of Bodhi is the ultimate of wisdom;
returning to non-attainment is the ultimate of principle. Merit is liberation (*vimukti*); wisdom is *prajñā*; principle is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Neither vertical nor horizontal, the secret treasury of the three virtues is fully manifested herein. Tracing its cause back to its origin, it truly arises from...
The beginner cultivates *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*; these are the merits of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*). Wēnlíng says:
"The Ocean of Sublime Adornments" is the fruit-ocean that unifies all virtues and harmonizes diverse streams; it is adorned without being adorned, and realized without being realized.
Since the previous section described the *Śūraṅgama* and myriad practices as the Path of Sublime Adornment, this [Ocean] is precisely what arises from that.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat and again addressed the Buddha: [up to] "it is like Yajñadatta, who, deluded, mistook his own head for its reflection.
(Xie Li says: This question has two parts. From "the thought-mind" (*saṃjñā-citta*) upward, he asks about the causes and conditions of arising;

from "conditioned by this" downward, he asks about the causes and conditions of returning to cessation. [Wenling says: Birth-and-death is false karma; the defilements are false conditions. Within the truly pure nature,]...

Since there is nothing that remains, it arises entirely from delusion. It is like being confused about one's own head; thus, among the characteristics of the five aggregates, it can be known that the five delusions are the root.

Wuxing said: "Essential reality" (*jingzhen*) refers to the Middle Way. "Subtle luminosity and tranquil illumination" (*miaoming jizhao*): because it is tranquil, it is the provisional; because it is illuminating, it is the empty.
The three truths are interfused, fundamentally free from dust and defilement; this is collectively termed "original enlightenment, perfectly pure. This section discusses the true nature alone.
Furthermore, the subsequent section discusses the arising of all phenomena through deluded thought alone. From "This is originally... onwards, both are explained together.
The arising of truth and falsehood constitutes the world. The reason for this is that without the preceding separate discussion, one would not know the meaning of "separation";
without the subsequent combined clarification, one would not know the meaning of "identity."
The delusion originally takes its cause within the midst of false conceptualization... (up to) the fundamental causes of the five aggregates are likewise all false conceptualizations.
(Changshui says: This breaks the sentiments regarding causes, conditions, and spontaneity. "Cause" refers to that which can produce; "condition" refers to that which can nourish.

A cause is able to produce through the assistance and support [of conditions], and once produced, it continues in succession. The power of conditions nourishes it; or, the cause may be singular while the conditions are manifold.)
That which is "spontaneous" (svayambhū) for the multitude is also called "self-arisen," or "self-characteristic," or "self-essence," or "the self-realization of the self-dharma."
Wenling says: To clarify that delusion has no cause is to show that it cannot be subject to conceptual calculation. If one knows where delusion arises, one may speak of causes and conditions;
but if one does not know where it arises, how can there be causes and conditions? Furthermore, to postulate "spontaneity" (ziran) is it not itself a false conceptualization?
"The substance of your body was originally produced from the thoughts of your parents... (up to) it is called the first solid false discrimination.

(Xie Li said: "The substance arises from thought; the mind arises from thought; life is transmitted by thought. As these various thoughts intersect and solidify, they form the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);
therefore, it is named 'solid false discrimination')."
Wenling says: "Thought is a false and illusory image, the residual body of deep-seated craving for desire.

Because it flows forth from one's own thoughts and cravings, it is said that 'the body arises from the thoughts of the parents. Within the aggregates (*skandhas*), one seeks in darkness through thoughts and cravings;

therefore, it is said that 'the mind transmits life within thought. Statements regarding sour substances and the like serve to verify the false knots of essence and function; thus, they accord with the principle of delusion."
This is consistent with reason. If it were not a false category, then the false could not produce such a result.
This teaching—that the mind conceiving of heights (up to what is called "empty clarity")—is the second delusion.

(Zhenji said: "Empty clarity and deluded thoughts serve as the causes and conditions for opposition and compliance. Wuxing said: "To be born due to causes means that one undergoes birth because of thought.
To depart from the substance of moving form is to receive the bitterness and astringency of form.
One should know that the three aggregates of form, sensation, and perception arise through mutual dependence upon deluded thought; they are necessarily not separate from one another.)"
Wenling says: To have a sense of longing and bitterness while contemplating the void is truly the arising of delusion regarding both the adverse and the favorable;

when benefit and harm manifest as fleeting movements, the *vedanā-skandha* (perception aggregate) constitutes its substance. Because it has an empty clarity, it is called the "delusory thought of empty clarity."
"Because of your thoughts and reflections, your physical body [is produced]... this is called the third deluded thought, that of pervasive integration (yōngtōng).
[Zhenji said: 'The deluded thought of pervasive integration is the causal condition for the grasping of form.']"
Wenling says: "Thoughts and considerations are empty phenomena; the physical body is substantial reality.

That the empty and the substantial, which are of different natures, can influence one another is due to their being fused by thought. The mind gives rise to empty thoughts, while the form grasps at substantial objects.

That the mind and the form, which have distinct functions, can correspond with one another is due to their being connected by thought. This extends even to the shifting changes between waking and sleeping, which cause the mind..."
Following after objects, causing the objects to follow the mind—all these are the delusions of interpenetration.
The principle of transformation does not abide, shifting and moving in secret and continuous succession; this is called the fourth subtle and hidden delusion.
(Zhenji said: "Its substance consists of hidden and obscure false conceptualization; it shifts as conditions subtly move, yet it is not you. How can its substance shift?

If it were identical to your own substance, it should naturally possess awareness. (Changshui said: "The former passage marked the subtle and hidden characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);
Ānanda’s subsequent response [the 'downward citation'] analyzes the principle of its falsity.")
Wuxing said: "If this were not you, it refers to the principle that transformations do not abide, and so forth. How could the essence (the body) undergo transition?

To interrogate [the opponent] regarding the growth of nails and hair and so on—as in the passage beginning 'If necessarily'—if these were the essence of you, why do you not perceive this phenomenon of one thing replacing another?
Because one does not perceive it, the arising and ceasing of the activity aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) is called 'subtly hidden.'"
Furthermore, from "where your clarity and brilliance are tranquil and unmoving" up to "moment by moment receiving perfuming," what calculation can there be?

[Zhenji said: "This aggregate (skandha) encompasses all eight consciousnesses; while their functions move, their substance is constant. Seeing, hearing, clarity, and brilliance are all one aggregate of consciousness.

Why does the text below indicate 'deluded habituated thoughts'? Regarding 'moment by moment receiving perfuming,' it refers to having previously beheld extraordinary things and thereby taking in seeds."
Within consciousness, if one does not receive [the seeds] from the elder brother, and were to look back upon the preceding differences, there would necessarily be no thought of memory.

Since there is no loss of memory, we know that throughout the interval, ignorance has constantly acted as a perfuming influence from moment to moment. The elder brother’s habituation is merely delusion;
what true essence could there be in it?
Xie Li said: "The term 'profound stillness' (zhàn) refers to the essence of consciousness; 'seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing' refer to the function of consciousness.
To claim that something is 'permanently constant' while it is not truly eternal is a delusion. The pure and true reality admits no false habituation;

yet now, the present can conceal the past without any loss whatsoever—this is precisely what constitutes false habituation. Thus, although the profound stillness does not waver, moment after moment it undergoes conditioning."
Its manifestations are largely illusory.
Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not true [up to] the fifth inverted subtle and refined conception.

(Wuxing says: The mutual functioning of the six sense organs and so forth is like the destruction of the afflictions of views and thoughts; thus, deluded thoughts are extinguished, and the coarse defilements are first [removed]).

[The text] ends here. Question: In the preceding passage, it was stated that "receiving perfuming" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, regarding the extinction of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), why does it stop at merely the *dṛṣṭi-heya* (views) and *bhāvanā-heya* (cultivation)?

Answer: That which is perfumed by ignorance also contains the seeds of *dṛṣṭi-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya*. Therefore, when the previous section pointed to the objects of perception, the presence of recollection and delusion constitutes precisely the coarse characteristics (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*).

Although both the seeds and their manifestations are now exhausted, the fundamental [ignorance] still remains. This does not mean that the six sense faculties have attained true mutual functioning (*anyonya-viniyoga*).
Wenling said: "This stillness is not true stillness; it is merely a state of profound concealment that one fails to perceive.
Therefore, it is likened to a torrential stream whose flow is hidden and deep, impossible to fathom. This is the very source of recollective thought and the substance of the vessel for delusion."
One must directly cause the six gates to be dissolved, so that deluded habits have no place to lodge; only then can they be extinguished. "Shuan" (串) means constant practice;

"ji" (幾) means the subtle and minute. That which seems non-existent is called *wang* (罔); that which seems existent is called *xiang* (象). Its substance is refined and subtle; therefore it is named *Wangxiang* (Entangled Image), *Xuwu* (Non-existence), *Dian-dao* (Inverted), and *Jingxiang* (Refined Conception).

Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) are formed by the five kinds of deluded imagination... [until] "the profound entry pervades the profound, returning to the limit of consciousness.
(Xie Li says: The aggregate of clinging is also called the aggregate of grasping (*upādāna-skandha*). The Buddha’s retribution body is conditioned and non-outflow (*anāsrava*);

it is called "grasping" because it is not produced by afflictions and karma. Because afflictions and karma constitute the "aggregate of grasping," and because [this body] arises from that grasping, it is named the aggregate of grasping.)

Wenling says: The five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are also called the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*). Due to a single moment of deluded ignorance, one thus grasps at these and thereby conceals oneself within them.
As for the statement regarding "causes and realms" (*dhātu*), fundamentally there are no realms; they arise solely from the cause of false conceptualization.
Therefore, form is not form by itself; it is because of emptiness that there is form, and thus the limit of form is established. This extends even to cessation, which does not cease by itself;
it is because of arising that there is cessation, and thus the limit of formations is established. Consciousness is called "lucid and aware," yet lucidity is not lucidity by itself.
Because the causal activities do not flow or stray, the nature enters the primordial clarity and accords with profound lucidity, thereby forming the limit of consciousness.
These five aggregates arise in successive layers; their cause of arising lies in consciousness, and their cessation begins with the removal of form.
(Changshui said: "The five aggregates arise from the subtle to the coarse; through delusion regarding wisdom there is consciousness, and so on, until through sensation there is form.
Their cessation proceeds from the coarse to the subtle: one must first destroy form before sensation manifests, and so on, until one destroys formations before consciousness manifests.)
Gushan said: "In terms of arising, one proceeds from the internal to the external, from the subtle to the coarse, like putting on clothes;

thus, when deluded regarding principle, consciousness arises, continuing down to the arising of form. In terms of cessation, however, one proceeds from the external to the internal, from the coarse to the subtle."
It is like shedding one's clothes. Thus, when one awakens to the principle, form is exhausted, and so on until consciousness is exhausted.
The principle is suddenly awakened to; with this awakening, [all delusions] are simultaneously eliminated. (Up to: What is there that is not clear? I inquire of you once again regarding this.
(Wu Xing said: "The preceding explanation also contains two meanings, sudden and gradual. The substance of the cloth is one, which serves as a metaphor for its nature;
awakening to this constitutes the sudden. The knots in the cloth differ, which serves as a metaphor for deluded thoughts; removing these constitutes the gradual.)
Zhendi said: "Consciousness is like the *karpāsa* cloth; form is like the final knot. Since the knots exist in dependence upon the cloth, birth exists in dependence upon consciousness.

Because liberation follows a sequence, cessation proceeds from the removal of form. As for the principle that 'one suddenly awakens to it, and by means of this awakening, both [birth and cessation] are simultaneously eliminated,' this means one knows that the cloth was originally without knots and thus they do not even exist. However, as for phenomena, they are not suddenly eliminated."

Regarding "exhausting [delusions] through gradual succession": although one may attain sudden enlightenment regarding the root, one must certainly rely on gradual cultivation. If one relies on enlightenment to neglect cultivation, then there will be understanding without practice;
by clinging to principle while being deluded about phenomena, one will inevitably fall into partiality and deviation. Ultimately, this is not the true Samādhi of correct cultivation.
Zizhong said: "To examine the origin of the celestial kerchief: it is tied in a sequence and untied in a sequence.
What it illustrates—the six sense organs and the five aggregates—share a superficial resemblance in their arising and ceasing, yet upon further investigation, they differ. Why?

Because the principle of the six sense organs is horizontal, while the principle of the five aggregates is vertical. For instance, when the six sense organs lose touch with the Truth and give rise to delusion..."
Roots are established due to delusion; there is certainly no sequence where the eye comes first, followed by the ear and so forth.
Even when returning from delusion to truth, there is no principle of proceeding from the coarse to the subtle. Is this not a forced interpretation?

As for my previous use of the sequence of untangling knots as a metaphor, I was merely taking up the distinctions among the six faculties and the selection of the perfect penetration—this is what I called "sequence. Now, to clarify...
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) likewise arise from delusion regarding the Truth and give rise to falsehood; because of this falsehood, the aggregates are formed.

Since it is said that their arising depends on consciousness (*vijñāna*) and their cessation proceeds from the elimination of form (*rūpa*), is this not a vertical sequence of meaning? If one uses the analogy of bondage and liberation, then the two stages possess a clear and orderly progression.
One should know that when the preceding text presents an analogy, one must not use the analogy to challenge the Dharma; this citation serves as an illustration.
One may use the roots to challenge the aggregates; this is an exposition suited to the occasion. One must understand the general outline:
you should take these roots of deluded thought (up to) knowing that there is nirvana and not being attached to the three realms.
(Gushan says: The preceding section explaining the "Aids to the Path" is concluded. The main body of the text ends here;
what follows is the "Propagation Section," which is not recorded).
Wenling said: "By means of this principle, one awakens oneself and awakens others, forever severing the root of delusion and together returning to the ultimate fruit.
After the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, [and so forth], were all greatly filled with joy, paid their respects, and departed.
(Wu Xing says: "Those who have first resolved their minds" refers to those at the stage of ordinary beings outside the Perfect Teaching, or perhaps those within it;
they all experience great joy, encompassing both ordinary beings and sages.)
Wenling says: "These are all members of the assembly listening [to the teaching]. The 'sages and immortals' (shengxian) are of the class of celestial immortals (tianxian).
The powerful ghosts and spirits, as well as the various Dharma protectors, all attain the joy of the Dharma according to their respective levels of realization."
The Epilogue to the Śūraṅgama Sūtra by Xingjian:
Indeed, when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, it was entirely for the sake of the causal conditions of the One Great Matter; he made a vow that was ultimately firm and steadfast.
First, the Four Noble Truths were discussed; next, emptiness and existence were explained. At the beginning of this sutra, Ānanda was seized by Māra and used as a pretext for his request.
Through repeated and earnest entreaties, the Bhagavān emitted light of a hundred jewels from the crown of his head and uttered the discourse of the One Vehicle from his tongue.

He investigated the mind through seven locations, leading [Ānanda] back to the realization of the nature of mind, and by refuting the false appearances of the sense organs and their objects, he clarified [the truth].

The seven great elements find their ultimate destination in every sense organ and every sensory object, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; thus, all phenomena and things are entirely composed of the ocean of teachings.
Yet, when one examines the various assemblies of sages to unify them within the Single Truth, all outflows are suddenly perfected.

When one accords with the single faculty, there is a subtle and intimate realization. By returning to hearing, reflection, and cultivation, how could Avalokiteśvara be sought elsewhere? Through this single gate, one transcends.
Complete penetration resides entirely within one's own body. Nineteen times he preached the Dharma, knowing that it does not depend on others to propagate it.
He manifested the four inconceivables through the transformation of the single mind. Ānanda requested again for their cessation;

by means of the non-arising of karmic fruits, the four prohibitions were purified, so that the five aggregates were cleansed and the twelve classes of beings no longer underwent rebirth as ghosts or demons. To realize this is to possess nothing at all. Twenty.

The transcendence of the five modes of existence is reached through realization; how sublime! The profound teaching encompasses all capacities, yet it is said that the definitive truth of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is the grand standard of this era.
If those on the stages (*bhūmi*) and those prior to the stages have not yet attained this certainty, then phenomena and dharmas will remain disparate.
If even the Greatly Wise and Great Sages do not enter this school, there would be no means by which to make a decisive selection. Therefore, the profound...
It is said that once this is accomplished for the present age, the Great Dharma will be further propagated during the final era.

May it be carved upon woodblocks and circulated so that every person may individually awaken to their own original mind, and may its influence pervade as many lands as there are motes of dust. [Seal] Respectfully stated.
